#5663. ‘We Started Buying Real Estate To Help Those in Need—and Built a Portfolio Worth Millions in the Process’

When Frank and Ann Ewing decided to purchase a rundown property in West Tennessee to renovate and rent out, they did so with the idea that they wanted to help provide affordable housing for others. What they didn't expect was that they'd also become millionaires in the process.

But that's exactly what happened as the Ewings quietly built a real estate portfolio over the past 20 years that's now worth around $10 million, while simultaneously making a small dent in the housing affordability crisis in their area.

"We decided that many of the world's problems start at home—all people deserve a safe, decent place to live and a lack of a decent place to live can cause social problems that affect us all," says Ann Ewing, the co-founder, with her husband, of Better World Enterprises and co-author of "Housing Into Homes," which illustrates how it's possible to make money in real estate while "doing good" at the same time.

Step by step, the Ewings amassed not only an entire portfolio of properties including a 33-unit townhouse complex, 20 duplexes, and single-family homes (about 90 rental units in total), but they stayed true to their initial mission, which was to help make the world a better place.

When Frank and Ann first met through an online dating site in the fall of 2000, they both lived in the Northeast. Their connection was immediate and their shared life goals aligned to the point that getting married in August 2001 felt like an easy decision.

During the time they were dating, however, Frank's mother tragically passed away. Though she'd been ill for some time, it was still a tough transition, but one they weathered as a couple. And in the process, they inherited a home in Jackson, TN. After the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, the couple decided to leave New York, where they'd been living, and move down south.

Once in Jackson, the Ewings "took some time to learn about Jackson, and learned that, at that time, West Tennessee was the bankruptcy capital of the world." As such, they realized they were actually in the perfect place to begin their Better World Project.

The couple planned to combine Ann's business acumen (she's a Dartmouth and Wharton School of Business alum) with Frank's expertise in home restoration, repairs, and improvements to make their dream come to life. And by 2002, they had started doing business as Better World Properties.

It was word of mouth that helped the Ewings find their first property to purchase in Jackson.

"We became aware of a somewhat neglected two-bedroom, one-bathroom home in a good neighborhood near our city's largest hospital and decided to check it out," says Ann. "We bought it, cleaned it up, and promptly rented it [out]."

They used some money they'd saved to purchase that first property for $55,000 (this was in 2002, so home prices were more accessible), and decided to rent it out for $550/month. The rent calculation was based on 1% of the investment property.

"As properties that are not in good condition sell for less than better maintained properties, and since we did much of the work on the property ourselves, we were able to rent it [out] for a bit below the standard rental rate in the area and still cover our costs," says Ann. ""The numbers meant that our investment should generate roughly a 10% return per year, not including the increased value of the property or tax benefits."

Today, after eventually adding an additional bathroom and bedroom, that first property is worth over $200,000.

Though it was personal savings that financed their first home acquisition, once they'd made that purchase they were able to use the collateral from that first home to purchase their second property—a neglected four-plex that had been constructed in 1938.

It needed significant work, much of which they did themselves again, including sanding all the wood floors and repainting the premises. But after purchasing it for $53,400 and restoring it to its original elegance, they had every unit rented out right away.

"We rented it [out] at rates ranging from $450 to $900 from 2002 to 2023 ... and in the process, we turned a 'dump' into a beautiful building," explain the Ewings. "It was hard work, but very rewarding psychologically as well as financially."

The calculations the Ewings use to determine what they rent their properties for include variables beyond simply making a profit. But in the balance, they also found themselves coming out ahead, which in turn allowed them to continue the process of buying, renovating, and renting to tenants.

"It is cheaper and quicker for an investor to buy a property that needs attention—everything from a little cleanup to a major renovation, bring it to good condition, and rent it out rather than tear it down and build a new property with new materials," says Ann. "Therefore, since housing is available to the community faster, and with a quicker return on investment, the owner can still make a profit while accepting a lower rent."

The Ewings intentionally rent out their properties for rents that are a bit less than market rate (5% to 10%), which they say helps with quickly renting them out and also keeping long-term tenants.

"Other landlords might think we are crazy, but it works for us," says Ann. "While we are a company and have to cover our expenses and generate enough money to invest in future renovations, we are also on a mission to improve communities."

And over the course of the last 20+ years, the Ewings have done just that.

"We rented [out] a one-bedroom property to an Army veteran who received a Section 8 voucher from the VA," says Ann. "We literally helped her move from a tent in the woods behind a fast-food restaurant into the first stable housing she had had in years."

Another example is an immigrant family that would not qualify for conventional bank financing to buy a home in the United States.

"Many years ago they rented from us for three years and always paid their rent on time and in full," says Ann. "They asked if they could purchase the house from us and we sold it to them, acting as the mortgage holder." Now, that family and their four children are very close to paying off their house.

The Ewings say they follow three principles in running their business.

First, treat everyone with respect and dignity. As they say, customer service is key to any business.

"Even if we don't have a property that would work for a particular person, we may be able to help someone else that they know," says Ann.

Second, they will not rent out a property that they would not live in themselves.

"While we may prefer a different number of bedrooms or a different layout, we will not rent [out] a property unless it is a clean, safe, decent place to live," says Ann.

Third, all of their renovations are done with an eye toward energy efficiency.

"We will invest extra money upfront to help people keep their utility bills low," the couple adds. "This is good for the tenants, it is good for us because happy tenants tend to renew their leases, and it is good for the environment. Win-win-win!"

The Ewings have also deliberately remained very hands-on throughout the process over the years.

"All of our properties are in Jackson, TN, or just beyond the city limits into Madison County," states Ann, explaining that she and Frank made a decision early on not to purchase a property more than a 15-minute drive from their home. "Managing property can be challenging enough when you are near it, and it gets exponentially more difficult the further away it is."

Though they recently turned management of a few properties over to a local property manager to free up some of their personal time for other pursuits, they are still managing several of their properties themselves and continue to look for ways to expand their mission.

"We are currently working on a duplex built in 1925 that we are bringing up to 2026 standards, and once this is complete, we may look for another property," says Ann.

After more than 20 years of turning "Housing Into Homes," the Ewings are now on a quest to teach other people how they can "do well by doing good" (their unofficial motto).

That was one reason they wrote their book—to give others the tools and a blueprint on how they can help others and help themselves at the same time by turning real estate investments into affordable housing.

"It is psychologically rewarding to turn a run-down property into a beautiful home," says Ann. "Making a difference in people's lives is an awesome bonus!"

Kimberly Dawn Neumann is a journalist based in New York City and the author of hundreds of articles on home-related topics for major publications, including Forbes, Real Simple, and Realtor.com. For more information, visit www.KDNeumann.com or IG @dancerscribe.

#5661. Aina’s smart AI ring promises a new way to interact with AI agents that anticipate user’s needs

Artificial intelligence has come a long way in a very short space of time, writing emails, answering questions, generating code, images, video and more besides. But as breathtaking as these advances are, using AI is still a hassle. People have to dig out their smartphone and find the right app, then enter a prompt before anything gets done.

Seeking to eliminate this friction is a startup called Aina Computers Inc., which has just emerged from 15 months in “stealth mode” to launch its flagship product: an AI-native smart ring equipped with an OLED display that’s purpose-built to control autonomous AI agents.

Aina founder Apoorv Shankar told SiliconANGLE that the development of hardware interfaces has not kept pace with the advances in AI. For people to access intelligence, they need to go fumbling through smartphone applications or switch on a laptop.

Even the most basic tasks, like ordering an Uber, require someone to open an app, enter their destination and click to confirm. To join a virtual meeting, the user still has to dig through their emails to find the right link. In Shankar’s view, AI is trapped behind a software layer and that means it cannot proactively serve people when they need it.

Aina’s Ring is meant to free AI from these binds and make it as simple to access as uttering a command. The Ring is made from titanium and comes equipped with a colorful OLED display, a microphone and a speaker, and an 18-hour battery. There’s also a mechanical “shifter” that can track thumb gestures in four directions.. “We started building Aina with a thesis that AI would evolve from following instructions to anticipating what we need,” Shankar explained.

The device is powered by Aina’s Context Aware Operating System software, which is designed to learn the Ring wearer’s behavior over time in order to anticipate their needs. It can connect to the user’s devices, such as their smartphone and computer, and also any AI agents they use. Once it’s up and running, it tries to anticipate what users will need at any given moment and surface the information they need on the Ring’s display before they even ask for it.

“With proactive agents, this shift has already begun,” Shankar said. “Agents like Muse, Instinct and Dots will soon run hundreds of our daily tasks, yet we still have to instruct them by text or voice. But soon, they’ll learn our patterns, build on our context and turn proactive for almost every interaction, waiting only for our approval.”

Shankar founded Aina last year. The startup was originally a human-computer interaction research lab. Its 40-person team experimented with dozens of different hardware concepts, including an adaptive three-key Mac keypad called Dune, before ultimately settling on the Ring as the ultimate interface for AI agents.

Aina’s $399 Ring is available for pre-order now and will ship to customers in January. That’s the date at which people’s relationship with AI is set to fundamentally change, Shankar believes. When someone wears Aina’s Ring, the way they interact with their AI agents will generally become a matter of simply saying yes or no, for they will quickly learn to anticipate what their users need, at the moment they need it, he said.

Users can interact with the Ring in three ways. The microphone is there to support voice interactions. The user simply presses and holds the button in the center to call up an agent and instruct it to do something, or else they can just use it to record some quick notes. It will also be able to relay phone calls, enabling people to converse by just holding their hand close to their ear.

The Ring also supports cues that are powered by the context-aware operating system. As it learns to anticipate user’s needs, it will be able to proactively order an Uber ride based on the time of day, their location and their schedule. All the user has to do is click or say “yes” to confirm and the Ring will book the ride. Alternatively, if someone is late for an appointment, the Ring will proactively draft a message to let the person they’re meeting know when they’ll arrive.

Shankar said the Ring can also be used as a remote control, so if someone is watching TV they’ll be able to tell it to pause or rewind the show they’re watching. It can adjust microphones and cameras during video calls, skip to the next track when someone’s listening to music on their iPod and so on.

“Every major shift in computing has come from software and hardware built together,” Shankar said. “The mouse and GUI brought us personal computing. The touchscreen and the app gave us mobile computing. Now with Aina we enter a new era, with personalized computing right at your fingertips.”

#5660. Mortgage Mix: Buyers Turning to ARMs Due to Elevated Rates; Compass Expands Its Mortgage Business

Editor’s Note: The Mortgage Mix is RISMedia’s highlight reel of need-to-know mortgage-industry happenings. Watch for it every other Friday afternoon.

The numbers: While mortgage rates had hit a peak and were nearing the high-end of the 7% range, they have now decreased for the third straight week to 7.18% for the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage and 6.57% for the 15-year fixed-rate mortgage. Notably, this was the lowest level seen in over a month.

What this means: A stronger jobs report was partially attributed to this week’s improvement, as Realtor.com® Senior Economist Hannah Jones said that “while solid hiring supports housing demand over time, a stronger-than-expected report could also lift bond yields and slow the pace of rate declines in the near term.

The “blue wave” that occurred in the elections this past Tuesday may also contribute to further improvements down the road, as Jones noted that “many newly elected representatives have voiced discontent with the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, which has contributed to rising inflation, so any progress toward resolution could mean lower inflation and softer mortgage rates ahead.”

Using their ARMs? Despite a come down, many buyers are still holding off from the market due to rates remaining over 7%. Mortgage applications this week were down 1.2%.

With the fixed-rate mortgage elevated, more buyers have turned to adjustable rate mortgages (ARMs) instead.

“As we have highlighted in recent weeks, more borrowers are choosing ARMs in this environment to lower their initial payments, with the ARM share at its highest level since September 2025,” said Mike Fratantoni, the Mortgage Bankers Association’s SVP and chief economist.

A Better battle comes to an end: After a tumultuous struggle between the lender and its founder, Better.com has dropped its federal securities lawsuit against Vishal Garg, who was ousted in August. The case was dismissed with prejudice, meaning it cannot be refiled.

The lender had been suing Garg for allegedly violating federal securities laws, arguing that he did not engage in the proper process to solicit shareholders in a bid to regain his position.

That bid ended up being successful, with Garg back in a leadership role.

Compass takes mortgage JV to the big leagues: Expanding its mortgage business to become a top-10 lender, Compass announced a merger between its own OriginPoint mortgage platform and Rate’s Guaranteed Rate Affinity to unite the two mortgage ventures under the OriginPoint brand.

Guaranteed Rate Affinity was founded in partnership with Anywhere Real Estate back in 2017, making the merger an unsurprising move due to Compass’s acquisition of Anywhere last year.

The merger expands OriginPoint’s resources and geographic reach, the companies noted in a release, while backing the business with Rate’s AI technology, products and lending platform.

Claudia Larsen is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5659. Ryan Serhant Reveals the Turning Point That Made Him a Real Estate Star—and How He Thinks Agents Can Cash in On AI

Before Ryan Serhant became a recognizable face in real estate, he was one of thousands of agents showing up to an open casting call—and declaring himself the best in the universe.

The opportunity would put him on “Million Dollar Listing” and turn him into what he described as a “walking billboard,” giving him a platform he was determined to make count.

Speaking at NAR NXT 2026 in New Orleans, Serhant reflected on that career-changing break, the relentless social media strategy that followed, and why he believes agents should now be looking to artificial intelligence to help build their businesses.

His message to agents navigating an uncertain market was straightforward: “Markets don’t dictate your income. They dictate your strategy.”

For Serhant, learning where to direct his energy was part of that process. He recalled spending too much time early in his career stressing about things he could not control, including what might happen in the months ahead.

Instead, he encouraged agents to focus on the work they can tackle now. The future will arrive regardless, and worrying about it does little to move a business forward.

"I try to plan ahead and I don't even—as an agent and a CEO— I'd be stressed about what is going to happen and one of the mistakes in the beginning of my career was stressing about what I can't control," he said, adding that agents should "attack" what they can control "without worrying about the future."

Branding himself a "futurist," he added, “At the end of the day, no one knows what they are doing."

Serhant acknowledged that his first few years were difficult and suggested that getting started as an agent is even harder today. His own breakthrough came after he attended an open casting call for “Million Dollar Listing” in 2010, joining roughly 3,000 real estate agents in Times Square.

He recalled not fully knowing what he would be doing there. But when asked why he had come, he delivered an answer that left little room for self-doubt: “I’m the greatest real estate agent in the universe.”

Serhant revealed the season was filmed with four people, but only three ultimately made the cut.

Once the show aired, he recognized that the exposure had given him an opportunity to distinguish himself—and he felt compelled to capitalize on it.

“Once the show came out, I became a walking billboard,” he said.

He also acknowledged the role timing played in his rise. He was finding his footing professionally as both cable television and social media offered opportunities to reach potential customers.

“I need to meet my customer where my customer is,” he said.

That approach led him to embrace Instagram in its early days, posting photographs of listings with himself in the images. He recalled posting every two to three hours, steadily building an audience that could become familiar with him before ever meeting him.

The goal was to establish a presence on people’s phones, creating recognition that could carry into an eventual conversation or business relationship.

Today, Serhant said, helping other agents succeed has become a source of excitement in its own right.

“It makes me tick. I enjoy it. I love it,” he said of teaching others.

Having encountered a wide range of challenges throughout his career, he described watching his agents win as the work that now gets him most excited.

He also emphasized his belief in investing in the future, describing Serhant’s mission as helping the world move forward.

For agents considering what that future looks like, artificial intelligence was a central part of his advice.

“The excitement within AI isn’t just language. It’s in creating work,” he said.

Serhant encouraged agents to identify administrative tasks that technology could reduce, freeing up time for the activities that depend on human connection and creativity.

“Humans should be doing only what humans do, which is meeting and creating,” he said.

He pointed to negotiation support and homeownership information as potential uses, while urging agents to think beyond individual tasks and consider how AI could help generate more business.

The measures that matter, he suggested, include increasing transactions per agent and improving gross profit. In that framing, the value of adopting AI lies in what it enables an agent to accomplish.

But he also shared an anecdote illustrating how the technology can influence a client’s decisions.

Serhant recalled a buyer pulling out of a $50 million deal after asking ChatGPT whether they were paying too much and receiving an affirmative answer.

The account underscored a challenge for agents: clients can now arrive with AI-generated conclusions that affect their willingness to move forward with a purchase.

His advice was to use the technology as support in their own work.

Across his reflections on television, social media, and AI, Serhant returned to the importance of approaching opportunities with a willingness to act.

“I learned that optimists are successful," he said.

Kelsi Karruli is a senior celebrity reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2025. She writes about trends encompassing real estate and celebrity properties. She previously wrote for Daily Mail, True Urban Culture, and JMedia Corporation, where she specialized in covering celebrities, relationships, psychology, and gender issues. She has a bachelor's degree in journalism from Pace University, where she received the James Rose Award for excellence in journalism. #5658. Oracle’s multicloud approach: Put the database wherever AI pipelines already run

Enterprises racing to put AI agents into production are learning that real-time data pipelines matter as much as the models. An agent working from a stale subset of corporate records delivers far less than one wired into live, mission-critical data.

That shift is changing how companies decide where their databases run. Oracle Corp. has pushed its database modernization strategy into other clouds, and customers are moving databases next to the applications and AI pipelines they are building, according to Nathan Thomas (pictured), senior vice president of product management for Oracle Cloud Infrastructure at Oracle.

“Customers are defining their AI pipelines, I think from an enterprise business perspective, with an eye towards trust, with an eye towards security,” Thomas said. “They are really looking at, ‘How do I get the mission-critical data into those pipelines?'”

Thomas spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how real-time data pipelines help improve agentic AI performance. (* Disclosure below.)

Oracle offers its database on its own cloud, on-premises through Cloud@Customer and inside Amazon Web Services Inc., Microsoft Corp.’s Azure and Google LLC’s Google Cloud. Customers rarely ask which cloud to pick, since existing relationships and the location of their applications usually settle the question, Thomas explained.

“They’re usually saying, ‘Hey, I’ve already got a relationship. Let’s put the database where my apps are and where my AI pipelines are,'” Thomas said.

Running the same Exadata hardware everywhere also takes the sting out of migration. AI projects are adding value to database migrations, and a like-for-like hardware move avoids most of the refactoring that once made them so painful, he noted.

“I’m coming from on-prem on an Exadata. I can move into the cloud on an Exadata,” Thomas said. “It’s the same hardware, same environment, same tools, same management, same performance.”

#5657. What real estate agents should watch on Election Day, per NAHB

NAHB’s Ken Wingert on housing and the midterms, from state ballot measures and the ROAD to Housing Act to tariffs, labor and mortgage rates.

Housing may not be on many ballots by name on Nov. 3, but it’s running through nearly every race.

With the midterms set for Tuesday, candidates from both parties are pitching voters on affordability. Lawmakers are campaigning on the recently passed 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, states from California to Massachusetts are voting on measures meant to make building easier, and homebuilders are grappling with tariffs and immigration enforcement that have driven up costs and thinned out job-site crews.

Inman spoke with Ken Wingert, chief advocacy officer at the National Association of Home Builders, about the races and ballot measures NAHB is watching, whether data centers are really competing with housing for land, and what agents should keep an eye on as votes are counted.

Inman: What are two or three outcomes to the midterms you think matter most for housing — on the federal- level and state-level?

Ken Wingert: The overall theme is that this is turning out to be, once again, an affordability election, and housing is at the top of that pain point … because we don’t have enough of it. So regardless of who controls Congress or who wins the governor’s race in any given state, I think housing will be near or at the top of the agenda going into 2027. That gives us, and other groups you’re probably talking to, a lot of opportunity to advocate for more housing supply.

On specific issues, people are starting to understand that supply matters. You’re seeing ballot initiatives in a number of states aimed at making it easier for builders to build and cutting some of that red tape. Members of Congress are running on the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. Congress is still debating permitting reform that may pass in the lame-duck session or get kicked to the next Congress.

From a congressional standpoint, if Democrats win at least one chamber, there will probably be more pushback and oversight on issues like tariffs and immigration, which have made it harder for builders to build more housing, or at least more expensive.

Are there specific races that NAHB is watching closely, at the state, federal or local level?

We’re not quite NAR size, but we’re involved in a lot. At the federal level, I think we’ll see how big a wave is, if one materializes, and whether it takes out some folks who have been very helpful on housing over the years.

Financial Services Chairman French Hill will be fine, I think, but he’s in a tighter race than expected. Mike Hill, chairman of the House Financial Services Subcommittee on Housing and Insurance, faces the same challenge. In Michigan, Bill Huizenga is a former Realtor and builder. Sherrod Brown, former chair of the Banking Committee, is potentially coming back to the Senate from Ohio. A lot of folks are watching that race.

But really, at the state level: California has a couple of ballot initiatives, one in particular we’ve been involved with on changes to CEQA, the California Environmental Quality Act. The legislature had made some changes, and this would codify them in state law. In Massachusetts, we’re supporting a ballot initiative that would reduce minimum lot sizes, meaning how big your lot has to be to build on it. And there are a bunch of funding ballot initiatives around the country. All of those aim to increase supply, so we’re keyed in on those state-level races.

I’ve seen candidates from both parties campaigning on the recently passed ROAD to Housing Act. Does that kind of policy achievement resonate with voters, or does a general affordability pitch resonate more?

Both parties are campaigning on the fact that Congress passed major housing legislation with overwhelming bipartisan support. Beyond affordability, another theme in this election is that people want less divisiveness and more collaboration to solve problems. ROAD to Housing was a great example of both parties giving up a few things to get a bill they wanted.

I don’t know that the average voter is digging into a bill with 60 titles, but they understand that Congress recognized a housing supply problem and is at least trying to fix it. If I’m running for Congress, that’s something I’m going to go out and tell people.

Have you noticed more local candidates running explicitly on pro-housing or YIMBY platforms? Any examples?

Our state and local associations make their own endorsements and funding decisions, so, honestly, I’m too far removed to say whether a certain state rep in Texas is doing X.

One interesting part of this election is that the NIMBY focus has shifted from housing to data centers. The recognition that we need more housing has shifted more in the YIMBY direction. That’s a dynamic we’re not encouraging, because data centers are a separate issue, but it’s been interesting.

Talking to our locals, more folks at the city council and county level, where the rubber really meets the road on development, are talking about the need to build more affordable and workforce housing.

We’ve seen in our own polling a real desire, and real angst, from younger voters who feel they can’t afford a home, and from their parents, who are also worried their kids can’t afford a home, may be living with them for a long time, and want them to stay in their state and area and raise their families there. That underlying affordability challenge is driving a lot of the rhetoric and, quite frankly, a lot of the ads. They may not mention housing specifically, but it’s embedded in broader affordability concerns.

You mentioned data centers. I’ve written a couple of stories about data centers competing with housing development for the same land. Is that something NAHB has seen? Is it a real phenomenon?

I think it’s a little overblown, at least right now. A lot of the areas where they’re looking to build data centers aren’t necessarily areas where you would build housing. So there may be some competition over land, but it’s not as big an issue as people may think.

The larger issue is competition for labor. Residential construction always competes with commercial construction for talent and labor, whether it’s somebody building an office building or a house. That competition is real, but it also means more investment in workforce training and more attention to the trades.

We’ve seen many large tech companies announce they’ll fund apprenticeship and training programs because they also need those workers. So there may be some trickle-down help for homebuilding. But it’s still too soon to see real impact, beyond utilities and similar things.

Speaking of labor, I’ve seen quite a few stories about how immigration policy and enforcement have affected construction labor. Has NAHB seen that, what’s your stance, and how have you worked with lawmakers on it?

We’ve definitely heard a lot about it, especially in the last few months. It’s been primarily in Southern states, but not exclusively.

The big concern from members is that the way enforcement is being carried out, whether at the local level, by ICE or some combination, is scaring off all Hispanic workers, regardless of immigration status or citizenship. They’re coming onto job sites, rounding everyone up and detaining folks for hours, repeatedly showing up or pulling people over in a van on the way to a job site. That’s made it very hard to retain workers or get them to show up, because there’s a fear factor in the Hispanic community about even U.S. citizens and green card holders getting roped in with folks who may not be here legally.

That’s caused delays on job sites and made it hard to find labor, period, because there’s no immediate replacement. That’s why we’re so focused on workforce training.

I think it’ll be a factor in places like Texas and Florida, and in the electoral outcome. You’re already seeing Hispanic turnout larger than historic levels. Some polling shows that even folks who supported the president on immigration, who maybe voted for him based on closing the border and enforcement, feel the enforcement has gone too far. It’ll be interesting to see what the exit polls show.

Inman’s core audience is real estate agents. What should agents pay the most attention to in these midterms? Does it depend on their local market, or is there something general to watch?

Disclosure: I used to work for NAR, too, so I understand where they’re coming from. I don’t know if there’s one particular issue, or whether it’s about the House or Senate flipping. It’s the overall voter mindset. If Congress changes control, or a governorship flips one way or the other, does it have an immediate impact? Does it change the [Trump] administration’s course? Those are all open questions.

Ultimately, voters hope inflation can be tamed, and interest rates obviously drive much of this for agents. Resolving the situation in Iran, and maybe dialing back some tariff policies, could affect the inflation numbers driving interest rates. If we can get rates back down, certainly below 7 percent and into the mid-6s, that will unlock a lot of demand that’s still out there but has moved to the sidelines over the last six months.

It’s hard to see how those things will change, no matter the outcome. They all feel very up in the air.

Yeah, but there’s a certain psyche to it. We saw this after the 2024 election. Everyone’s so wrapped up in politics now that people go into a weird holding pattern for the last month or two before an election. They say, “I’m going to wait until after the election and see, and then make a major decision.”

Uncertainty is a factor, and depending on your political outlook, you may be much happier on Nov. 4, or you may not be. But at least it resolves one more question mark for the next two years before we start a presidential cycle.

I hope that, whatever the outcome, having the election behind us will ease angst for potential buyers and sellers, calm the overall market, and get it moving again.

#5656. What to expect during KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA: Join theCUBE Nov. 10-12

Kubernetes has emerged as the default container orchestration standard, a foundational platform layer across the enterprise. Will Kubernetes also play a central role in positioning the next generation of AI workloads for production?

This is the question on the minds of the cloud-native community as it gathers this month for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA in Salt Lake City. With the rise of AI agents that have progressed from answering user questions to executing code and running business systems, customers are increasingly interested in controlling what autonomous agents are allowed to do.

“That brings us to OpenShell, an open-source secure agent runtime that Red Hat is helping develop alongside Nvidia and, of, course, the broader community,” said theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante, during a pre-event interview. “The approach puts enforcement into the environment where the agent operates, setting boundaries around what it can access and execute rather than relying on a model alone to follow the rules. We think this is a central question for the next chapter of cloud native: how do enterprises give agents enough freedom to be useful without giving up control?”

During KubeCon + CloudNativeCon, Nov. 10-12, theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio, will feature on-site reporting and exclusive interviews with executives from Red Hat Inc. and Nvidia Corp., among others. TheCUBE will examine the latest innovations in GPU orchestration, agentic workloads and platform engineering as inference and autonomous agents move into production. (* Disclosure below.)

OpenShell, while still an early-stage project, is actively being developed for Kubernetes environments. The activity reflects growing customer interest in using containerized environments for applications, according to theCUBE Research’s Paul Nashawaty.

“Fifty-one percent of organizations report that 51–75% of their applications now run in containers, representing a sharp rise from just a few years ago,” Nashawaty said. “Organizations now run the majority of their applications in containers which is a sharp rise that reflects the accelerating cloud-native transformation central to KubeCon + CloudNativeCon.”

OpenShell was accepted into the Cloud Native Computing Foundation as a sandbox project in September. One component of OpenShell allows agents to run in isolated sandboxes with limits on the files they can reach, an approach actively supported by the cloud-native community within the Kubernetes ecosystem.

“It builds on top of some core Kubernetes special interest groups,” said Pete Cheslock, principal AI community architect at Red Hat, during an interview with theCUBE. “The Agent Sandbox is one of them so that you can deploy these agents in a secure way using Kubernetes APIs.”

Cheslock’s point about security highlights the growing concerns and recent publicity surrounding AI agents and their ability to break out of isolated environments and compromise systems. Rapid enterprise adoption and integration of AI are increasing the risk profiles for organizations, a topic that will be on the agenda for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon.

“Our research data reveals that 41.3% of organizations cite increased vulnerability risk as the top security challenge, introduced by faster CI/CD cycles and a tension that cloud-native teams are increasingly turning to Kubernetes-native tooling to resolve,” Nashawaty said.

Enterprise reliance on cloud-native tools and open-source software requires confidence that these technologies are safe to use inside enterprise infrastructure. In May, Red Hat and IBM Corp. unveiled Project Lightwell, a $5 billion commitment to help enterprises secure open-source software.

“For the last year, especially since the Mythos moment, [security] has been the first thing that we’ve talked about in every customer conversation I’ve had,” said Stu Miniman, senior director of market insights for hybrid platforms at Red Hat, in conversation with theCUBE. “We’re trying to make sure that customers can feel secure and understand and use these tools. There’s even more effort being put on security than ever, which has always been a focus of Red Hat. If we don’t make sure that layer is as locked down and reliable and trusted as possible, everything else becomes secondary.”

At this month’s KubeCon gathering, theCUBE will explore how various practitioners are using Kubernetes to ensure workload portability across multicloud environments. Companies such as Vultr and ScaleOps are building Kubernetes-based tools that can support a range of platforms, reflecting enterprise computing trends.

“With our AppDev research finding that 94% of organizations now operate across two or more cloud providers, the demand for consistent, developer-friendly Kubernetes-based platforms has never been more pressing,” Nashawaty explained.

KubeCon also offers an opportunity to assess the progress of key technology projects under the CNCF umbrella. One of the major contributors in this arena has been Google LLC, which contributed the open-source service mesh Istio, serverless building blocks via Knative and Kubernetes itself. KubeCon is an annual reminder of how large the CNCF ecosystems has become, according to Red Hat’s Miniman.

“They’ve got a big ecosystem. I can give example after example of who created these technologies,” Miniman told theCUBE. “Oh yeah, the GitOps stuff came out of Intuit, and the platform engineering stuff came out of Spotify. Just find your focus and go in there, because there is no way you can cover all of it.”

Don’t miss theCUBE’s coverage of KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA from Nov. 10-12. Plus, you can access theCUBE’s exclusive content on demand after the event.

We offer various ways for you to watch theCUBE’s coverage of KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, including theCUBE’s dedicated website and YouTube channel. You can also get all the coverage from this year’s events on SiliconANGLE.

SiliconANGLE’s “theCUBE Pod” is available on Apple Podcasts, Spotify and YouTube, which you can enjoy while on the go. During each podcast, SiliconANGLE’s John Furrier and Dave Vellante discuss the biggest trends in enterprise tech, including AI, cloud, cybersecurity and infrastructure, with context and analysis.

SiliconANGLE also produces our weekly “Breaking Analysis” program, where Vellante examines major developments in enterprise tech, combining insights from theCUBE with spending data from Enterprise Technology Research, available on Apple Podcasts, Spotify and YouTube.

At KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, theCUBE will speak with Red Hat leaders and other industry executives about the latest innovations in GPU orchestration, agentic workloads and platform engineering as inference and autonomous agents move into production.

#5655. Why real estate agents wanted Barbara Corcoran for ICNY ’27

Barbara Corcoran (l) onstage at Inman Connect San Francisco 2015, Holly Meyer Lucas (r) onstage at Inman Connect San Diego 2026 |

As our team at Inman began planning Inman Connect New York this January, we asked real estate agents a fairly straightforward question: “In this market, who do you want to hear from most right now?”

The overwhelming response was Barbara Corcoran.

I’ve spent a lot of time thinking about that answer, because I think it tells us something interesting about the current state of real estate, the people who work in it and what they’re looking for from our industry’s leaders.

For context, before becoming Inman’s CMO, I spent years building a $100 million-plus producing real estate team in South Florida. I’ve personally sold more than 1,000 homes, ranging from properties under $20,000 to deals north of $20 million.

I’ve represented distressed sellers, helped families through extraordinarily difficult circumstances and negotiated transactions where getting to the closing table meant everything to the people involved. I’ve also mentored, trained and managed hundreds of agents through slow markets, busy markets and everything the last decade has thrown at us.

My point: I’ve carried the bag, and I understand my real estate agent brethren.

So, all summer when agents told me how much they are struggling (in what should be peak homebuying season), I took that seriously. For the past several months, I’ve heard from some of the most successful agents in the country who were going months without closing a transaction. These are experienced professionals who have built substantial businesses and survived multiple market cycles, suddenly finding themselves in unfamiliar territory.

Meanwhile, the industry around them is in a rather extraordinary state of upheaval. Major brokerages are consolidating, brokerages and MLSs are suing one another, the debate over private listings continues to divide the industry, and NAR is working to rebuild trust following several tumultuous years.

And somewhere in the middle of all this, agents are trying to sell houses while being told to post more on social media, stay hydrated and use more AI.

Our industry has some consequential decisions ahead of it, and the people making those decisions deserve to be questioned. Inman’s newsroom has an important responsibility to cover these issues, and our events should provide a place for the people involved to explain their positions.

But there’s another conversation agents want to have, and I think their overwhelming request for Barbara tells us exactly what it is.

They want to hear from someone who has been in their shoes, knows how to get scrappy in a down market to sell real estate, and can offer an experienced perspective without having to defend a corporate agenda.

One of my favorite anecdotes about Barbara is one that she shares often and seems to take enormous pride in — how gritty she was in her early life. Her LinkedIn bio opens with: “Barbara Corcoran’s credits include straight D’s in high school and college and 20 jobs by the time she turned 23.”

Tell me that doesn’t win the heart of a real estate agent. Our industry has a remarkable way of attracting people who struggled to find their place elsewhere.

Some weren’t great students. Others bounced around between jobs before finding real estate. I’ve met extraordinarily successful agents who can negotiate their way through an impossible transaction, recognize an opportunity before anyone else and build a relationship with practically anyone, and yet were kicked out of school when they were younger. (Looking at you, James Harris!)

Barbara herself has spoken openly about her struggles in school and dyslexia and how the challenges she experienced influenced the way she approached business. (I’ve got a completely unscientific theory about how I think many of America’s top-producing real estate agents who claim they struggled in school but are elite at selling are all actually just dyslexic, but I’ll save that for another time.)

Real estate agents find Barbara’s story particularly inspiring because real estate has always been an industry where people can build extraordinary careers around abilities that aren’t necessarily rewarded in a classroom, and Barbara took those abilities and turned a $1,000 loan into one of the most recognizable real estate brokerages in the country. She is one of us, and she made it out on the other side a literal Shark. And agents love her for it.

To boot, she built The Corcoran Group in New York City, where competition was fierce and standing out required creativity — something agents covet and understand deeply. Long before agents were being told to become content creators, Barbara understood how to make herself and her business interesting to the public. She launched market reports, generated publicity and became a recognizable authority on New York real estate.

She understood personal brand marketing before most of our industry knew what to call it.

She sold her brokerage in 2001 and went on to build another career as an entrepreneur, investor and television personality. And now, after all of that, there she is sitting in a chair on Shark Tank, evaluating other entrepreneurs and deciding which businesses deserve her money.

Barbara understands something that most successful real estate agents figure out, and the new ones need to hear: A willingness to take risks, build relationships and solve problems can take you a very long way in this business.

And she’s spent enough time carrying the bag to know how to find business when everyone else is convinced there isn’t any. Her perspective on this is particularly valuable for agents to hear, if we consider the voices dominating our industry’s conversations right now.

The real estate conversations are dominated by brokerage executives defending their business models, MLS leaders explaining their policies and industry organizations navigating enormous changes; senators are filing FTC complaints against industry leaders, too. It’s overwhelming, and yet, none of it helps Susie Realtor or Mike Agent close a home this quarter.

There are important questions being debated about how homes should be marketed, who controls listing information, and how real estate professionals will operate in the years ahead, and while I do believe all of those discussions deserve a place on highly influential stages such as Inman Connect New York, agents also desperately need to hear from voices right now who don’t have a dog in the fight, who can hunker down on a mic and say, “OK, listen up, this is exactly what I would do right now if I were in your shoes.”

Barbara Corcoran is the real estate fairy godmother who is uniquely positioned to say that, without an obvious bias, something to sell the audience or any other ulterior motive. That dynamic really appeals to agents right now, who are growing tired of the industry’s constant infighting.

A real estate agent trying to figure out how to get their listing sold after sitting for 90-plus days, so they can get their client the win and feed their own family, is less concerned with which brokerage executive launches their AI tool most effectively and who is winning the latest argument about private listings.

Agents need a change of scenery right now, and Barbara knows how to generate business, find the buyer and create buzz around listings that have been sitting for weeks.

She’s also famously candid, and I suspect she will have plenty to say about what is happening in our industry.

My takeaway from the overwhelming request for Barbara is that agents are craving an independent voice of reason. Someone who understands the realities of selling real estate and can speak from experience.

And when our community made that request, we listened.

I want to give credit to Inman CEO Tom Bohn for taking the feedback seriously and making Barbara a priority for New York. One of the things I’ve appreciated about working with Tom is his willingness to listen to the real estate professionals who make up our community with fresh perspectives, while also prioritizing the industry leadership who are critical to our ecosystem as an industry.

We have an opportunity to put some of the smartest people in the business on our stages. I think we should pay particular attention when the people in our audience tell us whose perspective they value.

So, we got Barbara, and she’s going to tell our audience exactly what she would do right now. And we can’t wait to hear it.

Join us at Inman Connect New York, Jan. 26–28, 2027, at the New York Hilton Midtown.

#5654. Same model, better answer: Enterprise data is what turns generic AI into a business tool

Generic AI models can write SQL, but they don’t know a company’s orders, customers or revenue definitions. Now, Oracle Database aims to give AI agents the context to move a stalled order forward.

But that shift raises questions about complexity, lock-in and security as AI agents start acting on live transactions. Oracle Corp.’s answer is a converged platform that keeps vectors, graphs, documents and transactions in one engine, according to Hasan Rizvi (pictured), executive vice president of product and research, database engineering, at Oracle.

“If you ask a generic AI assistant, you get a generic answer,” Rizvi said. “If you ask an AI assistant that knows your business, you get a much better answer. Where is the stock? How can I fix the transaction? How can I expedite the delivery?”

Rizvi spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed database convergence and the safeguards needed for AI agents. (* Disclosure below.)

AI lets teams spin up applications and data stores very quickly, making data sprawl everybody’s problem. Skeptics favor specialized databases for each workload, but new data types built inside Oracle’s engine inherit proven availability, security and scale, according to Rizvi.

“We’ve been working on this engine for 40 years, which is highly available, highly secure, highly scalable, highly performant,” Rizvi said. “If you build a new data type or a new workload in the same engine, you get all that benefit, multiple decades’ worth of investment.”

Choice is the other half of the pitch. The database runs on-premises, through Oracle Cloud@Customer and across multiple public clouds, and Oracle used the event to expand Iceberg support in its Autonomous AI Lakehouse, Rizvi noted. But security is where AI raises the stakes most, with Oracle’s Deep Data Security defining access policies in the database itself, so a user’s identity travels with every request from an agent or AI-generated app.

“Before, it took a lot of time and effort to find vulnerabilities to exploit them,” he said. “Now, with AI, it’s made it very easy to reverse engineer fixes for attackers to attack.”

#5653. 7 ways to breathe new life into a listing that isn’t selling

Don’t jump straight to a price cut when you have a listing not selling. These seven strategies refresh your marketing and put it in front of new buyers.

Listing not selling? If I had a listing that had been sitting on the market for 30, 60 or even 90 days, and I needed to get it sold in the next 60 days, I wouldn’t simply keep doing the same things and hope a buyer eventually showed up. I also wouldn’t immediately call the seller and ask for a price reduction.

I’d start by developing a specific plan to create new interest in the home. These are the seven strategies I’d use.

The first thing I’d do is give the listing a completely fresh look. I want someone who has already seen the property online to notice something different when it shows up again.

I’d start with the MLS description. I’d use AI to help me rewrite it to highlight the most compelling features of the property, tell a better story and give potential buyers a reason to schedule a showing.

Act as an expert real estate MLS copywriter. Rewrite the following MLS description in a fresh, creative and compelling way that helps potential buyers imagine living in this home and encourages them to schedule a showing. Avoid generic real estate language, highlight what makes this property unique and naturally include relevant location and property keywords for SEO and AEO optimization. Ask me any questions needed before writing the new description.

Next, I’d also take a close look at the photos and videos. If the property has been on the market for several months, it may be time for new photography, updated staging or a different approach to showcasing the home.

I’d consider whether an accurately represented twilight photo or a newly staged room could make the property more appealing. If AI-assisted photo editing is involved, I’d make sure any alterations are properly disclosed in accordance with MLS rules and accurately represent the property and its surroundings.

One of the simplest changes you can make is updating the primary listing photo. I’d take five or six of the strongest photos and ask other agents which one would most likely make them stop scrolling. Sometimes it’s the front elevation, but sometimes it’s a beautiful outdoor living area, an incredible kitchen or a view that immediately captures someone’s attention.

I’d also refresh the social media posts promoting the home. Instead of recycling the same graphics and captions, I’d create fresh content tailored to each platform where I’m marketing the property.

The goal is simple. Before doing anything else, make the listing look fresh to give people who may have previously overlooked it a reason to take another look.

The next thing I’d do is identify exactly who the most likely buyers are for this property. Instead of marketing the home to everybody, I’d identify two or three distinct buyer groups who might align with its features and benefits.

For example, a home with a first-floor primary suite, a dedicated office and a low-maintenance yard might appeal to several types of buyers for different reasons. One buyer may be focused on working from home. Another may be interested in reducing the amount of exterior maintenance required. A third may value the floor plan and flexibility of the living spaces.

Once I identified the potential buyer groups, I’d use AI to help me understand which property features, lifestyle benefits and potential concerns might matter most to each group. Then I’d ask AI to help me create separate marketing campaigns that speak to those different priorities.

The key is to focus on the property’s features and the benefits they provide, rather than making assumptions about who should live there. That helps keep the marketing inclusive and aligned with fair housing requirements.

This is a different approach from simply posting the same listing description repeatedly and hoping someone responds. We’re identifying what makes the property attractive to different buyers and creating marketing that helps them recognize those benefits.

When you understand what someone is looking for, you can do a much better job of showing them why a particular property deserves their attention.

The third strategy I’d use is a focused, 10-day campaign to make sure the agents most likely to have a buyer for the property know about it.

I’d start by reviewing MLS data to identify agents who have recently sold comparable homes in the area. I’d also look for agents who have active listings or, where available, buyer activity that suggests they’re working with people interested in similar properties.

Then I’d create a list of the agents most likely to have relationships with buyers who might be interested in my listing. Over the next 10 business days, I’d personally call two of those agents every day.

I’d say something like, “Hey, I know you do a lot of business in this neighborhood and price range. I’ve got a listing I wanted to make sure was on your radar. I’d love to get your feedback on it and see if you might have someone who’s looking for something similar.”

That’s 20 personal conversations with agents who have demonstrated experience selling the type of property I’m trying to get sold. I’d also create an email campaign to share the property’s most compelling features with a broader group of agents, using appropriate contact information and respecting communication preferences.

Another opportunity is reaching out to agents who have competing listings. I’d ask what kind of activity they’re seeing and what feedback they’re receiving. I’d also offer to share information about my listing so that if one of their buyers doesn’t find the right fit in their property, they know about mine. And I’d do the same for them.

The goal isn’t simply to promote my listing. It’s to build relationships with agents who are actively working with the buyers I’m trying to reach. Sometimes the best opportunity to sell a home isn’t through another social media post. It’s through a conversation with the agent who already has the right buyer.

One of my favorite ways to generate new interest in a listing is to stop focusing exclusively on the house and start showing what it might feel like to live there. I’d create videos that help potential buyers imagine the experiences the property and its location make possible.

For instance, I might create a video titled, “Here’s what a Saturday could look like living in this home.” The video could start with coffee on the back porch, move to a nearby farmers’ market, showcase a local restaurant for lunch and end with an evening enjoying the outdoor living space.

Another idea might be, “Here’s what date night could look like if you lived here.” The video could highlight nearby restaurants, entertainment or a relaxing evening at home. If the property is close to a park, I’d show the actual route and how convenient it is to get there. If it’s within walking distance of restaurants or shopping, I’d create a short video showcasing that experience.

I’d also think about the lifestyle opportunities inside the home. Maybe there’s a great outdoor kitchen for entertaining, a flexible bonus room or a covered porch that creates a natural gathering place. The key is to help people see something they may have missed when they first looked at the listing photos.

A buyer may not remember that a home has a 12-by-20-foot covered porch. But they may remember the video showing what a Saturday evening with friends could look like in that space.

Features tell people what a home has. Lifestyle marketing helps them imagine what living there could feel like.

The fifth strategy I’d use is finding ways to make the property more financially attractive than competing homes. We hear a lot about affordability, and for many buyers, the challenge isn’t simply the purchase price. It’s the monthly payment, closing costs or the amount of cash required to purchase the home.

That’s why I’d evaluate potential incentives before assuming that a price reduction is the only option. Maybe the seller could offer a closing-cost credit. Maybe a mortgage rate buydown would make the monthly payment more attractive. Maybe covering a portion of the HOA dues or offering an allowable allowance for improvements could help the property stand out.

I’d approach this the way a new-home builder might. Builders don’t always compete exclusively on price. They often use incentives to create a more attractive financial opportunity for buyers. I’d work with the seller and a qualified lender to determine which incentives are appropriate, what they would actually cost and how they compare with a price reduction.

For example, if a seller is considering a $10,000 price reduction, I’d want to know whether a properly structured $10,000 concession could provide greater value to the right buyer. The answer will depend on the buyer’s financing, the property, lender requirements and the local market. But it’s a conversation worth having.

Then I’d make sure those incentives were clearly communicated in the listing and marketing materials, including any important terms or limitations. Sometimes the opportunity isn’t simply making the house less expensive. It’s finding a way to make purchasing the house more attractive.

Once I’ve refreshed the listing, identified ideal buyer groups, connected with active agents and evaluated potential incentives, I’d launch a 21-day marketing blitz. This is where I’d get creative.

The mistake I see agents make is posting the same property photo and listing information over and over again. They may think they’re marketing the property 10 different times, but in reality, they’re often repeating the same message 10 times. I’d rather create 21 different pieces of content that give people different reasons to take notice.

For example, if the home is listed at $450,000, I’d create a video titled, “What does $450,000 buy you in this neighborhood?” Another video might be, “What the listing photos don’t tell you about this home.” I’d create content about the history of the neighborhood, the builder, nearby amenities and what makes the location unique. I’d showcase individual features that deserve more attention and answer questions buyers might have about the property.

I’d also create content comparing the home with other available options in the same price range. The goal would be to help buyers understand the value and opportunities the property offers. Some content would be short-form video. Some might be photo carousels. Some would be longer walkthroughs, neighborhood videos or educational posts.

I’d also use AI to brainstorm additional angles. I’d ask it to develop a 21-day content campaign that highlights the property from different perspectives without simply repeating the same sales message. The goal is to create enough variety that someone who wasn’t interested in the original listing post might see something new that changes their perspective.

One piece of content might attract someone because of the price point. Another might attract someone because of the neighborhood. Another might reveal a feature a buyer didn’t realize the home offered.

That’s a marketing campaign. Not simply posting the same listing over and over again.

If I’ve done everything I can to refresh the marketing, identify potential buyers, communicate with agents, highlight the lifestyle, create financial incentives and execute a 21-day content campaign, but the property still isn’t generating the activity we need, it’s time to have the conversation most agents dread: the price reduction conversation.

But here’s the difference. I don’t want this to be the first time the seller has heard that a price adjustment might become necessary. I’d communicate with them throughout the entire process. Before launching the marketing blitz, I’d explain exactly what we’re going to do and why. I’d also let them know what happens if those efforts don’t generate the results we’re looking for.

“I want you to know we’re going to make a significant push over the next 21 days to create new interest in your home. We’re going to refresh the marketing, reach out to agents who are active in this price range and launch a series of new campaigns. But if we get through that process and still aren’t seeing the activity we need, my responsibility is to bring you the most current market information so you can make the best decision for you and your family.”

That conversation sets the expectation before the difficult decision arrives. I’d actually recommend having a version of this conversation when you first take the listing. I’d explain that we have a comprehensive listing launch program designed to generate exposure and buyer interest. But if the market doesn’t respond the way we expect, we need to be willing to evaluate what it’s telling us.

Then, when the time comes, I’d bring the seller updated comparable sales, competing listings, properties that have gone under contract, showing activity and buyer feedback. I’d explain what the information suggests and present a specific recommendation.

But I wouldn’t simply ask for a price reduction. I’d show the seller what a strategic price improvement could allow us to do. Maybe it means reaching buyers searching in a different price range. Maybe it creates an opportunity to reconnect with agents who previously showed the property. Maybe it gives us a reason to host another open house, relaunch the marketing and communicate the new value proposition. I’d create a list of the specific activities we would execute following the adjustment.

I’d also be strategic about the timing. Depending on the market, I’d consider making the adjustment before the period when buyers are most actively scheduling weekend showings. I’d review the local data and how the major real estate portals display price changes rather than assuming every market or platform behaves the same way.

The important thing is that we’re not simply changing a number in the MLS. We’re using the new price as an opportunity to create renewed interest through a coordinated marketing plan. And ultimately, I’d remind the seller that the decision is theirs. It’s their home, and my responsibility is to give them the best market knowledge, professional guidance and clear recommendations they need to make an informed decision.

When a listing isn’t selling, continuing to do the same things and hoping for a different result isn’t a strategy. Neither is immediately asking the seller for a price reduction without first evaluating what else can be done.

The most important part of this entire process is communication. Your sellers should never wonder what you’re doing to get their home sold or be surprised when you recommend an adjustment. They should know you’re working on their behalf, evaluating the market and doing everything possible to help them achieve their goal.

This is a market that rewards professionals who are willing to think differently, market more creatively and communicate more effectively. Remember, your sellers didn’t hire you simply to market their home. They hired you to help them get it sold. Our job is to bring the creativity, strategy and professional advice necessary to give them the best opportunity to make that happen.

Jimmy Burgess is the Chief Coaching Officer for HomeServices of America and President of Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices. Get connected on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5652. Gemini AI Predicts a Brutal Unwinding of the TRUMP Memecoin

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

In the just-concluded 2026 midterms, Democrats delivered a decisive sweep, flipping control of both the House and Senate in a broad rebuke of Republican governance. As a result, Google’s Gemini AI predicts the TRUMP crypto memecoin could crash catastrophically heading into 2027.

The Democratic Party made significant gains in traditionally Republican states, flipping several Senate seats and securing a clear House majority. This outcome substantially weakens the Republican control in Washington, limiting the administration’s ability to advance its agenda and shifting legislative power toward Democratic priorities for the remainder of the term.

Historically, Democrats have taken a more skeptical, regulatory approach to cryptocurrency. With majorities in both chambers, they are now better positioned to advocate for tighter oversight, expanded enforcement, and potentially restrictive legislation on digital assets.

#5651. Oracle wants to pull stalled AI agents out of demo mode and into production

Companies want AI agents faster than they can build the AI architecture to run them. Most can put together a convincing demo. Far fewer can move agents into production without exposing data, hurting uptime or blowing their budgets.

That gap is pushing database providers to rethink what a data platform for agents has to deliver. Nearly 70% of organizations plan to deploy AI agents, yet very few get them into production, according to Çetin Özbütün (pictured), executive vice president of product and research, data warehouse and autonomous database, at Oracle Corp.

“AI is very easy to demonstrate, but when you try to bring it into production, enterprises usually encounter four different deployment difficulties,” Özbütün said. “The first of them is around security. It’s very hard to securely provide access to AI agents, and that’s one of the top challenges.”

Özbütün spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed AI architecture and the challenges of moving agents into production. (* Disclosure below.)

Security is the first hurdle. AI agents are finding vulnerabilities at unprecedented levels, and customers often can’t patch their databases before attackers exploit those flaws, Özbütün noted. Oracle’s Autonomous AI Database encrypts data at rest and in transit by default, and users can’t turn those protections off.

“As soon as the vulnerability is found, before it’s released anywhere else, we bring it into production in Autonomous AI Database,” Özbütün said.

Resiliency is the next test, because agents run around the clock and put heavy, unpredictable demands on the data platform. Oracle commits to 99.995% availability with no exclusions. That figure is measured by whether a client can connect and run queries, not by whether the underlying infrastructure is running, Özbütün explained.

“We patch our systems on a weekly basis, for example,” Özbütün said. “All of our patches are online patches, so the database is up and running, accepting new connections, accepting new requests while we’re running the patch.”

The same always-current approach applies to Oracle’s Deep Trust AI architecture, in which the database enforces the security profiles that customers define. New capabilities such as the expanded Deep Data Security features show up in Autonomous AI Database as soon as they’re announced, ahead of on-premises releases, according to Özbütün.

“You do nothing as the user or administrator of Autonomous Database to get this functionality,” Özbütün said. “As soon as a new functionality is available, like Oracle Deep Data Security, it becomes available for you to use on day one.”

#5650. Jeff Glover goes indie after 17 years with Keller Williams (EXCLUSIVE)

Jeff Glover, founder of Live Unreal Companies |

Jeff Glover takes Glover Agency independent after 17 years with Keller Williams, telling Inman the move is about keeping Glover U broker-agnostic.

Glover Agency, the Michigan team Jeff Glover founded in 2008, became fully independent on Nov. 1, ending a 17-year run with Keller Williams. The move comes roughly three months after Glover sold his three Keller Williams market centers.

The team says it has been Michigan’s top homeselling team across all brands in 11 of the past 13 years and has sold more than 10,000 homes. It operates out of four offices in Birmingham, Plymouth, Fenton and Grand Rapids.

Glover Agency will now operate only in Michigan and isn’t affiliated with any franchise or national brand.

With Glover Agency out of the franchise system, none of Glover’s Live Unreal Companies are tied to a single brand, which Glover says frees Glover U to work with agents and leaders at every brokerage in the U.S. and Canada.

In an exclusive interview with Inman, Glover said the decision had a lot to do with Glover U, the coaching and training company where he now spends most of his time. Glover U has long pitched itself as broker-agnostic, but Glover said his KW ties kept closing doors, even after the market center sale.

In August, Glover sold his ownership stakes in three Keller Williams market centers across Michigan, where he served as majority owner and operating principal. He said the sale supported Glover U’s broker-agnostic approach to serving agents across the U.S. and Canada. The three market centers combined closed nearly $1 billion in sales volume in 2025.

“Most of [the potential Glover U clients], if they don’t know me and their agents don’t know me, they’re not going to return my call,” Glover said of leaders at rival brands. “I had leaders of large companies — I mean, the largest that exist today — say, ‘Hey, Jeff, that’s great you sold your franchises, and we’re definitely open to you helping our agents, but I’m sorry, I can’t put a Keller Williams guy on our stage.'”

Joining another brand would have recreated the same problem. Going independent, Glover says, removes it.

“This move furthers the brand-agnostic approach we’ve been working toward, and now there should be little to no objection to somebody trusting me with their agents, because I don’t have a dog in the fight,” Glover said. “They don’t have to worry about me pushing their agents to go to any one company when I’m independent.”

The second driver is marketing. Glover Agency has advertised under its own name for years on TV, radio and billboards, and Glover said most Michigan consumers already assumed the team was independent.

Franchise rules on how the team could advertise, down to how large its name could appear, made it harder for individual agents to build their own brands.

“It’s very hard for them to create a brand within a brand within a brand,” Glover said. “It’s confusing to consumers. It’s confusing to other agents and other companies.”

Glover said top teams that understand marketing already know where consumer loyalty sits.

“The everyday seller and everyday buyer generally doesn’t say, ‘ We’re listing our home with Keller Williams or with Coldwell Banker,'” Glover said. “They say, ‘We’re listing our home with ‘Joe Smith’ or ‘Amy Duncan.'”

For the consumer, Glover said that the brand is “just the gravy on top.” “The brand helps, but today’s consumer resonates more with an agent’s or a team’s brand than with the company’s brand,” he said.

Day-to-day operations at Glover Agency are run by CEO Taylor Kerrigan. Glover remains involved and still lists and sells. He said he was prospecting in front of the team’s agents just before speaking with Inman on Friday.

“For our clients, nothing changes about how we serve them, other than a more personalized approach,” Kerrigan said in a statement. “What does change is that the name on the door is entirely ours.”

Glover joined Keller Williams in 2009, and the company says the team climbed as high as No. 3 nationally among all groups and No. 1 among expansion teams for homes sold. Asked what would be hardest about leaving, Glover didn’t hesitate.

“Without question, my relationship with Gary Keller,” he said, pointing to Keller’s early top 100 mastermind and a smaller circle of about a dozen agents, the Pirate Group, who got regular access to the KW co-founder. “I wouldn’t be where I am today if it weren’t for him.”

Glover said he still considers Keller a mentor and expects to keep speaking at KW events “so long as I’m welcome.”

The timing puts Glover on the opposite side of an industry trend. Consolidation has dominated brokerage headlines this year, including Compass–Anywhere and Real–REMAX, and independents face growing pressure to align with a larger platform.

Glover doesn’t think independence is right for everyone. He said it works for owners who know what agents need today, such as database growth, leverage and help building personal brands, and who have the energy to deliver it.

“For the person who somewhat wants the easy button, and maybe they’re at a point in their life where they don’t have the energy or time to pour into their company,” he said, joining a franchise or a company like Real, eXp or LPT “makes a lot of sense for that individual.”

For Glover, the bigger bet is on Glover U.

“The biggest thing is neutralizing Glover U so that it will be the No. 1 training and coaching company on the planet for real estate agents at the rate we’re growing,” he told Inman. “And I can’t do that if I’m affiliated with any one brand. So that’s a big part of it. The other part is the freedom and flexibility this gives us to help our agents grow their brands even bigger.”
