#5627. 7 steps from the National Cybersecurity Alliance to shrink your digital footprint

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Seven steps to check and shrink your digital footprint, from asking why to posting with care, plus what each protects.

Most people think of their online trail as a record of what they posted or searched for. It is really a collection of personal details, such as names, addresses, locations and purchases. Apps, retailers and platforms hold those details, and many of them are companies a person signed up with years ago and has since forgotten. Two very different groups will pay for that information or take it. Companies buy and sell location data in an industry worth $12 billion, according to TIME. Criminals target the same kinds of records. A single breach at AT&T $T, reported in early 2024, potentially affected 73 million people, according to the Aiken Standard. Some businesses treat your data as a product, and thieves treat it as something to steal. Every detail you have handed over adds to what either group can get.

A leak can do harm long before anyone notices it. Worldwide, companies took an average of 241 days to find and contain a breach, according to IBM $IBM 2025 figures reported by CBC News. People can search for their own names, delete old accounts, adjust settings and assert legal rights. Each of those steps helps, but most of them come into play after a person's details are already out, and each one has limits. The protections that last are the ones that keep data from leaving your hands at all.

Saying no is the cheapest protection you have, but it works only if the company honors your answer. A group of users sued Meta on the claim that the company went on following where they were even after they had switched the feature off, and in 2022 Meta settled that class action for $37.5 million without admitting guilt, according to TIME. You can't tell from a permission screen whether an app respects your refusal, so the protection holds only where the company takes you at your word.

Asking why limits what you share from now on, but it can't recall what you've already given away, and finding that is the work of the steps that follow.

Most people never see their own name the way a stranger, a recruiter or a scammer does: typed into a search bar. Searching for yourself lets you see what strangers can already find, according to the National Cybersecurity Alliance, and checking breach records tells you which passwords you need to change. In 2023, Google $GOOGL was accepting requests to remove some results from its search pages, CNBC reports, so you could start a cleanup from the same search you used to take stock. Both checks still tell you only what has already escaped. A list of compromised passwords is a record of damage already done, and neither search stops the next leak.

The cleanup that follows a search is narrower than it sounds. When Google removes a link, the page that hosts your information stays online, according to CNBC, and anyone who reaches that page another way can still read it. Google describes the purpose of these tools in terms of how people feel. "It's just one of the many things we're trying to do to help people feel control of their online experience," said Danny Sullivan, Google's public liaison for search. A removal request changes how easily strangers can find you, not how much of your information exists.

Some of what you find may stay put no matter what you ask. In 2023, Google could turn down any removal request that fell outside its rules, according to CNBC, so spotting something damaging about yourself did not mean you could get it taken out of the results. Google's tool for removing explicit photos was available only to U.S. users searching in English when it launched in 2023. People outside that group had less help with one of the most damaging kinds of exposure. Results change and requests can fail, and a single search proves little. Repeating the search on a regular schedule keeps you aware of your exposure.

You can learn where you stand by Googling yourself, but you will rarely change where you stand that way.

Accounts you have forgotten about are still part of your digital trail, and each old sign-up holds a login you no longer think about. The National Cybersecurity Alliance recommends a password manager for reviewing those accounts, because with all of them in one place you can see how many you hold and clean up the ones that are old, unused or weak. That makes the tool more useful as an audit of your past sign-ups than as a safe for your passwords. You get that benefit only when you close the accounts you no longer need and fix the weak logins on the ones you keep. Treat the list as a to-do list, not a record.

Cleaning up old logins matters most for passwords you have reused, because one shared password links every account that uses it. When a password is reused, "the bad guys only need to break your password security once to get at all those accounts," Suelette Dreyfus, a senior lecturer in computing and information systems at the University of Melbourne, said, as reported by ABC News. Unique logins break that link, and a manager can create a strong one for every site, so criminals who steal one password can get into only that one account. You get the most from a manager when you replace your old logins with unique ones, not when you only store them.

Many people pick a manager for its breach warnings, which have a real limit. The Australian Cyber Security Centre lists an alert for passwords exposed in a breach as a feature to look for, according to ABC News. Even a good alert comes late. Gohar Rind, managing director of Intaris, says a manager can check for a leaked password only after it has been made public, appeared on the dark web or been flagged in a notice from authorities. By that point, other people can already see the password. Rind advises changing an exposed password immediately. Treat any alert as a signal to act at once, not as a sign that the problem has been handled.

A password manager reduces your trail only when you use it to close and fix accounts yourself, and its warnings tell you only what has already leaked.

Every account you open leaves another company holding your name, your email address and a record of your habits long after you've stopped thinking about it. The National Cybersecurity Alliance says that each signup widens your exposure to junk mail, tracking and leaks, and that shoppers who check out as guests sidestep that exposure. The reasoning holds up as far as it goes. When fewer companies keep your details, you have fewer places to watch and less to defend.

Protection from leaks is where the promise falls short. A guest checkout still asks for your name, address and payment details, and the retailer keeps that information after you click "buy." Canada Computers says the shoppers hit by its breach bought without an account and typed in personal details, and its current investigation counts 1,284 of them, according to company figures reported by CBC News. Skipping the signup did not keep those shoppers' information out of the breach. What shoppers who check out as guests mostly gain is less follow-up, with fewer marketing emails and less tracking of what they do next. That is a choice about future contact, not a security measure.

The risk from a stolen guest order does not end when the purchase is over, because criminals can hold on to the details they take. Once personal data is taken, "cybercriminals can get to it weeks, months, years later," Terry Cutler, CEO of Cyology Labs in Montreal, told CBC News. Passing on an account is a good start, but what you type into a checkout form still counts, so give each order only what it needs.

Nobody can steal a detail from an account you never opened, or one you never typed in.

Some of the more protective choices start switched off, and a user has to turn them on. The alliance names Facebook $META as a hard platform to avoid, along with Google $GOOGL, Apple $AAPL and Microsoft $MSFT. Meta agreed to a child-safety settlement worth roughly $18 billion, and Facebook's non-algorithmic feed is an opt-in setting, according to TIME. Even with that much money at stake, people get the gentler feed only if they go looking for it.

Every setting also assumes the platform knows who is using the account. Zvika Krieger, former director of Meta's responsible innovation team and now a consultant for technology companies, told TIME that "if young users are just using adult accounts, all this is worthless." Meta has offered little information on how it will check users' ages, so that gap remains open. For a family, the first task is to make sure each person, especially a child, is on the account meant for them. Choosing the options comes after that.

Settings can also shift as legal pressure pushes companies to change them, which is one reason to check them on a schedule. The three-month review is the alliance's own suggestion, not a legal or industry requirement. Meta's settlement includes a $5.3 billion payment that depends on YouTube and TikTok adopting similar settings, according to TIME. It is not yet known whether either company will make that change. If one does, a user who reviews settings regularly will see the new options.

Even where a deletion right exists, it gives you the power to ask, and the company still decides how to answer. CBC News reports that officials named some grounds on which a company could refuse a deletion request and described them as only some of the exceptions. A request you file could therefore meet a refusal on grounds no one has fully spelled out.

Use these rights wherever they apply, but treat them as a backstop for data already out of your hands, not a way to take it back on demand.

The details that cause trouble are rarely secrets. People who would never share a password will still mention the town they grew up in or the name of a childhood pet. People often share those answers in online quizzes, and the same answers often protect an account's security questions. The risk is higher when the same detail also appears in a password. Before you post, ask what accounts a stranger could get into with the detail, not just whether it is private.

Care matters most when you pay for something online. Debit cards lack some of the protections that come with credit cards, according to the Aiken Standard. On a site you don't know well, a credit card is the safer way to pay. Caution also has to continue after a company announces a breach. The link in a breach notice could lead to a scam, and scammers may also call while posing as a retailer, a bank or a card issuer. The safe response is to go to the company's own website rather than click a link in the message.

Careful habits can't stop every breach. A company you trusted with an ordinary card purchase can still lose your details, and nothing you do on your end prevents that. You can get free credit reports from the official site, AnnualCreditReport.com, according to the Aiken Standard. Read your reports regularly to spot any account or activity you didn't create.

When you post and pay with care, less of you is out there to steal, and when you check your reports, you learn when someone has taken something anyway.

#5626. IBM Unveils Its Most Advanced Quantum Computer in Chicago, Marking a Milestone for Illinois's Quantum Future

Hosted by the University of Chicago, IBM Quantum System Two is now operational at Hyde Park Labs and will be a prominent fixture of Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park (IQMP) upon the site's completion.

IBM's first quantum computer in Illinois extends the company's industry and academic partnerships across the state, enabling the Illinois ecosystem and beyond to scale quantum algorithms and applications.

CHICAGO, Nov. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- IBM (NYSE: IBM), the University of Chicago, the State of Illinois, and Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park (IQMP) today unveiled an IBM Quantum System Two in Chicago, IBM's first quantum computer in Illinois and the company's most advanced system available. Initially located at Hyde Park Labs and hosted by the University of Chicago, the system is fueled by IBM Quantum Nighthawk, the most powerful quantum chip IBM has ever built.

Today, organizations across Illinois are already working with IBM to explore how quantum computing can scale to computationally difficult challenges. The new system aims to catalyze the state's robust ecosystem of scientists, universities, national laboratories, startups, and enterprises, many of whom are collaborating with IBM in Chicago within IQMP's National Quantum Algorithm Center (NQAC) to develop the next generation of algorithms and applications. As the anchor system of NQAC, which was established in 2024 by Illinois Governor JB Pritzker with IBM as a leading member, the new quantum computer will ultimately be moved to IQMP, a first-of-its-kind campus in Chicago currently being built to develop and scale quantum technology and microelectronics innovation.

"IBM is proud to deploy our first quantum computer of IQMP â an IBM Quantum System Two. Today, it can deliver scientifically useful results to organizations across the state of Illinois and beyond," said Arvind Krishna, Chairman and CEO, IBM. "As IBM's first quantum computer in Illinois, the system's deployment marks a milestone for Illinois' quantum community and builds on IBM's partnerships across the state as we expand quantum research across academia and industries."

"I want the next generation of breakthroughs to happen in Illinois and the jobs and opportunity that come with them to benefit the people of Illinois," said Governor JB Pritzker. "With the unveiling of IBM's Quantum System Two in Hyde Park, we are giving researchers and businesses the tool to turn big ideas into real-world solutions. With our growing partnership with IBM, we are building an industry that will give Illinoisans more career opportunities and build a future right here at home."

"The presence of IBM's first quantum computer in Illinois, the company's most advanced system available, is a testament to what's possible when partners across government, industry and academia work together toward a shared vision," said Harley Johnson, CEO of the IQMP. "Today reflects the unique strength of Illinois' quantum ecosystem. We're thrilled to see IBM Quantum System Two at Hyde Park Labs while the Park is under construction, and we're more energized than ever to welcome it to the IQMP, where it will anchor the National Quantum Algorithm Center and further establish Illinois as the global destination for quantum innovation."

"The deployment of IBM's Quantum System Two represents the culmination of a years-long partnership that brought together academia, government, and private industry to usher in a new generation of discovery. I am delighted that this machine is being unveiled here in Hyde Park, where our neighbors and community will have a view into the future," said University of Chicago President Paul Alivisatos.

"IBM Quantum System Two brings another critical capability to Illinois' growing quantum ecosystem and showcases the collaboration that makes our state such a draw," said Illinois Economic Development Corporation President and CEO Christy George. "For companies developing quantum technologies and applications, access to advanced computing systems, leading researchers, and industry partners in one place is a powerful advantage. This investment strengthens Illinois' position as a destination for companies looking to innovate, grow, and help shape the future of quantum computing."

This new IBM Quantum System Two advances IBM's mission to bring useful quantum computing to the world and extends the company's commitment to advancing Illinois as a global epicenter for quantum innovation.

Since NQAC's founding, IBM has helped grow the center into a hub within Chicago where industry leaders work side-by-side with IBM researchers to build quantum applications that can scale alongside technical progress in the field. This includes NQAC Grand Challenge participants Deloitte and AbbVie, who are working with IBM and Northwestern University to build quantum molecular simulation approaches for researchers engaging in drug discovery.

Other Grand Challenges participants working with IBM include EPRI and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (U. of I.) to explore how quantum optimization algorithms could lead to more efficient power grids.

Additionally, research institutions and national labs such as Fermilab are working with IBM in Illinois to accelerate high-energy physics research with quantum and advance technologies for distributed quantum computing.

IBM is also teaming with leading universities such as the University of Chicago and U. of I. to push technological progress in quantum computing. For example, IBM and the University of Chicago recently demonstrated quantum advantage over leading classical methods using an approach with guaranteed correctness.

Now, IBM's quantum computing technology is being brought physically into Chicago. Through NQAC, the new quantum computer will empower Illinois' quantum community to develop new algorithms and applications that will translate to real-world impact. And it will serve as a catalyst for developing Illinois' current and future quantum workforce. Earlier this year, IBM announced it would establish the FutureNow Chicago center at the IQMP in partnership with City Colleges of Chicago, to bring 750 jobs to the region across AI, cybersecurity, data science, quantum computing and other technologies.

With the arrival of IBM Quantum System Two, Chicago and the State of Illinois will be cemented as a leading destination for quantum innovation, industrialization, and workforce development.

"IBM's continued partnership and the unveiling of IBM Quantum System Two mark an exciting moment for the industry and our state's quantum ecosystem," said Brad Henderson, CEO of P33. "Deepening collaboration between industry, our universities, national labs, and state government is what sets us apart and further cements Illinois as a global leader in quantum technology."

"We are proud to contribute the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign's expertise and decades of leadership in supercomputing alongside our higher education and corporate partners," said Illinois Chancellor Charles L. Isbell, Jr. "As a public-serving university, Illinois' mission is to advance education, research, and economic opportunity across the state, and we're excited to engage in work that translates the brilliance of Illinois faculty into tangible, real-world impact that affirms the state of Illinois and Chicago as the epicenter of the next generation of technological progress."

"This is a significant milestone in advancing Illinois' quantum economy and turning our state's world-class research capabilities into real-world economic opportunity," said Illinois Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity Director Kristin Richards. "Through the State's leadership and strategic investments in quantum, we are building an ecosystem for long-term industry growth, new business investment, and high-quality jobs."

IBM is a leading global hybrid cloud and AI, and business services provider, helping clients in more than 175 countries capitalize on insights from their data, streamline business processes, reduce costs and gain the competitive edge in their industries. Thousands of governments and corporate entities in critical infrastructure areas such as financial services, telecommunications and healthcare rely on IBM's hybrid cloud platform and Red Hat OpenShift to affect their digital transformations quickly, efficiently and securely. IBM's breakthrough innovations in AI, quantum computing, industry-specific cloud solutions and business services deliver open and flexible options to our clients. All of this is backed by IBM's legendary commitment to trust, transparency, responsibility, inclusivity and service.

For more information, visit https://research.ibm.com.

#5625. OpenAI makes new data center commitments, AI policy recommendations

OpenAI Group PBC today made a set of commitments designed to ensure that its data centers benefit the communities where they’re built.

It also proposed that lawmakers make some of the commitments mandatory for artificial intelligence companies.

The move comes two days after Democrats won both the House and the Senate on a campaign backing data center construction curbs. Additionally, voters approved dozens of ballot measures designed to scale back or limit AI infrastructure projects.

OpenAI today reiterated a commitment it made in January to fully pay for the electricity and grid upgrades that its data centers require. That covers items such as the construction of new overhead power lines. Additionally, the company pledged to provide “financial assurances” that will protect other grid users from potential project cancellations and delays.

It will also take steps to reduce grid strain. In particular, it will scale back its data centers’ power draw at times when energy demand is particularly high. That approach, which is known as a flexible data center model, has also drawn the interest of other industry players as Nvidia Corp. and Google LLC.

Some data center builders sign non-disclosure agreements with local officials to keep construction details under wraps. OpenAI today pledged not to use NDAs. It will instead only seek “narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.”

OpenAI will publicly share construction plans and noise projections before construction of a new facility begins. Additionally, it will provide information about the jobs that each data center is expected to create. The goal is to help local unions and training providers prepare residents for the positions.

The company plans to tailor its commitments to each data center. It will publish the customized project terms in a document it calls a local compact. Once construction is underway, the company will provide annual updates and designate a local contact to field residents’ questions.

OpenAI hopes to codify some of the best practices that it published today into law. It released a policy paper that calls on lawmakers to limit data center developers’ use of NDAs and require them to cover their electricity costs. Furthermore, it argues that AI companies should be offered incentives to lower their power usage at times of peak grid stress.

Some of the best practices that the ChatGPT developer is prompting are already being adopted by other industry players. Google, for example, today pledged to fully cover the electricity costs of a new $17 billion data center that it plans to build in Wyoming. It will also finance related grid upgrades. Anthropic PBC made a similar commitment in February.

#5624. NAR President Kevin Brown warns of outside forces threatening real estate marketplace

Outgoing NAR President Kevin Brown defended the MLS model as central to transparency and competition while warning that outside interests could seek more control of the marketplace. He also addressed NAR reforms, legislative priorities and member accountability ahead of a leadership transition.  AI Summary

As his term as president of the National Association of Realtors (NAR) comes to a close, Kevin Brown is warning real estate professionals that outside forces seeking greater control of the industry could threaten the transparency and competition that are the backbone of the current real estate marketplace.

In remarks prepared for NAR NXT in New Orleans this week, Brown drew parallels between the forces that contributed to the 2008 housing crisis and those he believes are now attempting to reshape how real estate is bought and sold.

“Today, outside forces have once again entered our industry, and this time around it is our marketplace instead of our financial system, motivated by profits, control and market share,” Brown said.

He did not identify the companies or organizations he was referring to, but his comments come as the industry debates the future of listing distribution, broker control of listing data and the role of multiple listing services (MLSs).

Brown said he believes the MLS system remains essential to maintaining competition and giving buyers and sellers access to comprehensive property information.

“America is home to the fairest, most accessible and transparent real estate market in the world,” Brown said. “That is because of a pro-competitive foundation that provides the broadest, most reliable view of the market, anchored in the MLS system.”

Perhaps in a nod to the increase in private listings, he emphasized that consumer choice depends not only on the ability to make decisions but also on access to the information needed to make them.

“A fair and transparent marketplace gives homebuyers and sellers both choice and clarity — the freedom to choose and the information to understand the consequences of that choice,” he said.

According to Brown, NAR is working with MLSs, associations and industry leaders to address marketplace concerns while advocating for the MLS system in Washington.

He also urged members to take a more active role in defending the existing marketplace. “Be prepared to support and defend a marketplace that doesn’t just benefit a select few, but a marketplace that serves us all — the consumer, the industry and Realtors,” Brown said.

When it comes to the association, Brown acknowledged shortcomings. “If NAR wants to lead change, we must be willing to change ourselves,” Brown said. “We cannot wait for outside forces to set our agenda or determine our direction.”

Brown pointed to organizational changes this year, including staff reductions, streamlined governance and a renewed focus on member services. These changes are part of NAR’s three-year strategic plan, which focuses on rebuilding the member experience and modernizing the association.

“That is why we have rightsized our staff, streamlined our governance structure and sharpened our focus,” he said. “But the real test is not whether we created a plan. It is whether that plan helps you get to your next transaction, better serve your clients and move our industry forward.”

Brown also strongly addressed criticism of NAR, acknowledging the association’s shortcomings while challenging critics to provide accurate information. “Accountability starts with being honest about where NAR has fallen short, what must change and whether we are delivering value for you,” Brown said.

But Brown also took aim at what he characterized as sensationalized coverage of the association. “For some, reporting on NAR’s progress is not a profitable story. Sensationalism sells,” Brown said. “We are not interested in fueling miscommunication and half-truths to boost views, profits or egos.”

Brown maintained that criticism is necessary but said it must be grounded in facts. “We respect our critics,” he said. “Honest criticism makes us better and helps hold us accountable.”

Brown also highlighted NAR’s legislative efforts, including passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act.

“It took Realtors to get it across the finish line,” Brown said. He also pointed to efforts to modernize credit scoring and help delinquent veteran homeowners avoid foreclosure.

As Brown prepares to hand over the presidency to Florida’s Christine Hansen, he acknowledged that the association still has work to do. “NAR is not perfect and our work is not finished,” he said.

And while he warns that criticism of the association should be based on facts, he insists that members continue to hold NAR accountable. “Keep asking us the hard questions,” Brown said. “Keep holding us responsible for clear communication and meaningful results.”

#5623. 10 states with kindergarten vaccination rates below 90% in CDC data

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Kindergarten measles vaccination rates, plus one all-vaccines figure, sat below 90% in these 10 states in CDC data for 2025-26, with Idaho lowest at 75.2%

Kindergarten measles vaccination rates in the CDC's 2025-26 state table run from 75.2% in Idaho to 98.9% in West Virginia. That 23.7-point spread separates the lowest and highest figures the agency lists for the school year.

The CDC table covers about 50 jurisdictions. Kansas and Montana show no data for 2025-26. They cannot be placed in the order used here. This selection covers 10 reporting states with figures under 90%. All 10 fall in the CDC's "Less than 90%" category. Several other states land in the agency's "95%+" category.

The slides run from the lowest percentage to the highest within this group. Idaho comes first at 75.2%. Wisconsin follows at 85.1%, a 9.9-point gap from Idaho. North Dakota closes the selection at 88.5%, 13.3 points above Idaho. The other seven states — Minnesota, Utah, Arizona, Colorado, Oklahoma, Ohio and New Hampshire — range from 85.7% to 88.2%.

Three more states sit just outside this group. Florida and Iowa each reported 88.9%. Georgia reported 89.1%. Those figures are also under 90%. This article is a selection of 10 states with low rates, not a full list of every state below that line.

The CDC lists each state's rate alongside a count and a second percentage. The count appears to show how many kindergartners were assessed. The second percentage appears to show how complete the reporting was. The slides treat both readings with that caution.

States also collected their numbers in different ways. Six states in this selection used a census. Wisconsin, Arizona, Oklahoma and Ohio used a census for public schools and voluntary response for private schools.

New Hampshire needs a separate note. The state did not assess coverage for individual vaccines. Its 88.2% is the share of kindergartners who received all doses of all vaccines required for school entry. It is not a measles-specific figure.

The table does not explain why any state's rate is low. It carries no exemption data, no outbreak data and no policy details.

Idaho reported a kindergarten measles vaccination rate of 75.2% for the 2025-26 school year. No reporting state posted a lower figure in the kindergarten coverage table from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

That rate leaves 24.8% of Idaho kindergartners outside the share the CDC recorded as covered.

Idaho is also the only reporting state in the table with a rate below 80%. Every other state that supplied data cleared that mark.

The CDC lists Idaho's survey method as a census. The entry shows no separate approach for private schools. Several other states in the table pair a public-school census with voluntary response from private schools. Idaho's entry names a census alone.

The table pairs Idaho's rate with a count of 21,728. If that count reflects the kindergartners assessed, the 75.2% figure describes a group of that size. The column label was not confirmed, so the number is described here only as the count the CDC lists beside the rate.

The entry also shows a second percentage of 100%. If that column measures how complete the reporting was, Idaho's figure would rest on full reporting rather than a partial return. That reading is also unconfirmed.

Wisconsin's kindergarten measles vaccination rate was 85.1% in the 2025-26 school year, according to CDC data. Among the states that reported figures, only Idaho posted a lower rate.

That leaves Wisconsin 4.9 percentage points short of 90%. It sits in the CDC's "Less than 90%" category.

Minnesota, the next state up the table, reported 85.7%. The two states are 0.6 points apart.

The CDC lists a count of 59,360 next to Wisconsin's rate. It also shows a second percentage of 96.6% for the state. The table used for this article does not label either number.

Wisconsin's figure combines two collection approaches. Public schools were covered by a census. Private schools supplied data through voluntary response.

Minnesota reported a kindergarten measles vaccination rate of 85.7% for the 2025-26 school year, according to CDC data. That is the third-lowest figure among the states that reported numbers for the year.

The remaining 14.3% of the state's kindergartners fall outside that coverage figure. Minnesota's rate is 4.3 percentage points below 90%, the upper edge of the CDC's "Less than 90%" category. It is 9.3 points short of the agency's "95%+" category.

Minnesota sits close to its neighbor Wisconsin in the table, 0.6 points higher. Idaho, the lowest state in the table, is 10.5 points below Minnesota. West Virginia, the highest state in the table, is 13.2 points above it.

The CDC lists a count of 63,451 alongside Minnesota's rate. That figure most likely reflects the number of kindergartners assessed.

Minnesota's count is the third-largest among the 10 states in this selection. Only Ohio, at 129,087, and Arizona, at 73,907, list higher counts. Wisconsin's count is 59,360, about 4,100 smaller than Minnesota's.

The table also gives Minnesota a second percentage of 99.9%. That figure appears to describe how complete the state's reporting was. Four states in this selection — Idaho, Utah, Colorado and New Hampshire — list 100%. If that reading holds, Minnesota's 85.7% rate rests on records from nearly every kindergartner the state counted.

The CDC lists Minnesota's survey method as a census. Its entry does not include the voluntary response from private schools that appears in some other states' entries.

The statewide figure does not show how coverage varies within Minnesota. Clearwater County has the lowest overall measles vaccination rate of any county in the state, according to tucson.com. Neighboring Wadena County has the second-lowest.

In Clearwater County, many children are recorded as partially vaccinated. They lack one of the two doses. They also have no exemption on file. That pattern ties the county's low rate to incomplete dose series rather than to recorded exemptions.

Utah reported measles vaccination coverage of 87.2% among kindergartners in the 2025-26 school year, according to CDC data. That figure places the state in the CDC's "Less than 90%" category.

Utah's rate falls 2.8 percentage points short of the 90% line. Among the states that reported data for the year, only Idaho, Wisconsin and Minnesota posted lower rates. Minnesota, the next state down, sits 1.5 points below Utah.

Utah's figure sits 11.7 points below West Virginia's, the highest in the CDC table. It is 12 points above Idaho's, the lowest. The two gaps are close to equal. Utah sits near the midpoint between the table's highest and lowest rates.

The CDC lists a count of 44,001 next to Utah's rate. That number most likely reflects how many kindergartners were assessed, though the column heading is not confirmed.

A second percentage in Utah's row reads 100%. That figure appears to measure how complete the state's reporting was. If it does, Utah's rate rests on a full set of returns rather than a partial one.

Utah gathered its numbers through a census of kindergartners. That approach differs from the mixed method some states used, which pairs a census of public schools with voluntary responses from private schools. Under a census with full reporting, Utah's rate does not depend on which private schools chose to respond.

Utah requires each child enrolled in kindergarten to receive specific immunizations, including a two-dose series of the MMR vaccine, according to The Salt Lake Tribune.

The CDC table does not explain how Utah's coverage relates to that state requirement. It offers no breakdown of kindergartners by number of doses received. It also carries no exemption counts for the state.

Arizona's kindergarten measles vaccination coverage stood at 87.4% in the 2025-26 school year, according to CDC data. Among the states that reported a figure, that is the fifth-lowest rate in the agency's table.

That figure places Arizona in the CDC's "Less than 90%" category, 2.6 percentage points under the line. Utah sits just below Arizona at 87.2%. Colorado sits just above it at 87.7%. Fractions of a point separate the three states.

Arizona collected its numbers in two ways. Public schools were covered by a census. Private schools took part through voluntary response. Under that approach, private-school data come only from the schools that chose to submit them.

The CDC lists a count of 73,907 next to Arizona's rate. The table excerpt does not label that column, though it most likely reflects the number of kindergartners assessed. Among the 10 states here, only Ohio shows a larger count. If that reading holds, Arizona's rate draws on one of the bigger groups of children in this selection.

A second percentage of 92.5% also appears in Arizona's row. That column likely measures how complete the state's reporting was, but the label is not confirmed. Oklahoma is the only state in this group with a lower figure there. Oklahoma used the same mix of a public-school census and private-school voluntary response. The table does not say whether the method and the lower figure are connected.

At the other end of the table, Arizona trails West Virginia, the state with the highest reported rate, by 11.5 percentage points.

Colorado's kindergarten measles vaccination rate stood at 87.7% in the 2025-26 school year, according to CDC data. That places the state sixth in this 10-state selection, which runs from the lowest rate to the highest.

The figure falls in the CDC's "Less than 90%" coverage category. Colorado sits 2.3 percentage points below the 90% line that marks the top of that group.

Colorado belongs to a tight cluster near the middle of the selection. Arizona, one place lower, reported 87.4%. Oklahoma, one place higher, reported 87.8%. Only 0.4 points separate those three states. Margins that narrow decide their order in the table.

Colorado's rate is 12.5 points above Idaho's, the lowest figure in the table. It is 11.2 points below West Virginia's, the highest. On those two measures, Colorado sits slightly closer to the top of the table than to its lowest point.

Colorado collected its figures through a census of kindergartners. It did not pair that census with voluntary responses from private schools, as some other states in this selection did.

The CDC lists a count of 60,049 next to Colorado's rate. The source material does not label that column. The number may reflect how many kindergartners were assessed, but that reading is not confirmed.

Colorado's second listed percentage is 100%. That column's label is also missing from the source material. It may describe how complete the state's reporting was. Idaho and Utah, which also used a census, show the same 100% in that column.

Oklahoma's kindergarten measles coverage stood at 87.8% in the 2025-26 school year, based on CDC data. That figure puts the state seventh in this selection of 10 states with low rates, counting from the lowest.

The rate falls in the CDC's "Less than 90%" coverage category. It is 2.2 percentage points below the 90% line that caps that group.

Oklahoma sits in a tight cluster of nearby states. Colorado reported 87.7%, just 0.1 point lower. Ohio reported 88.1%, 0.3 point higher. Arizona, at 87.4%, and Utah, at 87.2%, also fall within one point of Oklahoma's rate. Taken together, the five states span just 0.9 point, from Utah's 87.2% to Ohio's 88.1%.

The CDC lists a count of 47,844 alongside Oklahoma's rate. The table's column headers were not part of the material reviewed for this article. The number most likely reflects the kindergartners assessed, but that label is not confirmed. Oklahoma's count is larger than Utah's 44,001 and smaller than Colorado's 60,049.

Oklahoma gathered its data through a mixed approach. Public schools were covered by a census, while private schools took part through voluntary response. A census reaches every school in a group. Voluntary response includes only the schools that chose to report.

The CDC table also pairs Oklahoma's rate with a second percentage of 90.7%. That figure most likely describes how complete the state's reporting was, but the label is not confirmed.

Oklahoma's 90.7% is the lowest second percentage among the 10 states in this selection. Arizona, the next lowest, shows 92.5%, which is 1.8 points higher. Idaho, Utah, Colorado and New Hampshire each show 100% in that column. Minnesota, at 99.9%, falls just short of that mark.

Four states in this selection combined a public-school census with private-school voluntary response. Wisconsin, Ohio, Arizona and Oklahoma all show second percentages below 97%. Oklahoma's figure is the lowest of those four.

Ohio reported a kindergarten measles vaccination rate of 88.1% for the 2025-26 school year, according to CDC data. The figure sits 1.9 percentage points under 90%. That places Ohio in the CDC's "Less than 90%" category.

Ohio is eighth among the 10 states in this selection, which runs from the lowest rate to the highest. Oklahoma, at 87.8%, sits just below it. New Hampshire's 88.2% sits just above it, though that figure covers all required school-entry vaccines rather than measles alone. Among the measles-specific figures in this group, the next one above Ohio's is North Dakota's 88.5%.

Ohio's rate is 12.9 points higher than Idaho's 75.2%, the lowest in the CDC table. It is 10.8 points below West Virginia's 98.9%, the highest. Measured in points, Ohio sits closer to the top of the table than to the bottom. Florida reported 88.9% and falls just outside this selection, 0.8 points above Ohio.

The CDC lists a count of 129,087 alongside Ohio's rate. The column label for that number is not confirmed, though it most likely reflects kindergartners assessed. It is the largest count among the 10 states here.

Arizona's 73,907 is the next-largest count, 55,180 lower than Ohio's. North Dakota's 9,344 is the smallest in the group. Ohio's count is nearly 14 times that figure. If the count does reflect kindergartners assessed, each percentage point of Ohio's rate covers far more children than the same point in a smaller state.

Ohio's row also shows a second percentage of 95.9%. That number most likely describes how complete the state's reporting was. The CDC table does not confirm that label either. Each state in this selection that paired a public-school census with voluntary private-school response shows a second percentage below 100%.

Ohio collected its figures through a census of public schools and voluntary response from private schools. Under that approach, private-school results depend on which schools chose to respond.

The CDC data does not give reasons for Ohio's rate.

In the 2025-26 school year, 88.2% of New Hampshire's kindergartners had received all doses of every vaccine required for school entry, according to CDC data. The state did not assess coverage for individual vaccines. That makes the number broader than a measles rate.

New Hampshire's number measures something different from the other nine states in this selection. Each of those states reported a measles figure. New Hampshire's figure counts only children who were fully up to date on the whole school-entry schedule. A kindergartner missing a single required dose of any required vaccine falls outside the 88.2%.

That difference limits what the number can show. It does not reveal how many New Hampshire kindergartners had measles vaccination specifically. It also does not show which vaccines or doses the remaining children lacked. A gap in one required vaccine registers the same way as gaps in several.

The figure is also not a direct match for its neighbors in this list. The CDC places New Hampshire in its "Less than 90%" category. Its 88.2% sits 1.8 percentage points below that line. In this selection, it falls between Ohio at 88.1% and North Dakota at 88.5%. Both of those states reported measles figures. The order at this point sets two kinds of measurement side by side.

The CDC lists a count of 11,544 next to New Hampshire's rate. Among these 10 states, only North Dakota's 9,344 is smaller. A second percentage in the same row reads 100%. If that column reflects reporting completeness, New Hampshire's figure would rest on full reporting. The state gathered its data through a census, rather than relying on voluntary responses from any group of schools.

New Hampshire's rules call for proof of immunization to come in an authenticated written form. That rule concerns the documentation behind school-entry vaccination. The CDC table does not say how those records shaped the state's 88.2%.

North Dakota's kindergarten measles vaccination rate was 88.5% in the 2025-26 school year, according to CDC data. That is the highest figure among the 10 states in this selection. It still sits in the CDC's "Less than 90%" category.

In other words, more than one in 10 North Dakota kindergartners were not counted as vaccinated against measles in the CDC's figures.

The state's rate is 1.5 percentage points short of the 90% line. It trails West Virginia, the top state in the CDC table, by 10.4 points.

North Dakota is also 0.4 points behind Florida and Iowa. Those two states tie just outside this selection. The line between this group of 10 and the states next to it comes down to fractions of a percentage point.

The CDC lists a count of 9,344 next to North Dakota's rate. That is the smallest count among the 10 states covered here. New Hampshire has the next smallest, at 11,544. The table does not label that column, so the count's exact meaning is not confirmed.

North Dakota's row also shows a second percentage of 98.6%. That column is unlabeled as well.

North Dakota gathered its figures through a census, according to the CDC table. It did not combine a public-school census with voluntary responses from private schools, as four other states in this selection did.

#5621. Measles symptoms day by day: what the first 2 weeks look like

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Measles symptoms day by day, from silent incubation and cold-like fever to Koplik spots, the spreading rash and the contagious window, with CDC guidance on when to seek care

Measles can spread before anyone knows it is there. A person who catches the virus usually feels fine for one to two weeks. When illness does begin, it looks like an ordinary cold: a fever, a cough, a runny nose and red, watery eyes. The rash that most people picture when they hear the word measles arrives days later. By then, the infected person has already been able to pass the virus to others.

That gap between what people expect and how the disease unfolds is the reason a clear timeline matters. Knowing measles symptoms day by day helps a parent, a teacher or a traveler match what they are seeing to a stage of the illness. It also explains why public-health agencies ask people to call ahead before walking into a clinic with a suspected case.

Two clocks run through the course of measles, and they are easy to confuse. The first counts days since exposure — the moment someone shared air with an infected person. The second counts days since the first symptom appeared. Both matter. The exposure clock measures the incubation period and helps trace where an infection came from. The symptom clock tracks the illness itself, from the first fever through the rash and recovery. Each slide in this guide says which clock it is using. That lets a reader place any single stage without reading the rest.

The 10 slides follow measles in order. They start with how the virus travels through the air and the quiet days of incubation. They move through the cold-like early phase, the small white spots that can appear inside the mouth and the rash that begins at the hairline. Later slides cover the window when a person is contagious, the complications that can follow and the signs that call for urgent medical care.

The guide closes with prevention. The MMR vaccine protects against measles, and some protection is still possible shortly after exposure. The figures cited throughout come from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the World Health Organization. This is a stage-by-stage walkthrough of one illness, not a ranked list.

Measles spreads when an infected person coughs or sneezes and releases the virus into the air. The virus can stay in that air, and on nearby surfaces, for up to two hours after the infected person has left the room.

Face-to-face contact with a sick person is not required. Walking into a waiting room, a classroom or a store aisle shortly after an infected person has passed through can be enough. Exposure can be as brief as sharing a room.

Measles is highly contagious. About nine in 10 susceptible people who are close to an infected person will catch it, according to the CDC. Susceptible here means a person who is not immune. That is someone who has not been vaccinated and has not had measles before.

The cause is the measles virus, a member of the paramyxovirus family. Humans are its only natural host. The virus enters through the nose, mouth or eyes and first takes hold in the airways. Touching a contaminated surface and then touching the face is another route to infection.

On the first of two clocks, the count of days since exposure, the moment of exposure is day zero. The exposed person feels nothing. There is no sore throat, no fever and no sign that anything has changed. Many people never know the exact moment they were exposed.

That gap makes measles hard to contain. The person spreading the virus may not look seriously ill. An infected person may still be going to work, school or a clinic. The people around them have no reason to take precautions.

Public health agencies trace measles exposures by place and time for this reason. When a case is confirmed, officials work backward to identify where the infected person spent time. That includes shared indoor spaces where the virus may have lingered after the person left. Anyone who was in those spaces during that window may be told to watch for symptoms over the following weeks.

Counting from the day of exposure, measles usually takes seven to 14 days to produce its first symptom. The full reported range stretches to 21 days. Throughout this measles incubation period, the infected person feels well and shows no outward sign of illness.

The count here runs on the exposure clock. Day zero is the day a person shared air or space with someone who had measles. Every later day in this stretch is counted forward from that point. There is no symptom yet to count from.

The silent stretch is what makes measles hard to trace. A person who falls ill may have to think back one to three weeks to find where the infection came from. By then, a brief encounter in a waiting room, a shop or an airport gate may be forgotten. The person who passed on the virus may also have moved on without realizing they had measles.

That is why the exposure date is the most useful piece of information in this phase. A school, clinic or health department may report a possible exposure at a specific place and time. That date then becomes the starting line. Knowing it lets a person and their doctor work out when symptoms would most likely appear. It also shows when the risk of illness from that exposure has passed.

The wide range matters for planning. A person who reaches day 14 without symptoms has not yet cleared the full reported window. Illness can still begin in the third week after exposure. The reported range ends at day 21.

Feeling well during these days is not proof of having escaped infection. It is not proof of having caught it either. Nothing a person notices on their own separates someone who is incubating the virus from someone who was exposed and stayed healthy. The window in which a person can spread measles is counted from the rash, not from the exposure date. It does not cover the early days after exposure.

Measles symptoms usually begin about seven to 14 days after a person is exposed to the virus, according to the CDC. The rash typically appears around 14 days after exposure, within a reported range of seven to 21 days.

This stage sits where two clocks meet. Days since exposure count from the day an unprotected person shared space with someone carrying the virus. Days since the first symptom count from the start of the illness itself. Here the timeline switches from the first clock to the second, as a silent infection becomes a noticeable illness.

The exposure clock is the one a household can use in advance. Someone who knows the date they were near an infected person can count forward from it. The first signs most often fall somewhere in the second week after that contact.

The outer limits matter as much as the typical figures. The rash can appear as late as 21 days after exposure. That stretches the full watch period to three weeks. A person who feels fine on day 10 after exposure has not yet cleared that window.

Measles does not begin with spots. The illness opens with fever and respiratory symptoms. The rash comes later. Anyone waiting for a rash as the first clue will miss the start of the illness. By the time the skin changes, the person has usually been sick for several days.

Once the first symptom appears, the count restarts. From that point on, clinicians describe the illness in days since symptom onset rather than days since exposure. Each later stage — the mouth spots, the rash and its spread down the body — is timed against that second clock.

An exposure date is not always known. Measles can be caught in a shared indoor space from someone who was never identified as sick. Some patients therefore have no exposure date to count from. In those cases, the symptom clock is the only one available. The first day of symptoms becomes day one of the timeline.

Measles begins with a phase doctors call the prodrome, which brings fever, cough, a runny nose and red, watery eyes. These signs start on day one of illness, counted from the first symptom, and arrive before any rash.

Each of the respiratory and eye symptoms has a clinical name. A runny nose is coryza. Red, watery eyes are conjunctivitis, an inflammation of the thin membrane that covers the white of the eye and lines the eyelids. Together with cough, these make up the "three Cs," a shorthand common in clinical teaching about measles.

Fever is part of the picture from the start. It can run high in measles, and it often keeps rising over the following days rather than settling. A high temperature together with the three Cs is the pattern that points clinicians toward measles in this early stage.

The cough is usually dry and persistent. The irritated eyes can make bright light uncomfortable, a symptom known as photophobia.

The difficulty is that these symptoms look like a bad cold or the flu. A parent or patient seeing a temperature, a cough and a runny nose has little reason to think of measles. The distinguishing marks of the illness — spots inside the mouth and then the skin rash — have not shown up yet. That is why measles is easy to miss at this stage.

Circumstances around the illness change how these symptoms are read. A recent known exposure, travel to a place where measles is circulating or an incomplete vaccination record all make measles more likely. Telling a clinician about any of these gives them a reason to consider the diagnosis before the rash appears.

The person can already pass the virus to others during these cold-like days. Close contacts without immunity, such as unvaccinated household members, are the people most at risk.

The prodrome is the stage where measles is hardest to recognize. A clinician who suspects measles at this point can order laboratory tests, such as a swab from the throat or nose, to confirm the diagnosis.

Koplik spots are tiny white spots on a red background inside the mouth, most often on the inner cheeks. Counting from the first symptom, they typically appear two to three days into the illness and one to two days before the rash.

The spots are small and easy to overlook. They are often compared to grains of salt scattered across the reddened lining of the cheek. They usually sit on the inner cheek across from the back teeth. Seeing them there takes a light and a deliberate look.

The sign is named after Henry Koplik, a New York pediatrician who described the spots in the 1890s. His description gave doctors a way to recognize measles before its best-known feature, the rash, had appeared.

That timing is what makes the spots useful. In the first days of illness, measles looks much like a heavy cold or flu. Nothing on the skin points toward a specific diagnosis yet. Koplik spots are linked to measles itself rather than to respiratory infections in general. Clinicians treat them as one of the few early clues that set measles apart from other common illnesses.

An early clue matters for more than the patient. A person with measles can already spread the virus before the rash appears. Recognizing the infection a day or two sooner gives a household or clinic more time to limit contact with others.

The spots do not appear in every case. Some people with measles never develop them. In others, the spots are faint or short-lived and go unnoticed. Their absence does not rule measles out. A doctor weighing a possible case looks at the full picture. That includes the exposure history, the pattern of early symptoms and, when needed, laboratory testing.

The spots also tend to fade around the time the rash takes hold on the face. That leaves only a short window to see them. A parent who notices white specks inside a sick child's cheek can mention them when phoning a doctor. The detail can point toward measles even before any rash shows on the skin.

The measles rash typically shows up three to five days after the first symptoms. It begins as flat red spots along the hairline and across the face, often including the area behind the ears.

This slide follows the symptom clock, which counts from the first day of illness. By the time the rash appears, a person has usually had several days of fever, cough, runny nose and red eyes. In measles, the rash is not the first sign of illness. It arrives after the cold-like phase is already underway.

The first spots are flat. Clinicians call flat, discolored skin spots macules. Small raised bumps, called papules, may then form on top of the flat areas. The combined pattern is known as a maculopapular rash. The term describes a mix of flat and raised spots, not blisters or fluid-filled bumps.

That difference helps separate measles from chickenpox. A chickenpox rash forms itchy blisters filled with fluid that later crust over. A measles rash does not turn into blisters. It remains a pattern of flat and slightly raised red spots.

As more spots appear, they can run together. Neighboring patches merge into larger red areas, and the skin may look blotchy rather than dotted. The medical word for spots that join this way is confluent.

On darker skin, the redness can be harder to see. The spots may look darker than the surrounding skin rather than bright red. In that case, the rash's location and pattern are more useful clues than its color.

The person is usually still feverish and unwell when the rash appears. A new facial rash does not signal that the illness is ending.

For many households, the rash is the point at which measles first becomes a likely explanation. The days before it can look like a bad cold or flu.

A rash alone does not confirm measles. Doctors typically confirm a suspected case with laboratory testing. That can mean a swab from the throat or nose, or a blood test that looks for antibodies to the virus.

The rash's arrival also gives clinicians a fixed reference date. Guidance on how long a person can spread measles is counted from the day the rash appears. Recording that date, along with the date the fever began, helps a doctor place the illness on the timeline.

After it starts at the face and hairline, the measles rash moves downward to the neck, the trunk, the arms, the legs and finally the feet. Fever often reaches its highest point while this spread is under way.

This slide uses the clock that counts from the day the rash first appears. On the other clock, which counts from the first symptom, this stage falls a few days into the illness, after the cough and fever have already set in. The downward spread happens in the days that follow the rash's first appearance at the hairline.

The rash does not appear everywhere at once, and it does not begin on the hands or feet. It travels in one direction, from head to toe. That ordered progression is one of the features clinicians look for when they examine a patient with a fever and a rash.

The fever can climb high during this stretch. CDC notes that a person's fever may rise above 104°F (40°C) once the rash appears.

The rash does not replace the earlier symptoms. The cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes that began before the rash typically continue while it spreads. A person at this stage may have a high fever, a cough and a rash covering much of the body at the same time.

The rash also leaves in order. It fades first from the head and face, then from the trunk, and last from the arms, legs and feet. The time this takes varies from person to person. What stays consistent is the sequence: the first areas to show the rash are the first to clear.

For families tracking an illness at home, the pattern offers a way to place the day. A rash on the face alone points to the early part of this stage. A rash that has reached the feet while the face is clearing points to the later part.

A person with measles can pass the virus to others from four days before the rash appears until four days after it, according to the CDC. This slide counts days from the rash, not from exposure or from the first symptom.

Anchoring the count to the rash gives families and clinicians a fixed reference point. The rash is the most visible sign of measles. Fever and a cough can build gradually, and people often cannot say which day they began. The day spots first appear at the hairline or on the face is usually easier to pin down.

Counting the day the rash appears, the window covers about nine days. Four of those days come before anyone has seen a single spot.

That front end of the window is what makes measles hard to contain. During those four days, the person typically has only the cold-like symptoms of the early phase. Nothing at that point clearly signals measles. A child may still go to school or day care. An adult may still go to work, ride public transport or sit in a waiting room. Each of those settings lets the virus reach other people before the illness has a name.

The back end of the window matters for a different reason. Once the rash is visible, measles is easier to recognize. The household can then take steps to limit contact with others. Isolation guidance follows from the same window, with the fourth day after the rash appeared marking its end point. Local health authorities set the specific rules where a person lives.

The window also explains why a confirmed case prompts questions about the days before anyone suspected measles. Places the person visited during the four days before the rash count as possible exposure sites, as do places visited in the days after. Anyone who shared indoor space with the person during that stretch may have been exposed.

Most people with measles recover with supportive care. There is no specific antiviral treatment for measles.

Doctors instead treat the symptoms. That usually means rest, fluids and medicine to lower fever while the immune system clears the virus.

This stage sits at the far end of the clock that counts days since the first symptom. It covers the period as the rash fades and the weeks that follow. One complication described below can surface years later. Recovery is the usual outcome, but measles can also cause complications, and some leave lasting harm.

Ear infections are among the more common problems. About one in 10 children with measles gets an ear infection, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Some of those infections cause permanent hearing loss.

Diarrhea is another common complication. It is reported in fewer than one in 10 people with measles, according to the CDC. The agency lists it alongside ear infections as the two common complications of measles.

Pneumonia is a more serious risk. Up to one in 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, according to the CDC. It is the most common cause of measles death in young children.

Encephalitis is rarer and more dangerous. It is a swelling of the brain. About one child in 1,000 with measles develops it, according to the CDC. The agency notes that it can lead to convulsions and can leave a child deaf or with an intellectual disability.

Measles can also be fatal. The CDC estimates that roughly one to three in every 1,000 children in the U.S. who get measles die.

A separate threat can surface long after the illness ends. Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, or SSPE, is a rare brain disease that is fatal. It can appear years after measles, even in someone who seemed to recover fully from the original infection.

The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends vitamin A for children with measles. It is a recommended part of care, not a cure for the infection.

Anyone who suspects measles should phone a doctor's office, clinic or emergency room before going in. The call gives staff time to keep other patients from being exposed to the virus.

That advice holds at any point on either clock, whether counted from exposure or from the first symptom. It applies to someone who has just learned of an exposure. It also applies to someone already several days into fever and rash. Clinic waiting rooms can hold babies too young for the vaccine and people with weakened immune systems. A short call lets staff arrange a separate entrance, a set arrival time or a direct route to a private room.

Certain symptoms call for urgent care rather than a routine appointment. Trouble breathing, a stiff neck, seizures, confusion and a fever that will not come down are all reasons to get help quickly. Breathing trouble can be a sign of pneumonia, one of the more serious complications of measles. A stiff neck, seizures or confusion can signal that the infection is affecting the brain. Even in an emergency, telling the hospital or the dispatcher that measles is suspected helps staff prepare.

Prevention centers on the MMR vaccine, which protects against measles, mumps and rubella in a single shot. CDC puts the effectiveness of two doses at about 97% against measles. One dose is about 93% effective, according to CDC.

CDC recommends that children get the first dose at 12 to 15 months of age. The second dose follows at four to six years. Adults who are unsure whether they were vaccinated as children can ask a doctor to check their records.

The vaccine can also help after someone has already been exposed. An MMR dose given within 72 hours of exposure may help protect a person who is not vaccinated. That window is short. An unvaccinated person who learns of an exposure should contact a doctor or the local health department right away.

Immune globulin offers a second option with a longer window. This antibody preparation can be given within six days of exposure for some high-risk people. It is a separate treatment from the vaccine, and a doctor decides who should receive it.

Elizabeth Warren is expected to chair the Senate banking committee in January after Democrats flipped Congress. The role would expand her investigative authority and could increase scrutiny of banks, lenders, private equity and crypto, alongside oversight of CFPB changes.   AI Summary

Sen. Elizabeth Warren is expected to become chair of the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs when Democrats take control of Congress in January, giving the Massachusetts Democrat expanded authority to investigate financial institutions and advance legislation affecting the sector.

The move is expected as a result of this week’s midterm elections, which saw both the Senate and House of Representatives flip from Republican to Democratic majorities.

Several outlets, including The Wall Street Journal and Reuters, anticipate that Warren is lined up for the role, even though other senators could theoretically rank ahead of her for the chairmanship.

The transition would give Warren, who is currently a ranking member of the legislative committee, more staff and subpoena powers, potentially increasing scrutiny of major banks, consumer lenders, private equity firms and cryptocurrency companies.

Warren, who would replace current Chairman Tim Scott (R-S.C.), is also expected to examine the Trump administration’s mass firings of financial regulatory employees and potential conflicts of interest involving companies with ties to the president.

Warren has built her political career around financial regulation and consumer protection. A former Harvard University law professor and bankruptcy expert, she became involved in developing the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau in the wake of the great financial crisis under President Barack Obama before winning a Senate seat in 2012.

Her expected chairmanship comes as the CFPB faces significant operational challenges and restructuring under the Trump administration, a move that she has publicly criticized.

The administration, meanwhile, has argued that the CFPB over-regulates consumer lenders and has been used to target political opponents and disfavored industries, going so far as to scale back enforcements this year.

The CFPB has undergone a leadership shuffle as a result of the administration’s efforts to scale back the agency’s power. In September, the committee advanced the nomination of Brian Johnson, Trump’s newest nominee to become director of the bureau, a move that Warren opposed.

#5619. Five9 buys contact center intelligence startup Level AI after posting narrow earnings beat

Contact center company Five9 Inc. flexed its acquisitive muscles today as it announced a $325 million all-cash deal to buy an artificial intelligence-native rival called Level AI as it posted its third-quarter financial results.

The deal is expected to close in the fourth quarter, subject to customary closing conditions. Five9 is a leading player in the cloud contact center software industry, selling tools and services that enterprises use to manage their customer service interactions. Its web-based software spans traditional phone calls, video calls, emails, messaging, social media and other channels.

As for Level AI, it’s the developer of a contact center and customer experience intelligence platform that uses artificial intelligence to support human agents on calls and analyze, score and augment their interactions with the callers they serve. Its platform is designed to listen into customer service agent’s calls, so it can provide real-time guidance throughout and support workflow automation. The insights it generates can also be used to assist in agent coaching.

Level AI also develops autonomous AI agents that can automate some simpler customer inquiries and background operational tasks, freeing up human agents to focus on more complex customer issues. “Level AI’s AI applications help organizations improve agent performance, automate more customer interactions across voice and digital channels, and turn conversations into insights the whole organization can use,” Five9 said in a blog post announcing the deal. “Its applications are in production with enterprise customers today and handle more than 1 billion customer interactions a year.”

Five9 said it intends to continue offering Level AI’s applications as standalone tools for organizations that don’t want to shift their on-premises contact center operations to the cloud, also those who are using other cloud contact center platforms. However, it also plans to integrate the startup’s tools with its Genius CX Platform.

“As AI reshapes the customer experience landscape, we believe adding Level AI strengthens our competitive position, expands the customers we can serve, and deepens the AI talent behind our continuous innovation,” said Five9 Chief Executive Amit Mathradas.

Level AI founder and CEO Ashish Nagar said that by joining Five9, his company will be able to bring its applications and customer service-native AI models to thousands of new contact centers around the world, while allowing it to continue supporting its existing customers.

Investors don’t seem to have shared the CEOs’ enthusiasm for the deal, however, for Five9’s stock fell more than 23% in late trading after the deal was announced. That may be because of the cost of the acquisition. The $325 million cash outlay amounts to almost half of Five9’s current cash and marketable investments, which stood at $738 million at the end of the third quarter.

Five9’s results weren’t too bad. The company reported adjusted earnings of 82 cents per share on revenue of $323.3 million, surpassing Wall Street’s guidance of 80 cents per share in earnings and $318.3 million in sales. But it’s notable that the company’s full-year guidance excludes any contributions from the pending deal, and so its value hinges on Five9’s ability to rapidly integrate Level AI’s technology.

For the current quarter, Five9 said it’s expecting earnings of between 88 and 92 cents per share on sales of $328 million to $334 million. But that guidance was mixed. Wall Street is looking for significantly higher earnings of 99 cents per share and $330.7 million in revenue.

For the full year, Five9 said it’s looking for earnings of $3.17 to $3.21 per share on total sales of $1.27 billion. Wall Street wants to see higher earnings of $3.26 per share on similar revenue.

#5616. Autonomous combat drone maker Shield AI buys radar startup Echodyne for $5.3B

Defense technology startup Shield AI Inc. said today it has agreed to buy the Bill Gates-backed radar startup Echodyne Inc. in a deal valued at $5.3 billion.

The acquisition is intended to enhance Shield’s autonomous drone warfighting capabilities, it said.

Echodyne is a 13-year-old startup that’s best known for its Metamaterials Electronically Scanned Array or MESA technology, which is basically just a fancy name for its next-generation solid-state radar systems that can be integrated with a wide range of weapons and monitoring systems. The technology is designed to detect much smaller targets than traditional radar, including the kinds of compact autonomous drones that have terrorized soldiers on the battlefields of Ukraine and in other modern conflicts.

The deal comes just a couple of months after Echodyne landed a $250 million contract with the U.S. Defense Department’s counter-drone task force JIATF-401, which will see it provide drone tracking technology to the U.S. military.

Echodyne’s advanced radar systems look like a natural fit for Shield AI, which is the developer of the X-Bat and V-Bat vertical takeoff and landing systems, known as VTOL drones. Shield’s V-Bat hit the headlines in the last couple of years after assisting the U.S. Coast Guard in tracking down drug traffickers looking to bring illicit cargoes into the U.S. via speedboats, and notably participated in a number of large maritime drug busts. Shield AI is also the developer of Hivemind, an autonomous software system for piloting unmanned drones, as well as pilotless boats and spacecraft.

Shield AI Chief Executive Gary Steele said the deal will enable his company to accelerate its goal of branching into three different areas of unmanned systems. “We are building a new-generation defense technology company consisting of three fast-growing, high-margin, mutually supporting business units: autonomy software, autonomous systems and mission systems,” he said.

Echodyne co-founder and CEO Eben Frankenberg said Shield AI is a natural partner for his company because it shares the view that autonomous systems must be able to sense their environment to achieve their desired mission outcomes. “By joining Shield, we’re creating a company with the size and breadth to deliver even more value to our broad range of defense, government and commercial customers around the globe,” he insisted.

According to Steele, Echodyne will continue to operate as a standalone entity, as a separate business unit within Shield AI’s mission systems business. Frankenberg will remain with the company, where he will report to Steele as part of its senior executive team.

Echodyne is not going to layoff any staff, and nobody will be asked to relocate either, he said. In the longer term, the companies expect tighter integration of Echodyne’s radar systems with Shield AI’s drones.

The deal will see $4.8 billion paid out upon closing, with the other $500 million dependent on Echodyne meeting certain performance targets, which have not been disclosed. Shield AI said it was able to fund the deal with a combination of its own cash and a $2.5 billion cash injection that came via a Series H funding round led by Blackstone and JPMorgan Chase, which was also announced today.

Shield AI has a history of making decisive acquisitions. Its V-Bat and X-Bat drones are heavily based on technology developed by a company called Martin UAV Systems Inc. that it acquired in 2021. In June, it purchased Aechelon Technologies Inc., a developer of high-fidelity simulation and physics-based sensor modeling software, for an undisclosed price.

Steele added that the company may not be done with acquisitions, and will continue to look at making more deals in order to accelerate its growth strategy.
