#5615. Lost your vaccine card? What to know about measles immunity and MMR

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A measles booster isn't needed for adults with two documented MMR doses, but people in several groups should check their vaccine records and may need another shot

For most adults, the answer to whether they need a measles booster is no. The harder question is whether they can prove they are already protected. The shot in question is MMR, which covers measles, mumps and rubella. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention does not recommend a routine extra dose for adults with two documented MMR doses. Producing proof of measles immunity is often the sticking point.

The vaccine works well. Two doses are about 97 percent effective against measles, and one dose is about 93 percent effective, according to the CDC. The agency still recommends two doses for certain adults, including college students, health care workers and international travelers. For people in those groups, one documented dose falls short of that recommendation.

Records go missing for ordinary reasons. Childhood shot cards get lost in moves. Pediatric offices close or merge. School files stay with the school. An adult who has lived in several states or countries may have records spread across many places, or none at all. Without written proof, a clinician may suggest a blood test or another dose.

Birth year also matters. People born in the U.S. before 1957 are generally considered immune, because measles circulated widely at the time. Adults born in 1957 or later who lack evidence of immunity should get at least one dose, according to the CDC. The agency also advises revaccination for people who received the inactivated measles vaccine used from 1963 to 1967, or a vaccine of unknown type in that period.

MMR is not right for everyone. It is a live vaccine, and it is not recommended during pregnancy or for people with severely weakened immune systems. Anyone in those situations should talk with a clinician before acting on a missing record.

The 10 slides that follow are a selection, not a complete guide. Six cover specific groups, defined by birth year, vaccine history, schooling, work or travel. The other four cover practical steps. They explain where to find old vaccination records, how a blood test can show immunity, who should skip the shot and why two documented doses settle the question.

People born in the U.S. before 1957 are generally presumed immune to measles and do not need a measles booster. The CDC counts birth before 1957 as one accepted form of evidence of immunity, alongside vaccination records and laboratory results.

The cutoff reflects history rather than any medical test. Measles circulated widely in the U.S. during the years when this group was growing up. Exposure was so common that a person born before 1957 was very likely to have caught the disease as a child. A measles infection generally leaves lifelong protection. Public health guidance therefore treats that birth year as a stand-in for past illness.

No vaccine was available to this generation in early childhood. The first measles vaccines came into U.S. use in 1963, years after this group had passed infancy. Their protection, in most cases, came from the virus itself.

The presumption is practical. People in this age group may have no childhood vaccine card or record of a measles diagnosis from decades ago. Birth year spares them from having to reconstruct paperwork that may never have existed.

The 1957 line works in one direction only. Anyone born in 1957 or later cannot rely on birth year and needs a different form of evidence, such as written vaccination records.

The rule has limits. It is a general presumption, not a guarantee that every individual had measles. The CDC's guidance frames it as evidence of immunity, which is different from proof that a specific person carries antibodies. A laboratory test can confirm that directly.

The presumption also rests on measles circulating in the U.S. People born before 1957 who grew up in another country, or who are unsure about their own history, can raise the question with a clinician.

Some workplaces and institutions set their own requirements for documented immunity. Anyone in this group facing such a requirement should check what that employer or school accepts before assuming birth year alone will satisfy it.

Adults born in 1957 or later who cannot show evidence of measles immunity should get at least one dose of the MMR vaccine, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. For this group, the absence of proof is enough reason to vaccinate.

The 1957 cutoff reflects how measles spread before a vaccine existed. People born earlier in the U.S. grew up while the virus circulated widely. Adults born in 1957 or later cannot lean on that presumption of immunity. Their protection depends on vaccination or on a lab-confirmed past infection.

The CDC accepts four forms of evidence of immunity. The first is written documentation of vaccination. The second is a laboratory result showing immunity. The third is laboratory confirmation that the person had measles. The fourth is birth before 1957, which by definition does not apply to anyone in this group.

That leaves three routes for adults born in 1957 or later. Each one depends on a written record or a lab result. A memory of getting shots as a child does not appear among the CDC's accepted forms of evidence. Neither does a parent's recollection of a childhood measles case.

The one-dose recommendation is a baseline, not a ceiling. Some adults in this birth range belong to groups for which the CDC recommends two doses. Those groups include college students, health care workers and international travelers. Adults in any of them should confirm whether their situation calls for a second shot.

MMR is a combined shot. An adult who gets a dose to fill a gap in measles records also gains protection against mumps and rubella.

For many adults, the practical first step is to search for old records before booking an appointment. A clinician can review whatever turns up and decide whether a dose or a blood test makes more sense. People who are pregnant or have a severely weakened immune system should mention that at the start. MMR is a live vaccine, and it is not recommended in either situation.

Adults who received the inactivated measles vaccine used in the U.S. from 1963 to 1967 should be revaccinated, according to the CDC. The same advice applies to anyone vaccinated during that window who cannot confirm which type of measles vaccine they received.

Two kinds of measles vaccine were in use in the U.S. during those years. An inactivated vaccine contains virus that has been killed. A live vaccine contains a weakened form of the virus that can still replicate in the body. The CDC's revaccination advice applies to the killed version.

Today's MMR shot is in the live category. It protects against measles, mumps and rubella in a single injection. The combined MMR vaccine did not exist during the inactivated-vaccine years. It was licensed in the U.S. in 1971, several years after that window closed.

That history shapes who belongs in this group. Many people who got a measles shot between 1963 and 1967 were children born in the late 1950s or early 1960s. People born in 1957 or later do not fall under the CDC's birth-year presumption of immunity. For them, a mid-1960s shot may be the only measles vaccination on record.

The unknown-type clause covers a common gap in old paperwork. A childhood card from that era may list a date and the word "measles" without naming the product. A parent's memory of a shot does not identify the vaccine either. Under CDC guidance, a dose of unknown type given in that window calls for revaccination, just as an inactivated dose does.

The remedy is a dose of the current MMR vaccine. That shot replaces an uncertain mid-1960s dose with one whose type is documented.

Anyone who is pregnant or has a severely weakened immune system should raise that with a clinician before getting the shot.

Anyone who finds a measles vaccination dated between 1963 and 1967 on an old card or school file can bring it to a doctor or local health department. A clinician can review the record and decide whether another dose is needed.

The CDC recommends that students at colleges, universities and other schools after high school have two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, known as MMR, or other evidence of immunity. For this group, one dose falls short of the CDC recommendation.

The campus setting is the reason for the higher standard. Residence halls, lecture rooms, dining halls and gyms put large numbers of people in shared indoor spaces. Students arrive from many states and countries, and they mix closely for months at a time. Measles spreads through the air and is one of the most contagious infectious diseases.

The recommendation is not limited to 18-year-old freshmen. It covers students in education after high school, which includes community colleges, graduate programs, trade schools and adults returning to study.

Documentation carries practical weight for this group. Many colleges and universities ask incoming students for proof of MMR vaccination before enrollment or before they move into campus housing. Requirements vary by school and by state. The student health office or admissions office can confirm what a specific campus accepts.

A parent's memory that the shots were given does not count as proof. The CDC accepts written documentation of vaccination as evidence of immunity. The record should show which vaccine was given and when.

Students who received both doses on the standard U.S. childhood schedule may already have the proof a college wants. Pediatric records and high school health files are common places for that history to sit.

Students who grew up abroad or moved between health systems may find only one dose recorded, or no record at all. A student with one documented dose generally needs one more to meet the CDC recommendation for this group. A student with no documented doses needs two. When two doses are needed, the CDC calls for them to be given at least 28 days apart.

MMR is a live vaccine. A student who is pregnant or has a severely weakened immune system should talk with a clinician before getting it.

Health care workers need two documented doses of the MMR vaccine under guidance from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That is a higher bar than the single dose the CDC sets for most adults born in 1957 or later who lack evidence of immunity.

The shot covers measles, mumps and rubella together. There is no separate measles-only vaccine in routine U.S. use. A second measles dose means a second MMR shot.

Hospitals and clinics are places where measles can spread quickly. The virus travels through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. It can linger in a room after that person has left.

Some patients in those settings cannot rely on the vaccine themselves. MMR is a live vaccine. The CDC does not recommend it during pregnancy or for people with severely weakened immune systems. Staff immunity is part of how those patients are protected.

The same limit applies to staff. MMR is not recommended for a health care worker who is pregnant or has a severely weakened immune system. That worker should talk with a clinician or occupational health office about immunity and job duties.

In clinical work, immunity has to be shown on paper rather than assumed. Under CDC guidance, written documentation of vaccination counts as evidence. A worker's memory of childhood shots does not.

A worker with one documented dose meets the general adult minimum but not the health care standard. A second MMR dose closes that gap. A laboratory result showing immunity is another accepted route.

Birth before 1957 also counts as evidence of immunity under CDC guidance. Health care workers born before that year should ask their employer how the rule applies to their role.

Workers who switch employers may need to show proof again. Keeping copies of vaccination records or lab results in one place makes that step faster.

Adults born in 1957 or later should have two documented MMR doses before traveling abroad, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention advises. That is a higher bar than the single dose the CDC asks of most other adults who lack evidence of immunity.

Travel raises the chance of exposure. Measles still circulates in many countries. Airports, long flights and busy tourist sites put travelers in close contact with people from around the world.

The U.S. declared measles eliminated in 2000. Elimination means the disease no longer spreads continuously within the country. It does not mean the virus is gone. Cases still appear when someone catches measles abroad and carries it home, where it can spread to people who are not protected.

Measles spreads through the air. The CDC reports that the virus can remain in the air of a room for up to two hours after an infected person has left. A traveler does not need direct contact with a sick person to be exposed.

Timing matters for anyone who needs both doses. The two shots must be given at least 28 days apart. An adult with no record of vaccination should plan the first dose well ahead of departure. A traveler who already has one documented dose needs only the second.

Checking records early also leaves room for other options. A traveler who cannot find paperwork can ask a clinician about a blood test for immunity, or get vaccinated. The CDC states there is no harm in getting another MMR dose for someone who may already be immune. The same shot also protects against mumps and rubella.

MMR is a live vaccine, so it is not recommended during pregnancy or for people with severely weakened immune systems. Travelers $TRV in either group should discuss measles risk at their destination with a doctor before departure.

Families traveling with babies and young children face separate considerations. Parents should ask a pediatrician about their child's vaccination timing well before an overseas trip.

Measles vaccination records are most likely held by a state immunization registry, a doctor's office, a school or a parent's files. Under CDC guidance, written documentation of vaccination counts as evidence of immunity. A dated record can settle the question before anyone books another shot.

Start with the state immunization information system. That is the CDC's term for the confidential databases that record vaccine doses given within a state. Every U.S. state has one. Access rules differ by state. Some let residents request a copy online, while others route requests through a health care provider or the state health department.

These registries have limits. Many began operating after older adults were children. Doses given decades ago may never have been entered. A record missing from the registry does not mean the shot was never given.

Family papers are the next place to look. Many households kept a paper vaccination card from childhood doctor visits, sometimes stored with birth certificates or other important documents. If a parent is available, asking where those papers ended up can shorten the search.

Schools are another source. U.S. states require proof of certain vaccinations for school entry. As a result, primary and secondary schools may have kept a copy on file. Colleges and universities that checked immunization status at enrollment may hold records too. How long institutions keep these files varies.

Past doctors and clinics are worth contacting. A pediatrician's office or family practice may still have older charts. Former employers that required vaccinations may have kept a file. People who served in the military may find doses listed in their service health records.

Memory alone does not count. Under CDC guidance, a person's recollection of a past vaccination is not accepted as proof, and neither is a parent's. The record needs to be written and show the date of each dose.

Once a record is found, keeping a copy saves the same search later. A photo or scan stored with other health documents works.

A measles titer is a blood test that checks for antibodies to the measles virus. Under CDC guidance, a laboratory result showing immunity counts as acceptable evidence of protection. That makes the test a substitute for vaccination records that have gone missing.

A doctor or other clinician usually orders the test, and the blood is drawn at a clinic or lab. It measures measles IgG antibodies, the kind the immune system produces after vaccination or a past infection. Results generally come back as positive, negative or equivocal.

A positive result is the outcome that helps someone without paperwork. It gives them written, lab-based proof to keep on file. They can show it to a school, employer or program that asks for evidence of measles immunity. It also settles the question for adults born in 1957 or later who cannot find a record of their shots.

A negative or equivocal result means the test did not confirm protection. The CDC treats an equivocal result as lacking evidence of immunity. In either case, the usual next step is MMR vaccination. The number of doses follows the recommendation that fits the person's age, job or plans.

The blood test is not the only route for people without records. Getting an MMR dose is an accepted alternative. There is no harm in receiving another dose when a person may already be immune, according to the CDC. Some people choose to skip the blood draw and get vaccinated. Others test first to avoid an extra shot if they are already protected.

Antibody testing has limits for people who already have records. The CDC does not recommend routine blood testing after two documented MMR doses. Under CDC guidance for health care personnel, two documented doses count as protection even if a later test is negative or equivocal. Extra doses are not recommended in that situation.

Insurance coverage and cost for titer testing vary by plan and lab. People weighing a blood test against vaccination can ask a clinician or their local health department which option fits their situation.

The MMR vaccine is not recommended during pregnancy or for people with severely weakened immune systems, according to the CDC. Both limits come from one fact: MMR is a live vaccine.

A live vaccine contains weakened forms of the viruses it protects against. Those weakened viruses multiply in the body at a low level. That brief activity trains the immune system to recognize measles, mumps and rubella without causing the full diseases in a healthy person.

That same mechanism explains the restrictions. A healthy immune system keeps the weakened viruses in check. A severely weakened immune system may not be able to do so. That risk is why MMR is not recommended for people with severely weakened immunity.

Severely weakened immunity can have several causes. Some people are born with immune disorders. Others develop it through disease or medical treatment, such as certain cancer therapies or drugs that suppress the immune system after an organ transplant. The degree of suppression matters. A clinician who knows the specific condition and medication is the person to judge whether MMR is appropriate.

Pregnancy is the second situation the CDC names. A pregnant person should not receive MMR while pregnant, even without evidence of measles immunity. Anyone in that position can talk with an obstetrician or other clinician about their measles protection.

These limits do not make vaccine records irrelevant. Someone who cannot receive MMR now may already be protected by doses given earlier in life. Written vaccination records or a laboratory result can confirm that protection without a new shot.

People who cannot be vaccinated rely on the immunity of those around them. Measles spreads easily from person to person. When family members, coworkers and caregivers are protected, the virus has fewer paths to someone who has no protection of their own.

Anyone unsure about their own situation can bring a list of current diagnoses and medications to a doctor, pharmacist or local health department before deciding on vaccination.

Adults with written records of two MMR doses do not need a measles booster. The CDC treats a completed, recorded two-dose series as enough and does not advise adding a third shot as a matter of routine.

The second dose is not a booster in the usual sense. It does not top up protection that has faded with age. It is there to catch the small share of people whose immune systems did not respond fully to the first shot. Two doses give the vaccine two chances to produce that response.

The U.S. childhood schedule places both doses early in life. The first is given at 12 to 15 months of age. The second follows at four to six years. An adult who received both on that timetable, and still has the paperwork, has already finished the series the CDC recommends.

A dated record from a clinic, school or immunization registry is what makes the series count. A parent's memory or a general sense of having had the shots is not written proof. The record should show the vaccine and the date of each dose. Written documentation of vaccination is one of the forms of evidence of immunity the CDC accepts. With it, a doctor, employer or university can confirm the series without ordering another shot.

Two documented doses also meet the CDC's two-dose recommendation for college students, health care workers and international travelers. People in those groups who already hold that record do not need to repeat the series to satisfy the guidance. The same record covers mumps and rubella as well. MMR protects against all three diseases with each dose.

A complete record does not guarantee immunity. No vaccine is 100 percent effective, and a small number of fully vaccinated people can still get measles. Anyone who is exposed to measles or develops symptoms should contact a clinician or local health department for advice on next steps.

#5614. Massachusetts AG issues rule on shared appreciation mortgages, NCLC calls for broader protections

The Massachusetts Attorney General’s Office has implemented a new rule governing shared appreciation mortgages, a dual-lien structure that ties repayment to home price appreciation. The regulation clarifies when nonprofit lenders are shielded from consumer protection claims and requires stronger disclosures, including maximum potential repayment amounts. Stemming from a 2024 law that granted broad liability waivers to nonprofit SAMs such as BlueHub, the rule follows litigation alleging the products function as high-cost, subprime-style loans that can strip home equity.   AI Summary

The Massachusetts Attorney General’s Office has implemented a new rule governing shared appreciation mortgages, adding disclosure and consumer protection requirements for a niche home equity product that has faced recent scrutiny.

The rule, effective Nov. 6, clarifies when nonprofit shared appreciation mortgage (SAM) lenders are shielded from state consumer protection claims and sets new notice standards, including prominent disclosure of the maximum amount borrowers may have to repay, according to an announcement from the National Consumer Law Center (NCLC).

The regulation stems from a provision in the state’s economic development bill, passed in November 2024. That statute carved out a broad waiver of liability under Massachusetts consumer protection laws for certain nonprofit SAMs, including loans originated by BlueHub Capital. Advocates say the legislative change created a “dangerous loophole” that exposed distressed homeowners to complex and costly loan structures with limited recourse.

Under the BlueHub-style model, borrowers typically receive a fixed-rate first mortgage alongside a second lien tied to future home price appreciation. The SAM second lien requires the homeowner to share a portion of any increase in property value with the lender upon sale, transfer or refinance. Because the payoff amount is variable and not set in dollars at origination, borrowers can face unexpectedly large balloon payments when they attempt to exit the loan.

NCLC noted that the risks of these structures have been highlighted in Humes v. BlueHub Capital Inc., a Massachusetts class-action lawsuit alleging SAMs embed hidden, subprime-level costs that can strip significant equity and accelerate home loss. The court found BlueHub liable for violating multiple state lending laws and recently certified the class to move forward, according to NCLC.

“While presented as a lifeline, shared appreciation mortgages often become a trap,” Andrea Bopp Stark, senior attorney at the National Consumer Law Center, said in a statement. “The AG’s final rule protects people from BlueHub’s loan model and similar products, but Massachusetts must go further to prevent harm from more common home equity theft loan products, including Home Equity Investment Loans.”

The AG’s new rule does not eliminate SAMs but seeks to ensure that nonprofit and other lenders using these instruments do so transparently and within defined consumer protection boundaries.

The regulation spells out the limited circumstances in which a SAM lender can be insulated from claims under Massachusetts consumer protection law and establishes a framework for robust disclosures, including clear presentation of the maximum possible repayment obligation.

While praising the change, NCLC argues that the rule does not reach a far enough to impact a growing category of products — home equity investments (HEIs). These provide upfront cash to a homeowner in exchange for a share of the future home price appreciation. NCLC characterized these arrangements as high risk for borrowers, as the actual amount owed depends on home price growth and triggers large, lump-sum obligations.

A representative at the AG’s office did not immediately respond to HousingWire‘s request for comment on the changes.

Massachusetts AG Andrea Joy Campbell has already challenged one HEI provider, Hometap. The state alleges consumer protection violations tied to HEI structures. But NCLC noted that the latest rulemaking in Massachusetts does not specifically regulate HEI products.

“The new rules provide important safeguards and requirements for SAMs, and stronger and broader rules are needed to address the high-risk HEI loans that are now targeting Massachusetts homeowners,” Bopp Stark said.

Consumers in other parts of the country have challenged HEI providers in court. Last year, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals overturned a 2023 judgment from a district court in Washington state, ruling that Unison‘s HEI product amounted to a reverse mortgage under state law.

In August, HEI provider Unlock settled with the Office of the Minnesota Attorney General over allegations that the company’s home equity agreements (HEAs) were mortgage loans that violated state usury caps, disclosure rules and licensing requirements.

Companies say they are supportive of regulatory efforts, pointing to a legal framework passed earlier this year in Illinois that could serve as model at the national level. At the Mortgage Bankers Association‘s Annual Convention & Expo last month, executives at Point told HousingWire they believe universal regulations are coming.

“We believe that these companies are going to be regulated,” said Dan McPheeters, Point’s head of business development and partnerships. “The practical effect is, it’s difficult to comply with [mortgage regulations] for a product that doesn’t have a monthly payment, that isn’t self-amortizing. … That said, as long as you address those tactical issues, this should be regulated.”

The NCLC urges additional state action to close what they see as remaining gaps in oversight of shared appreciation equity-based mortgage products. Their recommendations include:

#5612. Dropbox acquires Tigris Data for $350M, releases new AI productivity features

Dropbox Inc. is acquiring cloud storage startup Tigris Data Inc. for $350 million.

The company announced the deal today in conjunction with a major update to its product portfolio. It introduced DBX Agent Cloud, a service that artificial intelligence agents can use to store their data. Dropbox is also adding new AI productivity features to its flagship file sharing platform.

Sunnyvale, California-based Tigris Data offers an object storage service that runs across multiple public clouds. The company says that it enables applications to read and write several times faster than competing offerings. Furthermore, the service includes several features designed to optimize AI workloads.

AI agents often run in sandboxes that include, among other resources, the data they need to carry out their work. Loading data into a sandbox can be a relatively time-consuming process, which slows agent performance. Tigris Data offers a feature called bucket forms that speeds up the workflow. Furthermore, it prevents agents from modifying information that is used by other workloads.

Tigris Data’s service monitors the locations from which agents access records. When it detects a new location, it moves a copy of the records to a nearby server in order to reduce latency. The service caches the most frequently used files on high-speed storage infrastructure to further reduce access times.

Dropbox said Tigris Data will support its push into the AI infrastructure market. The company debuted its first entry into that product category, DBX Agent Cloud, in conjunction with the acquisition announcement. Like Tigris Data’s service, it’s an S3-compatible object storage offering optimized for AI agents.

The storage stalwart plans to add a file system capability further down the line. Object storage is best suited for unstructured datasets, while file systems are used to store records that are organized into folders. Dropbox plans to release the technology alongside “content processing capabilities.” The company says that those features will make it easier for AI models to process information kept in DBX Agent Cloud.

The offering is rolling out alongside a major overhaul of Dropbox’s flagship file sharing platform. An enhanced search bar will enable users to look for images by entering a description of the file they seek.

Furthermore, Dropbox can now respond to questions about a file by generating a natural language summary. A worker could, for example, request an overview of the changes that colleagues have made to an important folder over the past week.

Dropbox can not only edit questions about files but also edit them. The company says that users can have the built-in AI models change a file’s format, move it to a different folder or combine it with other records into a PDF document. Several other actions are supported as well. Users can mix and match actions into multistep workflows.

The new AI productivity features are initially available to customers in the U.S., the U.K. and Australia with Standard and Advanced subscriptions. Dropbox plans to expand access next year.

#5611. 10 ways beginners can lower investing risk, from a cash cushion to clearing debt

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Ten ideas for new investors, from building a cash cushion and starting early to checking fund labels, plans and IRAs.

For many Americans, nerve, not access, is what keeps them from investing. The hesitant beginner is the norm, as only 47 percent of U.S. adults were confident in 2025 that they could pick and oversee their own investments, according to the Federal Reserve. Anyone unsure about where to start is in the majority, so advice for beginners is really advice for most people. Confidence and ownership tend to go together. Among adults with no retirement account and no other investments, just 32 percent felt at ease making those decisions, well below the share for adults overall. That points to a possible loop in which people without an account lack confidence and people without confidence never open one. A beginner's real task is to break that loop without risking much.

People who hold back from investing usually keep their money somewhere safe and familiar. Insured cash is common ground for most households, and 59 percent of adults keep money in a bank savings account, a money market account or a CD, according to the Federal Reserve. Only 37 percent hold any stocks, bonds or funds in accounts separate from their retirement savings, which means most beginners outside the workplace keep to cash. That gap shows the tension behind every choice that follows. Savers accept that insured cash will earn little in return for its safety, while investors get the chance at growth only if they sit through the drops. For a beginner, then, low risk should not mean owning something that never falls. It should mean arranging money so you never have to sell in a panic or dip into long-term savings.

Investor.gov, the investor-education site of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, set out to explain how beginners can build long-term wealth through steady, managed investing, from the choices for money needed soon to the price of starting late and the employer money in workplace plans. The aim is a habit kept for decades, not a hunt for winning picks. The groundwork comes before any fund: a cushion of cash, years for the money to grow and an honest sense of how much loss you can stand. Even familiar choices, such as a broad index fund or the default setting in a workplace plan, deserve a closer look before a beginner relies on them. Together, these choices give a beginner a plan to hold onto when markets drop.

A beginner's first decision is which bucket a dollar belongs in, not which fund to buy. Investor.gov describes saving as a safe, insured place for money needed soon and investing as a way to earn returns over time. That rule assumes a person already has a cushion set aside. For someone without one, the first investment is a savings account. Building that account isn't a detour from investing. It is the step that comes before it.

Without a separate cushion, people end up using their retirement money as their emergency fund. Pulling back from retirement savings is one way people respond to money trouble, and 14 percent of adults not yet retired borrowed from their retirement accounts, cashed them out or cut their contributions in 2025, according to the Federal Reserve. Losing a job makes that move more likely. Among non-retirees, 9 percent of those who were laid off cashed out a retirement account, compared with 4 percent of those who weren't. A layoff is exactly the kind of shock an emergency fund exists to cover. A worker who cashes out after one sells when the bills come due, at whatever the market pays that week, instead of at a time of their own choosing.

Putting every spare dollar into the market feels like the most ambitious move, but for a beginner without a cushion it is the riskier one. Savings and investing aren't rivals. With a cash cushion in place, a person can leave invested money alone long enough for it to grow.

A beginner with little to spare has one real advantage: the number of years the money stays invested, not the size of each deposit. Over time a saver earns returns on past returns as well as on the money put in, and a steady habit kept for a working lifetime ends up worth far more than the deposits alone. Investor.gov illustrates the effect with a saver who puts in $100 a month for 40 years at 7%, an ordinary amount that many working people can set aside. A beginner doesn't need to wait for "real money" to start, because patience matters more here than wealth. CNBC Select reports that beginners can start with monthly contributions of $50 or $100. A saver with a tight budget can make the deposit smaller, but no one can get back the decades lost to waiting. The habit itself is the thing to protect, and automatic recurring transfers from a linked bank account keep the deposits coming in months when motivation fades.

The 7% in that example is an assumed steady average, not a guaranteed or forecast result, and real returns rise and fall from year to year. A saver earns the long-run average only by staying invested through the down years. Compounding stops the day the saver takes the money out. An investor who sells in a slump turns a temporary loss into a permanent one and starts over with a smaller balance. The low-risk move is a decision made in advance: commit not to sell before the first drop arrives, and check the balance less often so a dip doesn't prompt a hasty choice.

A saver pays every fee out of the same returns that would otherwise have been reinvested. A charge paid today leaves a smaller balance to earn returns in every year that follows. A flat monthly fee is heaviest for beginners, whose balances are smallest. Betterment charges a $5 monthly base fee, according to CNBC Select, and a saver putting in $100 a month loses a meaningful part of each deposit before it has any chance to compound. One way off that flat charge is a balance of $24,000, at which point Betterment switches to a percentage of assets, and modest monthly deposits take years to build a balance that large.

A beginner should read the fee schedule before trusting any compounding example, because what a saver keeps depends on the fees as much as on the returns.

Putting off the first deposit feels free, because nothing is lost on the day a person decides to wait. The cost shows up later, in how much a person has to set aside each month to reach the same goal. Someone who starts saving at 18 can build $500,000 by putting in $127 a month, while someone who waits until 55 must set aside $3,016 a month for the same goal, according to Investor.gov. The early saver can cover that amount from a modest paycheck, but the late starter needs a sum many households can't spare. The difference comes from the years the money has to grow, and no amount of later effort fully buys those years back. That makes the start date the first decision about risk a beginner makes, even though it doesn't look like one.

A beginner doesn't have to wait until 55 to pay for hesitating, and losing a single decade early in a career already raises the monthly amount. A 25-year-old aiming for $1 million at 65 would have to invest about $240 a month if the money earns 9% a year, according to figures from Brian Stivers, a financial advisor and founder of Stivers Financial Services, reported by CNBC Select. At that age, reaching $1 million costs about as much as a modest monthly bill. Waiting until 35 means setting aside about $590 a month at the same return, which many people would find hard to fit into a typical budget. A beginner who holds off until a bigger paycheck arrives usually pays more for the same result. Starting small now makes more sense than promising a larger sum later.

A late starter who waits and then picks the calmest mix available pays the most of all. Reaching $1 million from age 35 on a 3% return takes about $1,750 a month, CNBC Select reports, and that return stands for a conservative portfolio made up mostly of bonds. A 35-year-old who chooses the steadier mix must set aside far more each month than one counting on the 9% return, even though the goal is the same. Waiting and staying conservative are the two choices that feel safest, and a beginner who makes both pays for each of them. That is why starting early matters most for the beginner who can't stand big swings.

The lower monthly amounts depend on returns that are assumed, not guaranteed, according to CNBC Select. The 9% figure is a higher assumption than the conservative 3%, and an assumed rate describes a possible average over many years rather than promising any one saver a result. A beginner can't choose the return but can choose when to begin, and the start date is the one input fully under their control. Starting early gives a beginner room to hold a mix they can live with, without counting on big returns to make up for a late start.

How much of a drop they can actually stand is the next question.

No investment is low-risk for everyone, and a beginner has to answer two questions about themselves before choosing any fund. When the money will be needed and how much loss its owner can tolerate determine which products suit a person, according to Investor.gov. A fund that fits one beginner's timeline and temperament can be the wrong choice for another. The two answers also depend on each other. A person who won't need the money for decades has time to wait for prices to recover from a fall, but only if they don't sell partway down. A long timeline is worth nothing to an investor who loses their nerve before the recovery comes.

Most people judge their comfort with risk while markets are calm, and a calm market tells them nothing about how they will react to a loss. The honest test is to picture the declines that actually happen, and they happen often enough to plan for. "Reassess how much risk you are comfortable with, recognizing that stocks go down 10% often, 20% with some regularity and more than 30% occasionally," TIME writer Dan Kadlec said. A 10% slide, then, is a normal event that a beginner should expect to sit through without doing anything. The rare fall of more than 30% is the one a long-term plan has to survive. The real question is whether you could hold on through that one, not through the routine dips.

If imagining those losses feels unbearable, the answer is to decide now to hold less in stocks, not to plan on selling when the drop arrives. Learning that you would rather take a more conservative approach is useful information, not a sign that investing isn't for you. Two cautious investors differ mainly in when they find out. One who measures their tolerance before investing can build a mix they are able to keep. One who finds out during a crash has to decide while prices are falling, when selling would turn a loss on paper into a real one.

An investor who knows their limit in advance can benefit from a long timeline, and the next decision is how to split money to match that limit.

The biggest risk decision a beginner makes comes before choosing any fund: how to divide money among stocks, bonds and cash. Investor.gov names those three as the basic types of assets, and spreading money across them weighs risk against how long the money can wait and how much loss its owner can stand. No correct ratio exists to look up. John Mullen, managing director, president and CEO of Parsons Capital Management, tells CNBC that no single percentage split suits every client. A split borrowed from a friend, a headline or a rule of thumb reflects someone else's patience and nerve. A beginner's first job is to set the split against their own.

A mix doesn't keep the shares its owner chose. After a strong run in stocks, an investor who does nothing ends up holding more in stocks than the plan called for, according to CNBC. That shift has been large in recent years, as the S&P 500's total return over the three years through 2025 came to 88.11%. Over that stretch the stock portion of a typical mix outgrew the bonds and cash meant to balance it. The index's 2026 total return through Oct. 28 was another 14.17%, and anyone who set a mix before this run probably needs to check it now.

The extra stock matters most when prices fall. The S&P 500's total return in 2022 was a loss of 18.11%, according to CNBC, and an owner whose mix has tilted toward stocks loses more in a year like that than they had agreed to accept. That is the cost hidden behind a "balanced" mix: the label stays the same while the owner carries more risk than it suggests.

The fix is to bring the mix back to the limit its owner chose, measured against their own tolerance and timeline rather than a forecast. "If there are investors who are overexposed to stocks because of the multiyear bull market we've been in, then it's not a bad idea to bring yourself back to the risk tolerance you set for yourself in a calculated and non-emotional manner," Michael Gibb, president and CEO of Godsey & Gibb Wealth Management, told CNBC. The discipline works in both directions, and Mullen warns that investors who keep revising a mix that has served them well risk ending up unhappy with the results. An occasional reset is the only change a mix built to be held through swings should need.

For a beginner, low risk here means choosing a mix they can live with, checking it against themselves from time to time and otherwise leaving it alone.

A broad index fund appeals to a beginner because one purchase buys a small stake in hundreds of companies, with no need to pick winners. Investor.gov explains that spreading money across many holdings means a loss in one can be offset by gains in others. That works only when the holdings differ from one another. The five largest companies in the S&P 500 are Nvidia $NVDA, Apple $AAPL, Microsoft $MSFT, Alphabet $GOOGL, and Amazon $AMZN, according to CNBC, and all five are tech giants whose shares tend to react to the same news. Stocks tied to the same story don't offset each other. They tend to move together.

Spreading money around is meant to reduce losses when the market drops. Zachary Evens, a manager research analyst at Morningstar, tells CNBC that a slowdown in AI would mean falling prices for the AI and big tech stocks that already account for much of what many investors own. A beginner who bought the broad fund to play it safe may therefore hold a sizable bet on a single trade without meaning to. Diversification still helps, but it protects less than the word suggests when one theme leads the market.

Many workers in a 401(k) hold a target-date fund without ever picking one, because many plans use it as the automatic choice for savers who don't select their own, according to CNBC. Marta Norton, chief investment strategist at Empower, says some of that AI exposure falls on its own as the fund moves from stocks toward bonds over the years. The reverse also follows. A young saver decades from the target date holds mostly stocks and keeps more of that exposure, so the saver furthest from retirement gets the least help from the shift.

The answer is to learn where your broad funds overlap, not to give them up. "Dig down one layer below the top, and look at the top 10 or top 20 holdings across your ETFs in your portfolio, and try to get an understanding of how correlated those ETFs might be," John Sedunov, a professor of finance at Villanova University, told CNBC. Owning three funds adds little protection if all three rely on the same few giants.

For a beginner, being diversified is something to confirm once a year, not something to assume from a fund's label.

A workplace retirement plan is the one account where an employer adds money to a worker's own savings. Workers who join get tax benefits and an employer match that amounts to free money, according to Investor.gov, yet many people who are offered a plan never sign up. In 2014, 68 percent of workers offered a defined-contribution plan took part, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, which left a sizable share of the offered money unclaimed. Staying out is not a neutral choice in the way that leaving cash in savings can be. A worker who skips the plan gives up money the employer had already set aside to pay. Joining is the low-risk move because the worker receives the match on each contribution before any investment gain or loss.

Signing up only starts the claim, and the size of the match depends on how much the worker puts in. Investor.gov advises workers to save at least enough to collect every dollar of the employer's match. A worker whose employer adds 50 cents for each dollar saved, up to 6 percent of pay, gets the largest possible match of 3 percent of pay only by saving the full 6 percent, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. A beginner who contributes a token amount to be careful is turning down part of an offer that costs nothing extra to accept in full.

The match is also less of a gift than it sounds. Employers that automatically enrolled workers showed no statistically significant difference in total compensation costs from those that didn't, according to research the Bureau of Labor Statistics published in 2015. That finding suggests employers pay for the match out of a fixed pay budget, so a beginner should count it as part of their pay.

Many beginners assume their employer will sign them up and handle the rest, but automatic enrollment was the exception. In 2009–2010, only 14.5 percent of workers in plans were in ones that enrolled them automatically, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Even employers that used the feature often left existing staff out, and 82 percent of plans with automatic enrollment applied it only to new hires, according to one survey reported by the Bureau of Labor Statistics in 2015. A worker hired earlier who never signed up stays out until they act. A worker enrolled by default should check right away whether the default contribution rate reaches the match ceiling and raise it if it falls short.

An IRA is the retirement account a beginner opens without an employer's help. It comes with tax breaks, and a saver can hold one in addition to a job-based plan, according to the SEC's Investor.gov. Opening one is a common step for ordinary savers, not a move reserved for experts, as Americans held about $18.2 trillion in IRAs across all accounts nationwide at the end of the first quarter of 2026, according to FRED. No employer enrolls a worker in an IRA, so the hardest part is the first step, and the decision to take it rests with the saver alone. That makes the IRA the account to consider when a job offers no plan, or when the workplace plan is already in place and there is money left over to invest.

A tax break does not protect an account from losses, and the money inside an IRA can lose value. For many investors, workplace plans and IRAs are "the foundational building blocks of their investment portfolio," Investor.gov said. Yet even the national total in these accounts can go down from one quarter to the next. That first-quarter 2026 total was lower than the $18.725 trillion recorded at the end of 2025, according to FRED. The dip came after a year of growth, and the total stayed well above the $16.32 trillion recorded at the end of the first quarter of 2025. One weak quarter is a pause in a longer rise, not a judgment on the account.

A beginner should open the account and then choose what goes inside it with care, picking holdings they can keep through a down quarter. Choosing those holdings is the saver's job, just as opening the account was.

Money set aside for a car, a move or a tuition bill due in a year or two can't sit where retirement money sits, since a saver has no time to wait out a market drop before the bill arrives. Investor.gov says near-term goals call for lower-risk choices that a saver can reach quickly, such as CDs and money market funds. For this money, avoiding a loss just before the deadline matters more than growth. That reverses the usual investing question. The aim is to have the full amount ready on the day you planned, whatever markets are doing that week.

The checking account a saver already uses is the easiest place to keep goal money, but money held for spending earns little, according to the Federal Reserve Board. A CD or a money market fund sits one step away from the account a person spends from. A beginner should move goal money into one of them on purpose and should not plan to spend from it as freely as from checking.

A new digital form of cash is only as safe as what it legally is. A tokenized deposit is still a bank deposit, and it remains eligible for deposit insurance, according to the Federal Reserve Board. A product's modern name doesn't tell a saver how well the money is protected. The useful question about any new form of cash is whether it is legally a bank deposit, not how new it looks.

Money you'll need soon usually belongs in a plain, insured account that you have confirmed is a bank deposit.

A beginner's safest financial move sometimes happens before they put any money into a fund. Investor.gov counts budgeting, paying off costly debt, keeping emergency savings and watching for fraud as ways to build wealth, alongside choosing investments. These habits are part of building wealth, not chores to finish once and forget. People who keep them avoid the same danger that every account and fund choice is meant to prevent: having to sell at a bad time or dip into money meant for decades. That makes the habits the base of a beginner's plan.

Card debt is where this matters most, because a beginner who invests while carrying a credit card balance can lose ground even in a strong year for markets. If a card balance goes unpaid, "you’ll be paying interest charges that may greatly exceed the amount you could earn on your savings or investments," Investor.gov said. The interest charge is close to certain, while investment gains are not. A beginner who leaves money in the market while a balance runs can come out behind. Paying down the balance carries no market risk, and every dollar repaid stops a charge. For a beginner with card debt, the low-risk order is to clear the costly balance first and start investing after.

Compounding, a target date fund and a workplace match all depend on money left over at the end of the month, and spending less than you earn is what produces it. Guarding that money is part of the same habit. A beginner who holds steady through a market drop protects little if they lose the savings to a scam or a careless decision.

Low-risk investing is mostly a set of habits a beginner can keep, and the account is where those habits pay off.

#5610. How a new Pulte Florida agrihood makes conservation a buyer desire

PulteGroup is developing The Grow, a 1,200-acre agrihood east of Orlando planned for about 2,200 homes anchored by a 9-acre working farm. Plans leave just over half the site undeveloped, positioning the project as a growth and conservation case study.  AI Summary

For years, Central Florida’s exploding population growth and rapidly expanding suburban sprawl have clashed with local efforts to protect the region’s dwindling green space and undeveloped land. PulteGroup’s new 1,200-acre community on Orlando’s eastern edge aims to balance these seemingly contradictory interests.

The community is called The Grow. Once undeveloped, rural land, the property is set to begin morphing into a roughly 2,200-home “agrihood” centered around a 9-acre working farm. In keeping with its conservation focus, the plan calls for reserving just over half of the site from development, including wetlands, conservation areas and shared green space.

The Grow offers a potential case study in balancing growth and conservation, a tension deeply felt in Central Florida and many other high-growth Sun Belt markets. Between 2000 and 2025, the Orlando metro area’s population grew nearly 80%, from 1.64 million to 2.95 million.

That growth reshaped once-rural communities on the region’s edges, replacing undeveloped land with new subdivisions, apartments and shopping centers. Many long-time Sunshine State residents now lament the loss of “Old Florida,” marked by a landscape of open land, working ranches and orange groves that are now developed.

When Pulte, the sole homebuilder at The Grow, purchased the community’s lots in 2023, it set out to build a premier community that responded to these tensions.

“One of our biggest selling features is the openness of the community and how much greenery we left. Everywhere you look, you’re surrounded by trees,” Patrick McNamara, a Sales Manager at Pulte, told HousingWire TBD.

However, the true distinguisher between The Grow and other local communities will be its working farm, a rare amenity that carries the conservation theme beyond protecting land to putting it to use.

For Pulte, which held a grand opening for the community in late September, the farm and the extensive conservation space give the builder a way to stand out to prospective homebuyers, a crucial edge considering the challenging sales environment homebuilders are facing.

The working farm is central to the community’s agrihood concept – providing fresh, sustainably grown produce. Residents will support it by buying products, volunteering and joining educational activities.

McNamara argued that the farm creates a direct connection between residents and their food. A professional third-party company will manage the farm, but residents and families will be allowed to volunteer and then buy the finished produce at a resident-only general store that will serve as an anchor for The Grow’s commercial and retail street.

The development will include two other farms: a small demonstration farm, covering about an eighth of an acre, and a separate community farm where homeowners can practice what they learn.

These smaller farms will serve as an educational, hands-on amenity for families, where residents can learn each stage of growing produce and then put what they learn into practice. An existing program, “Seed the Table,” will allow residents to plant crops, watch them grow and eat what they produced.

The farmers will also work with the lifestyle director to hold chef-led cooking classes at the community’s gathering barn, and will host seasonal celebrations and festivals that bring homeowners together.

Beyond conservation and sustainability, the farm is meant to build community, encourage learning and offer a unique lifestyle.

The Grow, which features homes from the low $400s to the high $800s, isn’t immune to the macro-level sales pressures impacting the local and national housing market. McNamara concedes that his team has to leverage generous incentives like mortgage rate buydowns to finish sales.

However, he also confirmed that The Grow has sold more than 100 homes since opening pre-sales about six months ago, and that prospective buyers have been anticipating the community’s opening for years.

The agrihood concept is the hook that draws buyers in.

“The farm is a big draw,” McNamara said. “I think the agrihood is what’s bringing people in, but what’s getting them to buy is once they see everything else that comes with it.”

In addition to the working farm and conservation space, The Grow will feature a main street with about 170,000 square feet of retail and commercial space, envisioned as a high-end retail and dining corridor that can work as a visitor magnet.

Other features include an indoor event and social space, an outdoor green space with a community pizza oven, a dedicated dog park, walking and nature trails, playgrounds and other resident-only amenities like a clubhouse, a gym and a pool.

“[Buyers] are shocked to find out that this isn’t a little farm community. This is a high-end resort neighborhood.”

The community’s preservation of nature is another big selling point. While many newly built communities lack mature trees and vegetation, The Grow’s preservation space means that residents can live alongside nature from day one.

“It’s really about getting immersed in nature, and that’s really hard to find in new construction,” McNamara said. “Homebuilders typically buy a piece of land and clear it out, start from scratch, and then plant a lot of trees. But you’ve got another 30 years until you can really enjoy the shade from it. In this neighborhood, we’ve left hundreds of 100-year-old oaks all throughout the community. We’ve made them focal points.”

“One of the big draws is the lifestyle and the outdoor feeling that you’re going to have in this community,” he added

#5608. Progress Residential to pay $49.8M to settle FTC, state claims over rental practices

Progress Residential, the single-family rental operator owned by Pretium Partners, agreed to a $49.8 million settlement with the Federal Trade Commission and state regulators over allegations it hid rental fees, mishandled security deposits and misled tenants about property conditions.   AI Summary

Progress Residential, the property manager of single-family rental homes owned by Pretium Partners, has agreed to pay $49.8 million to settle deceptive and unfair practices claims by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and state regulators. The company denies any wrongdoing.

In a complaint filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Georgia, regulators alleged that the company advertised rental prices that did not reflect the full amount tenants would be required to pay, imposed hidden or inadequately disclosed fees and charges, and mishandled security deposits.

The claims also included that Progress misrepresented the condition and move-in readiness of properties, restricted tenants’ ability to share reviews, and failed to adequately address tenant complaints and maintenance issues.

In a statement given to HousingWire, a representative of Progress Residential and Pretium said the companies have reached an agreement “with the FTC and four states to resolve the Commission’s Civil Investigative Demand related to certain aspects of our resident experience during the period of 2021 to 2025.”

“The agreement contains no admission of wrongdoing, and we maintain Progress’ practices have been transparent, fair, and consistent with industry practice,” the spokesperson said. “Although we disagree with the FTC’s claims, this resolution allows us to move forward with our mission of expanding access to quality, affordable rental housing in neighborhoods of opportunity.”

The deal was reached by the FTC, the attorneys general of Arizona, Indiana and Colorado, and the Utah Division of Consumer Protection. It combines monetary relief for renters across the country.

“We will always welcome investment in housing and recognize the important role private capital can play in increasing opportunities for Hoosier families,” Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita said in a statement. “But no company, regardless of size or financial backing, gets a free pass to mislead consumers, impose hidden charges or treat tenants unfairly.”

“Consumers searching for housing should have access to straightforward information about the costs associated with renting a home,” said Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection. “Transparency regarding rental prices and fees helps consumers compare options and make informed choices. Clear pricing practices also support competition by allowing housing providers to compete on the basis of price, quality and service.

“The FTC is monitoring the rental housing market and will continue to take action where appropriate to ensure that consumers receive clear and accurate information about the costs of renting a home.”

Per the settlement terms, Progress must disclose the total monthly rental price in advertisements and listings, along with mandatory fees and charges, before a consumer commits to rent. The company also must stop withholding funds for ordinary wear and tear and is prohibited from misleading claims about property conditions.

The consumer redress funds created by the settlement total $48.5 million and will be used for relief as directed by the stipulated order entered in the federal case. Arizona is receiving $1.25 million.

In 2024, Invitation Homes, the largest owner of U.S. single-family rental homes, agreed to pay $48 million to consumers and change some of its practices.

Editor’s note: This story was updated with a statement from the FTC.

#5607. Salmonella vs. E. coli vs. listeria: how to tell them apart

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Salmonella vs. E. coli vs. listeria comes down to timing, symptoms and the foods that carry them — here is how to tell three common foodborne bacteria apart

The meal that made you sick may not be the one you ate last night. Food poisoning tends to get blamed on the most recent thing someone ate. The bacteria behind it keep very different schedules. Some act within hours. Others stay quiet for weeks before symptoms appear, long after the food in question has been forgotten or thrown away.

That gap in timing is one of the most useful clues for sorting out Salmonella vs. E. coli vs. listeria. All three are common foodborne bacteria. Each one tends to travel in different foods. Each one produces a somewhat different pattern of illness. And the people at greatest risk of serious illness are not the same for all three.

The differences have practical consequences. Treatment that helps with one bacterium may be discouraged for another. That decision belongs to a clinician, not a guess. Knowing which foods carry which organism shapes how a household shops, stores and cooks. It also determines who at the table needs to take extra care.

This guide is not a complete map of foodborne illness. Campylobacter, norovirus — which is a virus, not a bacterium — and many other pathogens also make people sick. They are not covered here. The focus is narrower: three bacteria that frequently appear in food recalls and outbreak reports but behave in distinct ways once they reach the body.

The information draws on established public health guidance, mainly from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the U.S. Department of Agriculture. It does not replace medical advice. Anyone with severe or worsening symptoms should contact a health care provider.

The slides that follow start with a profile of each bacterium: what it typically causes, where it tends to come from and who is most vulnerable. A side-by-side comparison then looks at how symptoms and incubation times differ across the three, and why those signs overlap enough to mislead. The final slide covers how doctors confirm the cause with lab tests and which kitchen habits lower the risk of infection in the first place.

Salmonella infection usually causes diarrhea, fever and stomach cramps. Most healthy people recover within four to seven days without any specific treatment. Dehydration is the main risk.

Salmonella is a genus of rod-shaped bacteria that live in the intestines of many animals, including birds and reptiles. The genus takes its name from Daniel Elmer Salmon, a U.S. veterinary scientist whose research program isolated the bacterium in the 1880s. Scientists have identified more than 2,500 serotypes. A much smaller number cause most human illness.

Symptoms typically appear anywhere from six hours to six days after a person swallows the bacteria. Rest and steady fluids carry most people through the illness. Oral rehydration solutions replace the salts lost through diarrhea as well as the water.

Doctors generally reserve antibiotics for severe illness or for patients at higher risk of complications. CDC lists children under five, adults 65 and older and people with weakened immune systems among the groups more likely to become seriously ill. For everyone else, treatment focuses on staying hydrated.

Animals spread Salmonella too. Turtles, lizards, snakes and other reptiles can carry it while appearing healthy. Backyard chickens and ducklings can as well. Handling the animals, their enclosures or their bedding and then touching the mouth is enough to pass the bacteria along.

Typhoid fever belongs in a separate category. It comes from a different type, Salmonella Typhi, and causes a distinct illness marked by prolonged high fever. Humans are its only known host. It spreads through food and water contaminated with human waste. In the U.S., most typhoid cases occur in people who have traveled abroad.

Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, or STEC, causes severe stomach cramps, vomiting and diarrhea that is often bloody, usually with little or no fever. O157:H7 is the best-known strain in this group.

Escherichia coli is a large and varied group of bacteria. Most strains live harmlessly in the intestines of people and animals. Some cause illness, and the strains that produce Shiga toxin are behind the most severe E. coli infections.

The toxin takes its name from Kiyoshi Shiga, the Japanese microbiologist who identified Shigella dysenteriae. That bacterium makes a closely related toxin. Public health agencies in Europe often call the same group VTEC, for verocytotoxin-producing E. coli. The code O157:H7 identifies a strain by two markers. The O antigen sits on the bacterial surface, and the H antigen is found on its flagella.

Symptoms commonly begin about three to four days after exposure. The full range runs from one to 10 days.

The most serious complication is hemolytic uremic syndrome, or HUS, which damages the kidneys. It usually develops about a week after symptoms begin, often when the diarrhea is already improving. Children under five face particular risk. CDC lists decreased urination, unusual tiredness and loss of pink color in the cheeks and inside the lower eyelids as warning signs. People who develop HUS are usually hospitalized.

Common sources include undercooked ground beef, raw milk, raw flour, leafy greens and contaminated water. Ground beef carries extra risk because grinding spreads bacteria from the meat's surface throughout the patty. A whole steak is different. Contamination tends to stay on its outer surface, where cooking heat reaches it directly. Flour is a raw agricultural product that usually has not been treated to kill germs. That is why raw dough and batter can carry STEC.

Treatment differs from many other bacterial infections. CDC advises against antibiotics for suspected STEC infection. They may raise the risk of HUS. Whether to use any medication is a decision for a clinician rather than for self-treatment at home.

Listeria monocytogenes, the bacterium that causes listeriosis, can grow at refrigerator temperatures. That sets it apart from Salmonella and E. coli. It mainly threatens pregnant people, newborns, adults 65 and older and people with weakened immune systems.

Healthy adults who eat food contaminated with listeria often have a mild illness or no symptoms at all. The picture changes for people whose immune defenses are weaker. In those groups, the infection can spread beyond the intestines into the bloodstream or other parts of the body. That form is called invasive listeriosis. It is the form that can become life-threatening.

Invasive listeriosis usually begins with fever, muscle aches and tiredness. Those signs look much like the flu. They can also appear without the diarrhea and cramps many people associate with food poisoning. That can make the illness hard to connect to a meal at first.

When the infection reaches the nervous system, the symptoms change. A person may develop a headache, a stiff neck, confusion, loss of balance or convulsions.

Pregnancy carries a distinct set of risks. A pregnant person may have only a fever and other flu-like symptoms. The more serious effects can fall on the pregnancy itself. Listeriosis during pregnancy can cause miscarriage, stillbirth or premature delivery. The infection can also pass to the baby and lead to a life-threatening infection in the newborn.

The timeline makes listeria hard to trace. Symptoms often begin one to four weeks after a person eats contaminated food. The full range runs from the same day to about 70 days.

Ready-to-eat foods kept cold are a particular concern, because they are often eaten without further cooking. Listeria can also survive in food-processing plants and contaminate products after they have been cooked or packaged. The foods linked to listeria include deli meats and hot dogs eaten without being reheated until steaming hot. Heat kills the bacterium. Soft cheeses made from unpasteurized milk, refrigerated smoked seafood, raw sprouts and cantaloupe are also on the list.

Antibiotics are the standard treatment for listeriosis. The choice of drug and the length of treatment rest with a clinician, particularly for pregnant patients and newborns.

Timing is the clearest difference among these three foodborne bacteria. Salmonella often causes symptoms within hours to a few days. Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) usually takes about three to four days, and listeria can take weeks to appear.

Salmonella has the shortest window of the three. Symptoms can begin as soon as six hours after infection or as late as six days. Diarrhea and stomach cramps usually come with a fever. That fever helps separate Salmonella from STEC.

STEC falls in the middle. Most people notice symptoms about three to four days after exposure, within a full range of one to 10 days. Fever is usually absent or low. Diarrhea that turns bloody without much fever fits the STEC pattern more closely than the Salmonella one.

Listeria has the longest and widest window. Symptoms often appear one to four weeks after a person eats contaminated food. The full range stretches from the same day to about 70 days. A gap that long makes it hard to link the illness to a specific meal.

Listeria can also cause a short intestinal illness marked by diarrhea and vomiting. That form usually starts within 24 hours of eating contaminated food. It typically lasts one to three days.

The invasive form looks less like typical food poisoning. It tends to resemble the flu, with fever, muscle aches and tiredness, rather than centering on the gut. When the infection reaches the nervous system, a stiff neck and confusion can follow.

Salmonella and STEC overlap substantially. Both cause diarrhea and stomach cramps. Their onset windows overlap too. Salmonella can take up to six days to cause symptoms, and STEC can begin within one day. Listeria's onset range is wide enough to cover both.

Symptoms alone cannot reliably identify which bacterium is responsible. Timing and fever can narrow the possibilities, but they do not confirm a diagnosis. That takes a lab test.

A lab test, not a list of symptoms, confirms which bacterium caused an illness. Stool samples are the standard way to identify Salmonella and Shiga toxin-producing E. coli. Listeria is generally confirmed by culturing blood or, when the nervous system is involved, spinal fluid.

The choice of test follows where each infection does its damage. Salmonella and STEC infections center on the intestines. The evidence therefore shows up in a stool sample. Invasive listeriosis spreads beyond the gut. Clinicians look for that bacterium in the bloodstream or in the fluid surrounding the brain and spinal cord.

A confirmed result also lets public health officials connect individual cases to a shared source. That link is how a contaminated product can be traced and pulled from shelves.

Prevention starts with heat. CDC and USDA guidance calls for cooking ground beef to an internal temperature of 160°F and poultry to 165°F. A food thermometer is the only reliable way to check. USDA guidance holds that the color of meat is not a dependable sign that it is safe to eat.

Cold storage matters too. A refrigerator should hold at 40°F or below. The dial setting does not display an actual temperature. A separate appliance thermometer shows whether the refrigerator stays cold enough.

Bacteria also spread through cross-contamination, not only through undercooking. Wash hands with soap and water after handling raw meat. Keep raw meat away from ready-to-eat foods such as salads, bread and cooked dishes. That separation applies to cutting boards, plates and knives as well as to shelves in the refrigerator.

CDC and USDA guidance advises against drinking raw milk and eating soft cheese made from unpasteurized milk. Pasteurization heats milk to kill harmful bacteria. Skipping that step removes the protection. Pregnant people, adults 65 and older and people with weakened immune systems face added risk from cold, ready-to-eat foods. For them, heating deli-type foods until steaming hot lowers the danger.

Some symptoms call for medical care rather than waiting it out. These include bloody diarrhea, a high fever, signs of dehydration and diarrhea that lasts more than a few days. Any fever that comes with a stiff neck also needs prompt attention.
