#5595. From backyard chicks to hedgehogs: 10 animals that can pass on salmonella

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Pets that can carry salmonella include backyard chickens, turtles, bearded dragons, hedgehogs and dogs, and this guide explains how the germs spread and how to lower the risk

A pet can look perfectly healthy and still carry salmonella. Chicks, turtles, lizards, hamsters and even the family dog can harbor the bacteria in their intestines without showing any sign of illness. That makes appearance a poor guide to risk. The germs leave an animal in its droppings. From there, they spread to its fur, feathers or scales, and to its bedding, water, food and enclosure. People pick them up by touching the animal or anything it has touched, then touching their own mouths.

Food is the route most people associate with salmonella. Animal contact is a second, less obvious one. Salmonella is a group of bacteria, and the same germs that contaminate food can live in an animal's gut. Pet food can also bring the bacteria into a home, even before an animal touches it.

The illness usually brings diarrhea, fever and stomach cramps. Symptoms typically start between six hours and six days after exposure. Most healthy people recover in about four to seven days without treatment. Some people are more likely to become seriously ill, including young children, older adults and anyone with a weakened immune system.

Much of the exposure comes down to where an animal lives and what it touches. A backyard flock spreads germs through its coop and the shoes of whoever tends it. A turtle or frog sheds them into tank water. A hamster or guinea pig leaves them in its bedding. A dog or cat can pass them along through its food bowl.

This guide covers pets that can carry salmonella in 10 common categories, from chicks and ducklings to bearded dragons, snakes, hedgehogs, dogs and cats. It is a selection of familiar household and backyard animals rather than a complete list or a ranking. Each slide explains how the bacteria move from that particular animal to people and what precautions fit its habitat. Knowing where the germs collect makes it easier to keep them away from hands, kitchens and the people most vulnerable to them.

Backyard chickens and chicks can carry salmonella bacteria in their intestines while looking clean and healthy. A bird that seems well can still pass the germs to people who handle it or spend time around its living space.

The bacteria leave a bird's body in its droppings. From there, they reach the places and things the flock touches every day. Feathers, feet and beaks can all pick up contamination. So can the coop floor, nesting boxes, cages, feeders and water containers.

Salmonella generally does not make chickens visibly sick. An owner cannot sort safe birds from risky ones by looking at them. Every bird in a flock is best treated as a possible carrier.

Eggs can carry the germs too. Shells can become contaminated when hens lay in soiled nesting material. Salmonella can also be present inside an egg before the shell forms. Collecting eggs often, throwing away cracked ones, refrigerating the rest and cooking them until yolks and whites are firm lowers the chance of illness.

The germs travel on people as well as birds. Shoes worn in a run or coop carry droppings and bedding back toward the house. Clothing brushed against birds or dusty coop walls does the same. A separate pair of boots that stays outside the house limits how far contamination spreads.

The CDC advises keeping live poultry outside the home. That guidance covers young chicks, which are often raised indoors under a heat lamp during their first weeks. Housing a brooder in an outbuilding instead keeps feathers, dust and droppings away from living spaces.

Cleaning supplies belong outdoors too. Feeders, waterers and coop tools are safest scrubbed outside, away from household surfaces. Washing hands with soap and water right after collecting eggs, refilling feed or mucking out the coop closes a direct route from the flock to the mouth.

Ducklings, goslings and turkey poults can carry salmonella in their intestines while looking healthy. Holding, cuddling and kissing these young birds brings the bacteria close to a person's hands and mouth.

Young ducks, geese and turkeys all count as live poultry. They carry the same salmonella risk as baby chickens, and the same precautions apply to them.

Their soft down and small size invite close handling. A bird cupped in the hands or held against a cheek sits within inches of a person's face. Its feathers, feet and vent come along with it.

The CDC advises people not to kiss or snuggle poultry. That guidance covers lifting a bird to the face or holding it against the chest. A young bird can look clean and alert during that contact and still pass the germs to the person holding it.

Ducklings and goslings add another factor: water. They dabble in their drinking water and splash it into the surrounding bedding. The result is damp bedding mixed with droppings, which clings to hands that reach in to tidy it.

The CDC also says children younger than five should not handle poultry. That advice applies to ducklings, goslings and turkey poults as well as chicks. In a household with a toddler, an older child or adult takes on the holding and the brooder chores.

Washing hands with soap and water lowers the risk after contact with these birds. Wash right after holding a duckling, gosling or poult. Wash again after touching its brooder, bedding, feeder or water dish, including after refilling water or changing wet litter.

Pet turtles and tortoises often carry salmonella in their digestive tracts, even when they look healthy. Since 1975, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has banned U.S. sales of turtles with shells under four inches long, and the rule is still in force.

The size cutoff targets a specific problem. Small turtles fit easily into a child's hand. Young children are also more likely to put their fingers, or the animal itself, into their mouths. A turtle longer than four inches is harder to treat as a handheld toy.

The FDA rule covers selling and distributing small turtles as pets. It allows exceptions for scientific, educational and exhibition purposes. The rule does not mean larger turtles are free of the germs. A turtle of any size can carry salmonella.

Tortoises are land-dwelling turtles, and they are reptiles too. They can carry salmonella in the gut and pass it in their droppings. The substrate, hides and food dishes in a tortoise enclosure can become contaminated as a result.

Aquatic turtles add a second pathway: tank water. These turtles swim, eat and defecate in the same water. Germs can build up in that water and on the filter, gravel and decorations. Splashes during a water change can carry them onto counters, floors and clothing.

Tank water should never be poured down a kitchen sink. Tanks, filters and accessories should not be scrubbed there either. A sink used for dishes or produce puts the germs right next to food. Cleaning the tank outdoors keeps the mess out of the house. If a bathtub is the only option, it needs a thorough cleaning and disinfecting once the job is done.

Hands need soap and water at the end of every tank change. The same goes for after feeding and after lifting a turtle or tortoise out for a soak or a shell check. A turtle allowed to wander across the floor can leave germs behind. Keeping it in its enclosure limits the area that needs cleaning.

Buyers can check shell length before bringing a turtle home. A seller offering turtles under four inches as pets is breaking the federal rule.

A bearded dragon can carry salmonella in its gut and pass it in its droppings while appearing alert, eating well and showing no sign of illness.

Bearded dragons are lizards native to Australia. The species most often kept as a pet is the central bearded dragon, Pogona vitticeps, which comes from the country's arid interior. Its calm temperament and tolerance of handling have made it a common pet lizard in U.S. homes.

That same tolerance shapes how the germs move. Owners often hold a bearded dragon on a lap or shoulder, let it rest on furniture, or feed it greens and insects by hand. Each of those contacts involves skin, claws or a mouth that may have touched droppings.

The enclosure is the second main route. Bacteria shed in feces can spread across the substrate, rocks, branches, hides and the food and water dishes. Basking platforms the lizard climbs on and rests against belong to the same contaminated space.

The risk does not stay inside the tank. Dishes, decor pulled out for cleaning and the lizard itself can carry bacteria onto floors, rugs and countertops. A bearded dragon allowed to roam a room can leave germs on every surface it crosses.

Bathing is a common part of bearded dragon care. Owners often soak the lizard in shallow warm water, and a household bathtub used for that purpose becomes another contact surface. Cleaning and disinfecting the tub afterward, or using a dedicated plastic basin, keeps the soak separate from human bathing.

Live feeder insects add another route. Crickets and roaches released into the tank share the enclosure with the animal's waste. Their containers and any uneaten greens should be treated as part of that same space.

Washing hands with soap and water belongs at the end of every session with a bearded dragon. That means after holding it, after feeding it, after rearranging its enclosure and after removing waste.

Pet snakes can carry salmonella, and the risk comes from two places: handling the animal and cleaning its enclosure. All reptiles can carry the bacteria, according to the CDC. That includes common pet species such as corn snakes and ball pythons.

In reptiles, salmonella lives in the gut and leaves the body in droppings. Inside an enclosure, the germs can then reach the snake's skin, its water bowl, its substrate and the hides and branches it moves across.

Handling is the first route. Snakes are often held for long stretches, draped over hands, arms or shoulders. That brings the animal's skin into contact with sleeves, collars and bare arms, not only fingers. Washing hands with soap and water after returning the snake to its enclosure keeps the germs from reaching the mouth, a phone or a doorknob.

Enclosure cleaning is the second route. It carries risk even when the snake is never touched. Rearranging a hide, scooping out soiled substrate or refilling a water dish all mean contact with surfaces the animal has used.

The water bowl needs particular care. Many snakes soak in their bowls, and some defecate in them. That puts droppings directly into water the keeper later handles. Keeping the bowl and spot-cleaning tools separate from household dishes and cleaning supplies limits where the germs can travel. Handwashing after each cleaning session closes off this route.

Feeding adds a third point of contact. Many pet snakes eat whole rodents, often bought frozen and thawed before feeding, though some keepers offer live prey. Rodents can carry salmonella too. That means the bacteria can enter the home with the food itself.

Feeding tongs keep hands off the prey item. An uneaten thawed rodent goes in the trash rather than back in the freezer. Washing hands after thawing and offering a rodent covers the contact the tongs miss.

Leopard geckos and other pet lizards can carry salmonella on their skin and on the surfaces inside their enclosures. The risk matters most in homes with children younger than five, adults 65 and older, or anyone with a weakened immune system. Those groups are more likely to develop serious illness.

The leopard gecko, Eublepharis macularius, is a small ground-dwelling lizard. It is native to dry, rocky regions of Afghanistan, Pakistan, northwest India and Iran. In captivity it lives in a glass or plastic terrarium and eats live insects such as crickets and mealworms. Unlike most geckos, it has movable eyelids and cannot climb smooth glass.

None of those traits changes its germ risk. The CDC says all reptiles can carry salmonella. That applies to crested geckos, green anoles, blue-tongued skinks and green iguanas as much as to leopard geckos. A lizard that looks alert and eats well can still have the bacteria on its body.

Young children face a higher risk for two reasons. Their immune systems are still developing. That makes a serious infection more likely. They also tend to put their hands, toys and other objects in their mouths. That gives germs picked up from a lizard's skin a direct route inside.

The enclosure is a second source of exposure. Substrate, hides, water dishes and decorations can all hold germs from droppings. A child who reaches into a terrarium to touch a basking rock can pick up bacteria without ever holding the animal.

Adults 65 and older face the same exposures with a greater chance of severe illness. So do people whose immune systems are weakened by chemotherapy, HIV or drugs taken after an organ transplant. In these groups, salmonella is more likely to spread beyond the gut and into the bloodstream.

In a household with any of these higher-risk members, other adults can take on the handling and the tank maintenance. Scrubbing hands with soap and water right after touching the lizard or reaching into its tank removes germs before they reach a face, a snack or a toddler. Keeping the lizard off couches, beds and children's play areas limits how far the bacteria travel through the home.

Pet frogs can carry salmonella, and the CDC says amphibians share this risk with reptiles. For fully aquatic species, the main exposure is the tank water itself, which picks up the bacteria the frog sheds.

Amphibians are the animal group that includes frogs, toads, salamanders and newts. Many pet amphibians spend part of their lives on land. Fully aquatic frogs, such as African dwarf frogs and African clawed frogs, spend their whole lives underwater. The axolotl, a salamander kept in home aquariums, also stays in the water for life. Everything they shed ends up in the water around them.

The bacteria live in an infected animal's gut and leave the body in droppings. In an aquarium, those droppings break down in the same water that fills the tank. From there, the germs reach the glass, the gravel, any decorations and the filter.

A person does not need to touch the frog to be exposed. Reaching into the tank to move a plant, net out debris or adjust a heater puts hands in direct contact with the water. Changing the water or rinsing a filter cartridge does the same.

Splashes carry the water farther. Drips from a net, a siphon hose or a bucket can land on floors, tables and nearby surfaces. Those spots can then pass the bacteria to anyone who touches them later.

Washing hands with soap and water belongs at the end of every tank task, not only after picking up the frog. That includes feeding, topping up the water and wiping down the glass. Wiping up spilled tank water and cleaning the surfaces it touched limits how far the germs travel.

Nets, buckets, siphons and scrubbing pads stay in regular contact with the tank water. Keeping those tools for tank use only stops them from carrying the bacteria into other household chores.

Hamsters, mice and rats kept as pets can carry salmonella, and the CDC has linked outbreaks of human illness to pet rodents. A rodent that looks healthy and clean can still pass the germs to people.

Inside a cage, contaminated droppings can reach almost every surface. Bedding, food dishes, water bottles, exercise wheels, tunnels and chew toys can all carry the germs.

That makes the enclosure a source of infection in its own right. A person can pick up salmonella while changing bedding or refilling a bowl without touching the hamster, mouse or rat at all.

Regular cage cleaning is the first of two main precautions for these pets. Removing soiled bedding and wiping down cage surfaces and accessories limits the buildup of contaminated material. Wheels and tunnels have seams and corners where droppings collect, so they need scrubbing rather than a quick wipe.

Disposable gloves keep droppings off the skin during the job. They should come off carefully, because a glove's dirty outer surface can brush the skin as it is pulled away.

The location of that cleaning matters too. Doing it outdoors, or in a utility area away from shared living spaces, keeps dirty bedding and rinse water from spreading germs through the home.

The second precaution is washing hands with soap and water right after holding the animal or touching anything from its cage. Pet rodents are often carried around and passed between family members. Each of those contacts gives germs a chance to move from fur and paws to hands. When a sink is not nearby, hand sanitizer can serve until a proper wash is possible.

Many families buy a hamster, mouse or rat for a child. Adults can supervise young owners during handling and check that they scrub their hands afterward. Holding a rodent against the face gives the germs a short path to the mouth. Kissing a pet rodent carries the same risk. So does snacking while handling one.

Pet hedgehogs and guinea pigs can carry salmonella without showing any sign of illness. The bacteria pass in their droppings and settle into their bedding, where they can reach anyone who handles the animal or its cage.

The two animals are often grouped together as small pets, but they are not close relatives. Guinea pigs are rodents that were domesticated in the Andes of South America. The hedgehogs sold as pets in the U.S. are usually African pygmy hedgehogs. They belong to a separate group of insect-eating mammals. What the two share is a living arrangement: a small enclosure lined with bedding where the animal walks, sleeps and leaves its droppings.

The CDC has linked salmonella outbreaks in people to pet hedgehogs. A hedgehog's spines and skin can pick up germs from its own bedding. Letting the animal roam across a couch, bed or carpet gives those germs more surfaces to reach.

Hedgehogs are nocturnal and do much of their running at night. Their exercise wheels and litter areas often collect droppings overnight. Scrubbing a soiled wheel is a direct point of contact with fresh waste. Washing hands with soap and water right after cleaning the wheel limits the chance of carrying bacteria back into the house.

Guinea pigs bring a different pattern. They graze on hay and fresh vegetables through the day and produce a large volume of droppings. Their bedding gets soiled quickly. Hay racks, hideouts and water bottles all sit inside the same space. Bagging soiled bedding and sealing it, rather than shaking it out indoors, keeps dust and droppings contained.

Guinea pigs are social animals and are commonly kept in pairs or small groups. More animals mean more bedding to change and more handling. Children often hold guinea pigs on their laps. Washing hands right after lap time, and after refilling the hay, cuts the chance that germs from the pet reach a child's mouth.

Dogs and cats can carry salmonella without showing any signs of illness. The food and treats they eat can also bring the germs into a home. Raw pet food and some chews, including pig ear treats tied to a 2019 outbreak, have been linked to human infections.

A healthy-looking dog or cat can pass salmonella in its feces. From there, the germs can end up on fur, paws and bedding, as well as in the yard or litter box. People can pick them up by petting the animal, scooping a litter box or bagging waste on a walk.

Raw diets are one way the bacteria get in. Raw meat-based pet foods can contain salmonella, much like raw meat sold for people. Freezing or freeze-drying the food does not reliably kill the bacteria. A dog or cat eating a raw diet can shed the germs in its feces while appearing well.

Preparing a raw diet creates exposure separate from contact with the animal. Thawing raw patties on a counter, portioning food by hand or wiping up spills with a dish towel can move bacteria onto surfaces used for human meals.

Treats can carry the bacteria too. In 2019, the CDC linked a multistate salmonella outbreak to pig ear dog treats. Chews like these are handled often. They pass back and forth between a person's hand and a dog's mouth. Each handoff gives the germs another chance to reach skin and nearby surfaces.

For dog and cat owners, handwashing is tied to feeding and cleanup. Wash hands with soap and water after feeding a pet, handing out treats, cleaning bowls or picking up waste. Bowls and scoops need a wash with soap and hot water. Use a dedicated scoop for pet food rather than a cup or spoon from the family's dishes.

Pet food and bowls belong away from where people cook and eat. Store pet food separately from human food. Keep dogs and cats off kitchen counters and other food-preparation areas. Feeding pets in a mudroom or laundry room, rather than the kitchen, keeps their meals apart from the family's.

#5593. From raw oysters to leftover rice: 10 foods tied to foodborne illness

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These 10 foods that cause food poisoning, from raw oysters to leftover rice, carry specific bacteria and viruses, and simple handling habits lower the risk

A bout of food poisoning can usually be traced to a particular germ that found its way into a particular food. Salmonella travels with poultry and eggs. Listeria survives the cold of a refrigerator. Vibrio bacteria collect in oysters that filter seawater. Knowing which pairing is at work explains why some foods call for more care than others.

Foodborne illness is the broad term for sickness caused by bacteria, viruses, parasites or toxins in what people eat and drink. The foods linked to it tend to share a few traits. Some come from animals that carry bacteria in their gut or environment. Some are eaten raw, which removes the cooking step that would otherwise kill whatever is present. Others become a problem after cooking, through the way they are cooled and stored.

That last group shows that safe ingredients are only part of the picture. A pot of rice left on the counter can let bacterial spores that survived cooking germinate and produce toxins. Here, the risk comes from handling rather than from the raw ingredient.

The list below covers 10 foods that cause food poisoning when something goes wrong in how they are produced, prepared or stored. It is a selection, not a ranking, and the order carries no meaning. It spans animal products such as chicken, eggs, ground beef, raw milk, deli meats and oysters. It also includes raw produce such as leafy greens, sprouts and cantaloupe, along with one common leftover.

Home food safety comes down to four steps: clean, separate, cook and chill. Clean means washing hands, utensils and surfaces. Separate means keeping raw meat, poultry, seafood and eggs away from foods that will be eaten without cooking. Cook means heating food to a safe internal temperature. Chill means getting perishable food into the refrigerator promptly.

Each slide explains the pathogen tied to one food, how contamination happens and the handling habits that lower the risk for that item. Pregnant women, older adults, young children and people with weakened immune systems face higher stakes from several of these foods. For them, the details on each slide carry extra weight.

Raw or undercooked chicken is a common route to food poisoning because poultry often carries Salmonella and Campylobacter. U.S. government guidance is to cook all poultry to an internal temperature of 165 degrees Fahrenheit. That temperature kills both bacteria.

Both organisms live in the intestines of healthy birds. They can reach the meat during slaughter and processing. A chicken breast can look clean and smell fresh while still carrying bacteria on its surface. The same applies to turkey, duck and other poultry.

Thorough cooking is the step that makes poultry safe to eat. A food thermometer shows when the meat has reached that temperature. For a whole bird, check the innermost part of the thigh, the innermost part of the wing and the thickest part of the breast. Keep the probe away from the bone. Touching bone can produce an inaccurate reading.

Ground chicken and ground turkey follow the same 165-degree target as whole cuts. So does stuffing cooked inside a bird. Stuffing absorbs raw juices from the cavity and needs to reach the same temperature as the meat around it.

Washing raw chicken before cooking adds risk rather than removing it. Rinsing under the tap does not kill Salmonella or Campylobacter. Water splashing off the meat can carry bacteria onto the sink, nearby counters, dish towels and any food sitting close by. Cooking to 165 degrees Fahrenheit already destroys the bacteria. A rinse adds nothing to that protection.

Raw poultry juices create a second route for illness through cross-contamination. A cutting board used for raw chicken can pass bacteria to salad vegetables or bread chopped on it afterward. Knives, plates, tongs and hands can do the same. Separate boards for raw meat and ready-to-eat foods reduce that risk. Hot, soapy water cleans boards and utensils between uses. Hands need washing with soap after touching raw poultry.

Refrigerator placement matters too. Raw chicken kept on a lower shelf, sealed in a container or set on a plate, cannot drip onto foods below it. Marinade that held raw poultry should not go on cooked food as a sauce unless it is boiled first.

Salmonella can be present inside an intact egg, not only on its shell. Raw or runny egg dishes can cause food poisoning even when the egg looks clean and uncracked.

The obvious place to look for contamination is the outside of the egg, where dirt or droppings might touch the shell. Shell $SHEL contamination does happen. Salmonella can also reach the yolk or white before the shell forms, when a hen carries the bacteria in her reproductive tract. A spotless egg straight from the carton can still hold the bacteria inside.

Thorough cooking kills Salmonella. The concern centers on foods in which the egg is eaten raw or only lightly heated. Homemade mayonnaise is a common example. It is made by whisking raw yolks with oil, with no cooking step at all.

Pasteurized eggs offer a practical swap for recipes that call for raw egg. In-shell pasteurized eggs are heated in a warm water bath long enough to kill bacteria without cooking the egg. Pasteurized liquid egg products sold in cartons serve the same purpose in dressings, sauces and desserts.

For eggs eaten on their own, cooking until both the yolk and the white are firm kills Salmonella. Sunny-side-up, poached and soft-boiled eggs leave the yolk runny. That leaves more room for any bacteria inside to survive. Cracked eggs give bacteria an easier way in and are safer thrown away. Storing eggs in their carton on a refrigerator shelf, rather than in the door, keeps them colder and more consistent in temperature.

Ground beef should be cooked to an internal temperature of 160 degrees Fahrenheit under U.S. guidance, because grinding spreads surface bacteria through the whole piece of meat. E. coli O157:H7 is the pathogen most associated with undercooked burgers.

These bacteria live in the intestines of cattle. During slaughter and processing, they can end up on the outer surface of a cut of beef.

On a whole steak or roast, that outer layer is where the bacteria stay. The dense interior of an intact cut is generally protected. Searing the outside exposes surface bacteria to direct heat. For that reason, a rare steak carries a different risk than a rare burger.

Grinding removes that protection. The process takes whatever sat on the surface and mixes it through the entire batch. One batch of ground beef can also combine trimmings from more than one animal. Bacteria from a single source can then end up in many patties.

The center of a burger is no safer than its edge. A patty with a dark, seared crust can still hold live bacteria in an undercooked middle.

A food thermometer settles the question. For a burger, push the probe in through the side of the patty until the tip reaches the thickest part. A reading taken from the top of a thin patty can put the tip too close to the hot surface. That can overstate the temperature at the center.

E. coli O157:H7 produces a toxin known as Shiga toxin. In serious cases, an infection can damage the kidneys. Young children and older adults face a greater risk of these complications.

The 160-degree target covers every dish built on ground beef, not only burgers. Meatloaf, meatballs, chili and stuffed peppers all start from the same mixed meat. U.S. guidance sets the same temperature for ground pork, veal and lamb. Raw preparations such as steak tartare, made from chopped or minced beef, skip the cooking step entirely.

At restaurants, a burger served rare or medium-rare has not reached the temperature U.S. guidance sets for ground beef. Diners who want to meet that standard can ask for a burger cooked to 160 degrees.

Raw oysters can concentrate Vibrio bacteria and norovirus from the water they grow in. Eating them uncooked means swallowing whatever the oyster has collected, with no heat step to kill it.

The risk starts with how oysters feed. They are filter feeders that pump large volumes of seawater across their gills to strain out plankton and other particles. Bacteria and viruses in that water can build up inside the animal. Clams and mussels feed the same way. The concern therefore extends to other bivalve shellfish served raw.

An oyster is also eaten whole, gut included. A fish fillet is different. Its digestive organs are removed before it reaches the plate.

Vibrio bacteria occur naturally in coastal salt water and brackish water. Their presence is not a sign of sewage or pollution. Warmer water favors their growth. An oyster from a clean, well-managed bed can still carry them.

One species, Vibrio vulnificus, is a particular danger for people with liver disease or weakened immunity. In those groups an infection can turn severe. People with a chronic liver condition should avoid raw oysters entirely. The same caution applies to anyone whose immune system is suppressed by illness or medical treatment.

Norovirus reaches shellfish by a different route. It enters growing waters through human waste, from sources such as sewage overflows or boats discharging untreated waste. It is a common cause of vomiting and diarrhea. It also spreads easily from person to person once someone is infected.

Popular toppings offer no protection. Lemon juice and hot sauce do not kill the bacteria. A fresh smell and a clean, glossy appearance cannot reveal whether an oyster carries Vibrio or norovirus.

Heat is what lowers the risk. Fried oysters, oyster stew, grilled oysters and steamed mussels carry less risk than the same shellfish served raw on ice. When steaming clams, mussels or oysters in the shell, throw out any that stay closed after cooking. Shucked oysters should be cooked through until the flesh is firm.

Raw milk, meaning milk that has not been pasteurized, can carry Listeria, Salmonella, E. coli and Campylobacter. Pasteurization kills these organisms. That heating step is the main safeguard between a glass of milk or a wedge of soft cheese and a possible infection.

Bacteria can enter milk at several points before it reaches a bottle. An infected udder can shed germs directly into the milk. Traces of manure on the animal's skin or on milking equipment can add more. A clean-looking farm and a healthy-looking animal offer no guarantee. These organisms are invisible, and they do not change the taste or smell of the milk.

Pasteurization addresses that problem with heat. Milk is warmed to a set temperature, held there for a set time, then cooled quickly. The process takes its name from Louis Pasteur, the 19th-century French scientist whose work showed that heating could kill microbes in wine and beer. Pasteurization does not sterilize milk. Pasteurized milk still needs refrigeration, and it will still spoil over time.

Soft cheeses made from raw milk carry the same risk in another form. Styles such as brie, camembert and queso fresco are higher in moisture and lower in acid than many hard cheeses. When they are made from raw milk, bacteria in the milk can carry through into the finished cheese. Fresh Latin-style cheeses such as queso fresco are sometimes sold informally, outside regular stores. That makes their origin and production method harder to check.

Listeria is the main concern with these cheeses. Pregnant women, older adults and young children face greater risk from it than other people. In pregnancy, a Listeria infection can pass to the baby, even when the mother feels only mildly unwell.

The practical step is reading the label. In the U.S., look for the word "pasteurized" on milk and cheese packaging. Rules on selling raw milk differ from state to state. As a result, what shoppers find on shelves varies by location. At restaurants, farmers markets and when traveling abroad, asking whether a soft cheese is made from pasteurized milk is the most direct check.

Deli meats and hot dogs can carry Listeria monocytogenes, a bacterium that survives refrigeration. These foods are sold ready to eat, so there is often no cooking step at home to kill it.

Cold slows most foodborne bacteria sharply. Listeria behaves differently. It can keep growing slowly at refrigerator temperatures. A package of sliced turkey or a pack of franks can become riskier the longer it sits in the fridge.

Contamination usually happens after the meat has been cooked. Ham, bologna, salami and roast beef are processed, then sliced, handled and packaged. Listeria can reach the meat during those later steps, from equipment or surfaces in a processing plant. Meat sliced to order at a deli counter passes through one more machine before it reaches the customer.

Hot dogs follow a similar path. They are fully cooked before packaging, and many people eat them straight from the package. That habit skips the one step that would destroy bacteria picked up after the factory cooking.

Listeria poses a particular risk during pregnancy. An infection can pass to the fetus, even when the mother has mild symptoms or none at all. U.S. food safety guidance advises pregnant people to heat deli meats and hot dogs until steaming hot before eating them. The same guidance covers older adults and people with weakened immune systems. Thorough heating kills Listeria. A quick warm-up that leaves the center cool does not.

A refrigerator set at 40 degrees Fahrenheit or below keeps many bacteria in check. A refrigerator thermometer confirms that setting. Many refrigerator dials use numbered settings rather than actual degrees.

Cold storage alone does not stop Listeria, though. Eating opened packages of deli meat promptly limits the time the bacteria have to multiply. Keeping the liquid from hot dog packages away from other foods and kitchen surfaces also matters. That fluid can carry Listeria too.

Romaine lettuce, spinach and other leafy greens can carry E. coli and other bacteria straight to the plate. They are usually eaten raw, so no cooking step stands between a contaminated leaf and the person eating it.

That habit sets greens apart from many foods linked to foodborne illness. A chicken breast or a burger patty gets heated to a temperature that kills bacteria. A salad does not. Whatever reaches a leaf in the field or the packing shed can still be on it at dinner.

E. coli outbreaks in the U.S. have been traced to leafy greens, and romaine and spinach have both been involved. The strains behind these outbreaks produce Shiga toxin. They can cause serious stomach illness. In some people, especially young children, the infection can lead to kidney damage.

Contamination can start long before harvest. Irrigation water, runoff from nearby livestock operations and animal droppings in fields can carry bacteria onto growing plants. Harvesting, chopping and packing give those bacteria more chances to spread. Cutting damages the leaf, and bacteria can lodge in its torn edges and crevices.

Bagged salads go through a commercial wash, but a pre-washed label does not mean the contents are sterile. Bagged greens still need to stay refrigerated. They should be used before the date printed on the package.

Whole heads and loose bunches call for a few steps at home. Remove the outer leaves first. Rinse the remaining leaves under running water just before eating, rather than soaking them in a sink of standing water. Soap and bleach are not meant for produce and should not be used on it.

Rinsing removes some dirt and germs, but it cannot remove every bacterium clinging to a leaf. Greens that are damaged, slimy or wilted belong in the trash. Refrigerating cut or chopped greens promptly limits how much any bacteria present can grow.

Heat changes the picture. Spinach, kale and other sturdy greens cooked until fully wilted, as in a sauté or soup, no longer carry the same raw-produce risk.

Raw sprouts carry a food poisoning risk that begins before they ever reach a store shelf. The warm, humid conditions used to sprout alfalfa, mung bean and clover seeds also let bacteria multiply quickly.

Sprouting depends on moisture and warmth. Growers soak the seeds in water, then keep them damp and warm for several days while they germinate. Salmonella, E. coli and Listeria grow well in those same conditions. A small number of bacteria on a seed can become a much larger population by the time the sprouts are harvested.

The seed itself is often the source. Bacteria can sit on the seed coat, lodge in its cracks or get inside the seed. From there they travel into the finished sprout. That sets sprouts apart from many other raw vegetables. The contamination does not have to come from a dirty knife or a careless shopper — it can be part of the product from the start.

Rinsing does little to solve the problem. Water can wash some bacteria off the surface. It cannot reach organisms that have grown inside the sprout. A thorough wash at the kitchen sink does not make raw sprouts safe.

Growing sprouts at home does not remove the hazard either. A sprouting jar on a countertop recreates the same warm, wet environment a commercial grower uses. Contaminated seeds bring their bacteria into the jar with them. Home-grown sprouts can carry the same risk as store-bought ones.

The way people eat sprouts adds to the concern. Alfalfa and clover sprouts usually go raw onto sandwiches, wraps and salads. Mung bean sprouts often arrive as a fresh garnish on dishes such as pho or pad thai. They are served raw on the side or scattered on top.

Cooking is the step that lowers the risk. Stir-frying bean sprouts, or simmering them in soup until they are steaming hot, reaches bacteria that rinsing leaves behind. When ordering at a restaurant, diners can ask for sprouts to be cooked or left off the plate.

The stakes are higher for some people. Listeria poses a greater danger to pregnant women, older adults and young children. People in those groups, and anyone with a weakened immune system, can choose cooked sprouts instead of raw ones.

Cooked rice left at room temperature is a common source of food poisoning from Bacillus cereus. The bacterium's spores survive cooking, then germinate as the rice cools and produce toxins that reheating may not destroy.

Bacillus cereus lives in soil and dust. It can reach rice grains in the field, and dry, uncooked rice can carry its spores into a home kitchen. A spore is a dormant, hardy form of the bacterium. Boiling or steaming kills active bacteria, but spores can come through the pot intact.

The danger builds after the meal is served. A full pot left on the stove or counter cools slowly. On the way down, it passes through temperatures where the spores can become active again. Once they germinate, the bacteria multiply and release toxins directly into the rice.

One of those toxins causes vomiting. It withstands heat, so warming leftover rice does not necessarily make it safe to eat. A microwave or a hot wok can kill the bacteria while leaving the toxin behind. Bacillus cereus can also cause a separate, diarrheal form of illness.

This pattern is sometimes called fried rice syndrome. The name reflects a familiar sequence in restaurant and home kitchens. Rice is cooked in a large batch, held at room temperature, then stir-fried later. Fast, high-heat frying warms the grains. It cannot be relied on to break down toxin that has already formed.

Speed is the main defense. A deep pot keeps its center warm for longer, so cooked rice should not be left to cool in the pot it was made in. Spreading it in a shallow container lets heat escape faster. Then it should go into the refrigerator promptly.

Time limits apply as well. Perishable food, including cooked rice, should not sit out for more than two hours. When the air is above 90 degrees Fahrenheit, such as at a summer picnic, the limit drops to one hour. Rice that has passed those limits belongs in the trash, not the microwave.

The same habits apply to takeout, buffet trays and rice cooked ahead for weekday lunches. The risk is not limited to rice. Other cooked starches, such as pasta, can also carry Bacillus cereus and need the same prompt cooling.

A cantaloupe's rough, netted rind can trap bacteria, and a knife passing through it can carry them into the flesh. Listeria and Salmonella have both been linked to cantaloupe. The rind needs cleaning even though nobody eats it.

The netting on a cantaloupe is a web of raised ridges and shallow crevices. The fruit grows in contact with the ground. Soil, irrigation water and handling all leave material on the surface before a melon reaches a kitchen. Bacteria can settle into those grooves, where a quick splash of water may not reach them.

The main hazard comes during preparation. A blade enters at the rind and travels straight into the edible flesh. Anything sitting on the outside can ride along on the knife edge. The same transfer happens when cut slices are pushed across a cutting board that the unwashed fruit touched moments earlier.

Once inside, bacteria land on a moist, sweet and low-acid surface. Those conditions do little to slow bacterial growth. U.S. food safety rules for restaurants and stores treat cut melon as a perishable food that must be kept cold. A whole, uncut melon does not fall under that requirement.

Scrubbing the rind before cutting is the standard first step. A clean produce brush under cool running water can work into the netting better than fingers alone. U.S. food safety guidance calls for plain water rather than soap, detergent or bleach when washing produce. Patting the melon dry with a clean towel removes more of the loosened material.

Smooth-skinned honeydew and watermelon call for the same routine. Their rinds have fewer crevices to hide bacteria. They still grew in a field and passed through many hands on the way to a shopping cart.

After cutting, the pieces belong in a covered container in the refrigerator. A platter of sliced melon left sitting on a picnic or buffet table loses that protection. Pre-cut melon from a grocery store should come from a refrigerated case and go straight into the fridge at home.

The stakes are higher for groups more vulnerable to Listeria, including pregnant people and older adults. Washing and cutting a whole melon at home lets them know how the fruit was handled and how long ago it was cut. Pre-cut cubes of unknown age offer no such record.

#5592. AWS’ Colleen Aubrey: Stop inventing new AI metrics — it’s your business metrics that matter

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

There isn’t a business or information technology leader today who doesn’t have artificial intelligence at the top of their priority list. The challenge for most organizations is deciding what to measure and how to determine whether an AI initiative was successful.

To better understand how customers should approach AI metrics, I spoke with Colleen Aubrey from Amazon Web Services Inc,, who has some deep experience in this area.

As senior vice president of Applied AI Solutions at AWS and a member of Amazon’s S-team, she builds on that foundation with lessons from 20-plus years at Amazon, where she built customer-facing products for millions of sellers and advertisers. The playbook she drew from that experience gives enterprises a practical path to move out of AI pilot purgatory, and it starts with throwing out the AI return-on-investment slide.

She argues that understanding AI ROI requires thinking in terms of business metrics. “I worry that people start trying to come up with new metrics to measure the impact of AI, but it’s the same metrics,” she explained. “It’s your business metrics that matter.” AWS has spent 20 years building cloud infrastructure. AI business applications are a much newer opportunity.

When Aubrey joined AWS, she inherited 35 application-layer programs. “I would say Connect for the contact center was probably our most successful example,” she told me in a recent interview ahead of AWS re:Invent Nov. 30-Dec. 4.

She studied what made it work: The team had deep operational experience running Amazon’s customer service function; it chose a sharp wedge (outstanding voice quality on the AWS backbone rather than chasing feature parity; and the team knew its customers. The lessons from that success are now the blueprint for the expanded Amazon Connect family: Connect Customer, Connect Talent, Connect Health and Connect Decisions.

The playbook Aubrey built for the Connect family closely mirrors what IT leaders need to move their own AI programs out of pilot mode. Here are my five takeaways that should matter to IT leaders:

The first lesson Aubrey drew from her assessment was about where to start. Nobody runs a better supply chain than Amazon, which is exactly why the early version of AWS Supply Chain was such a useful learning experience. When Aubrey got close to the product, she saw a team working to catch up rather than lead. They had been building five modules that “largely were about getting to feature parity” with entrenched enterprise resource planning vendors that had a decades-long head start.

Connect had taken the opposite path, and it’s instructive. “They understood they weren’t going to achieve feature parity,” Aubrey said of the Connect team. Instead, they led with outstanding voice quality on the AWS backbone, started narrow and built from there.

Aubrey applied that same lesson to the supply chain. She rebooted it as Connect Decisions by asking a different question: where is the pain most acute, and where is the current tooling weakest? The answer was planners. “They’re firefighting the whole time,” she said. “They’re overwhelmed by a whole bunch of signals. By the time they get to decide, the moment has passed.”

The same applies to enterprises. AI projects that stall often try to replicate an entire workflow. The ones that succeed identify a painful decision point and make it dramatically better.

Aubrey’s point about measurement deserves unpacking. “Companies are stuck on what’s the ROI of AI, and they’re looking at return on tokens and this sort of stuff,” she said. “The question is, can you move your business metrics by working in a different way?”

Her proof point is Wells Vehicle Electronics, which, according to AWS, cut inventory by 7% in three months while expanding the SKUs they actively monitor from 20 to 2,000. Nobody at Wells is talking about tokens. They’re talking about working capital. If a project can’t be tied to a metric the chief financial officer already tracks, it’s an experiment, not an investment.

Amazon started where most companies start: with software development, making AI tools available across the company. Aubrey admits there’s a bit of chaos at first. “Everyone’s just experimenting with a bunch of things,” Aubrey said.

She sees that as a feature, not a bug, because that’s where the real learning happens. “You go through this learning period of, you know what, our test coverage sucks,” she said. Fix test coverage, and you find “our pipelines suck,” so you fix pipeline health, eliminate manual intervention and deploy faster. The result in her group this year: a twofold improvement in the velocity of pushes to production.

The lesson is that the velocity didn’t come from the coding assistant. It came from fixing everything downstream that the assistant exposed. Enterprises that buy the tool and skip the plumbing will see activity rise while output stays flat.

I asked Aubrey whether Amazon has adjusted its goals to reflect what employees can now do with AI. Her answer was an honest “yes and no.” In her user experience team, roles have collapsed: designers are being pushed to ship code to an alpha environment, and Amazon has created a new “UX tech” role.

The “no” is that org design and goal-setting are still catching up. Her message to her team is blunt: “The only choice you can’t make is to own the task. You have to choose to own the outcome.” Every IT leader should borrow that line. Task-based job descriptions will age poorly.

AWS’s design philosophy for the Connect family is what she calls “humorphism,” the idea that AI should fit the way people already work, not the other way around. Her biggest concern is the lag between internal prototypes and production.

“Shipping good AI with a bad user experience will fail, in my opinion,” she said. Her team has invested heavily in closing that gap, moving beyond traditional command-based interfaces toward AI that picks up cues, remembers decisions, and carries work forward. The goal, she said, is to make AI so usable that people change how they work, not because they’re told to, but because it makes sense.

She was equally candid about maturity. TE Connectivity has scaled Connect Decisions to 2,000 planners, but Connect Talent reached general availability only in September and has early customers in deployment. Aubrey said the team is focused on getting the product right before aggressively scaling, reflecting the same “pick a wedge” discipline she applied across the Connect solutions.

What made this conversation valuable was Aubrey’s willingness to share how she thinks about building AI products that work in production, from studying what made Connect successful to applying those lessons across supply chain, hiring, health care, and customer engagement. That candor is a useful model for IT leaders, because most enterprise AI programs are stuck for the same reasons AWS’s applications once were: too much breadth, too little focus and success measured by the wrong yardstick.

The AI era won’t reward companies with the most pilots. It will reward those that pick a sharp problem, fix the plumbing it exposes, redesign work around outcomes and move the metrics they already have.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5591. Mynd.ai Announces Change to American Depositary Share Ratio

ALPHARETTA, Ga., Nov. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Mynd.ai, Inc. (NYSE: MYND) ("Mynd" or the "Company"), a global provider of interactive technology and AI solutions for education and commercial customers, today announced that it will change the ratio of its American Depositary Shares ("ADSs") to its ordinary shares from one ADS representing ten (10) ordinary shares to a new ratio of one ADS representing seventy-five (75) ordinary shares. For the Company's ADS holders, the change in the ADS ratio will have the same effect as a one-for-7.5 reverse ADS split.

The ADS ratio change is expected to become effective on or about December 7, 2027 (U.S. Eastern Time), subject to completion of the applicable procedures with the Company's depositary, Citibank, N.A. (the "Depositary"), and other relevant parties. The ADSs will continue to trade on the NYSE American under the symbol "MYND," with a new CUSIP number of 628988206.

Following the effectiveness of the change, each ADS will represent seventy-five (75) ordinary shares of the Company, compared with ten (10) ordinary shares previously. The ordinary shares of the Company will not be affected by the change in the ADS ratio, and no ordinary shares will be issued or cancelled in connection with it.

The exchange of every seven and one-half (7.5) then-held ADSs for one new ADS is expected to occur automatically on the effective date, with the then-held ADSs being cancelled and new ADSs issued by the Depositary. Fractional new ADSs will not be issued in connection with the change in the ADS ratio. Instead, fractional entitlements to new ADSs will be aggregated and sold by the Depositary, and the net cash proceeds from the sale, after deduction of applicable fees, taxes and expenses, will be distributed to the applicable ADS holders in accordance with the terms of the deposit agreement.

ADS holders are not required to take any action. ADSs held in brokerage accounts will be adjusted automatically, and holders of certificated ADSs will receive instructions from the Depositary. The Company will pay the Depositary's fees and charges in connection with the surrender, cancellation, exchange, and issuance of ADSs effected as part of the ADS ratio change. ADS holders should consult their brokers, banks, or other financial intermediaries for information regarding the treatment of their holdings in connection with the ratio change.

#5590. 10 ways to tell if your mail-order meat or cheese arrived safe

Free daily briefing on global business news.

How to tell if mail-order meat or cheese is safe: 10 checks covering the 40°F rule, thermometer readings, thawed items, mold, dry ice and next steps

A food gift sent by mail spends hours, sometimes days, outside anyone's refrigerator. Once the box lands on a doorstep, the person who opens it becomes the last checkpoint in the cold chain. That chain runs from the producer's cooler through trucks, sorting centers and delivery vans.

A sealed exterior reveals little. A box can look intact, with clean tape and a crisp label, while the meat or cheese inside has spent too long at an unsafe temperature. A steak can smell normal and still carry bacteria that cause illness. A soft cheese can look perfect and still pose a risk to a pregnant relative.

Knowing how to tell if mail-order meat or cheese is safe comes down to a short set of physical checks. Temperature is the first. Time is the second, including any stretch the package sat on a porch. The packaging adds evidence, from the state of the gel packs to whether dry ice remains. The label fills in the rest, separating some shelf-stable dry-cured salami from fresh cuts that must stay cold.

The guidance behind these checks comes from U.S. federal food-safety agencies. The U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service publishes the temperature and time limits for perishable food. The Food and Drug Administration and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention warn about Listeria in soft cheeses for higher-risk groups. Several of the checks call for a food thermometer.

The 10 slides that follow are a selection of practical checks for a perishable shipment, not every food-safety step. They cover reading a thermometer correctly, deciding whether thawed items can be refrozen and handling mold on a cheese gift. They also explain what melted ice packs reveal, how to treat dry ice and why hard and soft cheeses carry different risks. The final slide covers what to do when a delivery fails these tests.

Each check stands on its own. A reader holding a box at the front door can jump to the one that matches the problem in front of them.

A perishable mail-order food gift passes the first safety check if its contents arrive at 40°F or below. That figure comes from U.S. Department of Agriculture guidance. It separates food that stayed cold enough from food that may not have.

The USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service treats 40°F as the upper limit for keeping perishable food safe. Raw steaks, fresh sausages, cooked meats and soft cheeses all fall under that guidance.

Above that line sits what the agency calls the danger zone. It runs from 40°F to 140°F. Bacteria multiply fastest in that range of temperatures.

A shipped box has to hold its contents below the bottom edge of that zone for the entire trip. Insulated liners and coolants are there to do that job. The temperature of the food when the box is opened shows whether they worked.

That makes 40°F the first question to answer for any gift of meat or cheese. It is a single, measurable number. A reading either meets it or misses it, however sturdy or intact the box appears.

A reading at or under 40°F means the shipment passes on this measure. A reading above it means the contents spent time in the range the USDA warns against.

The rule covers perishable items, meaning foods that need refrigeration to stay safe. A wedge of fresh cheese or a vacuum-packed cut of raw beef belongs in that group. Cooked meats meant to be kept cold, such as sliced ham, belong there too.

The same threshold also serves as the reference point for other decisions about a delivery. Whether thawed items can go back in the freezer, and what to do with a warm package, both start from this number.

A 40°F reading answers one question, not every question. It shows the food was out of the danger zone when the box was opened. How long a box sat outside, or whether a cheese carries mold, needs its own check.

A food thermometer is the only reliable way to know whether a mail-order meat or cheese gift arrived cold enough. The reading has to come from the product itself, not from the air inside the box or the outer wrapping.

Touch is not a substitute. A vacuum-packed steak or a wedge of cheese can feel cold in the hand. That feeling does not show whether the food sits above or below the 40°F line. A thermometer turns the guess into a number.

Where the probe goes matters as much as the tool. Air inside an insulated shipper reflects the packaging. So does the surface of the outer wrap. Neither one gives the temperature of the food that will be eaten. A reading from either can make a shipment look safer or riskier than it is.

Do not push the probe through a sealed package to reach the inside. There are two better options. The first is to place the thermometer flat against the product, with the tip pressed to the sealed surface of the meat or cheese. The second is to open the package and take the reading right away, before the item has time to warm on the counter.

Timing shapes the result. Have the thermometer out and ready before cutting the tape on the box. Unpack the perishable items one at a time and read each one as soon as it comes out. A stack of products left on the counter will warm while the rest of the gift is sorted. The reading then reflects the kitchen rather than the trip.

Check every perishable item separately. A gift box may hold a roast, a package of sausages and two or three cheeses. One reading does not speak for the others.

Give the display time to settle before accepting the number. A probe that is still adjusting can show a figure that is off in either direction.

Items that read at or below 40°F can go straight into the refrigerator or freezer. Anything that reads higher needs a closer look before it is cooked, eaten or stored.

Frozen meat that still has ice crystals when it arrives can go back in the freezer or be cooked. The same is true for meat that feels as cold as it would straight from a refrigerator. That is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's guidance on refreezing.

The rule answers a common question about mail-order gifts: can you refreeze meat that arrived thawed? The answer turns on how cold the meat stayed, not on whether it is still rock-hard.

Ice crystals are the clearest sign. They show the meat has not fully thawed. A steak, a pack of sausages or a roast can soften at the edges and still hold crystals near the center or inside the wrap. Under USDA guidance, that item can be refrozen or cooked.

Touch is the second sign. Meat that has lost its ice but still feels refrigerator-cold falls under the same guidance. It can also go back in the freezer or onto the stove.

A third case covers meat that has thawed completely. If it has no ice left but is still at 40°F or below, USDA says it can be refrozen as well. The catch is quality. Meat that thawed all the way and then refroze may not match the quality of meat that stayed frozen.

Safety and quality are separate questions here. USDA treats refreezing as safe in all three situations. The possible quality loss applies only to meat that thawed all the way.

A gift box can hold several cuts, and they do not always arrive in the same state. Check each package on its own. Look for crystals, then feel for cold. Return the items that still hold ice to the freezer first. After that, check any fully thawed pieces against the 40°F mark before deciding whether to refreeze them.

This guidance covers meat that stayed cold. A fully thawed item that has warmed above 40°F is a different situation, and refreezing is not part of the USDA advice for it.

USDA guidance says perishable food should not sit out for more than two hours. The limit drops to one hour when the air temperature is above 90°F, and time a mail-order box spends on a doorstep counts toward it.

The limit covers the time food spends outside refrigeration. For a shipped gift, the most visible part of that time is the gap between the carrier's drop-off and the moment someone carries the box indoors. A package that sits on a porch all afternoon has spent that afternoon unrefrigerated.

Porch time is not separate from the two-hour count. It adds to it. A box dropped off in the morning and opened in the evening has sat at the door all day before anyone checks what is inside.

The one-hour version of the rule applies in hot weather. A doorstep on a day above 90°F is where the shorter limit takes over. A recipient expecting a shipment during a heat wave has less room for a late pickup.

The first practical step is to control when the package lands. Scheduling delivery for a day when someone is home cuts down the porch time. For a gift sent to someone else, the sender can ask the recipient which days work before placing the order.

Tracking the delivery window is the second option. A tracking number, when the seller provides one, shows roughly when the box is due. Someone can then be ready to bring it inside soon after it arrives. For a gift, the sender can share the tracking number with the recipient so they know when to expect it.

The drop-off time is worth checking once the box comes in. A timestamp on the tracking record, if one exists, shows how long the contents went without refrigeration. That record also helps when the next step is reading the food's temperature against the 40°F threshold.

A normal smell or appearance does not prove that mail-order meat or cheese is safe to eat. USDA notes that Salmonella and Listeria do not reliably change how food smells, tastes or looks.

Opening a package and sniffing the contents is a common habit. For a perishable shipment, that step answers a narrower question than it seems to. It can detect spoilage. It cannot reliably detect the bacteria behind foodborne illness.

Two different groups of microorganisms are involved. Spoilage organisms break food down in ways the senses can pick up. They produce sour or off odors, and they can leave a slimy film on meat or cheese. Pathogens are the organisms that make people sick. They can multiply without leaving any of those clues.

That split makes the sensory check a one-way test. A pack of sliced turkey or a block of cheese might arrive with an off odor or a slimy surface. Those signs mean the food should be discarded. If the same items smell and look normal, the senses have not ruled out the organisms that cause illness.

Appearance carries the same limit. A sealed roast can show its normal color after a warm stretch in transit. A cheese can keep its usual aroma. Neither detail reveals whether bacteria multiplied along the way.

Taste offers no extra protection. The USDA guidance on these pathogens covers taste along with smell and appearance. A small bite from a questionable package is not a safety check. It exposes the person eating it to whatever the food carries.

The sensory check still has a use. It is quick, and it can flag spoilage before anyone eats the food. It works as a reason to reject a delivery, never as a reason to accept one.

The decision to keep a perishable shipment should rest on measurable evidence, such as a thermometer reading taken from the product. Smell and appearance cannot supply that evidence.

Gel packs that arrive fully melted and warm suggest the shipment's cold chain failed somewhere in transit. Dry ice, the other common coolant in food gift boxes, is solid carbon dioxide and should be handled only with gloves or tongs.

The coolant is the first piece of evidence a recipient sees after lifting the lid. Sellers pack gel packs or dry ice to keep meat and cheese cold for the length of the trip. Their condition on arrival offers a quick read on how that trip went.

A gel pack that is still frozen solid, or firm and icy at the center, suggests the coolant was still working when the box landed. A pack that has turned completely liquid and feels warm to the touch tells a different story. The coolant gave out at some point before the box was opened. How long the food sat without that protection cannot be judged from the outside.

That signal is a warning, not a final verdict. The product itself still needs a temperature reading against the 40°F threshold before anyone decides what to keep. Warm, melted packs make a failed reading more likely, but they do not settle the question alone.

Dry ice behaves differently from gel packs. It does not melt into a puddle. It turns straight from a solid into carbon dioxide gas. A box with little or no dry ice left does not by itself show whether the food stayed cold, so the food still needs its own check.

Dry ice also calls for care in handling. Never touch it with bare hands. Its extreme cold can injure skin on contact. Use gloves or tongs to lift any remaining pieces out of the box.

Never put leftover dry ice in a sealed container, such as a screw-top jar, an airtight plastic tub or a zip-top bag. As the solid turns to gas, pressure builds inside a closed space. That pressure can cause the container to burst.

Open the shipment in a ventilated room. Carbon dioxide gas can collect in a closed, cramped space. Opening a window, or unpacking the box near an open door, lets the gas disperse while the remaining dry ice turns to vapor.

Hard cheeses such as cheddar and Parmesan carry less food-safety risk in a mailed gift than soft cheeses such as Brie, fresh mozzarella and queso fresco. The difference comes down to moisture. It shapes how closely each cheese in a delivered box needs to be checked.

Cheddar and Parmesan are low-moisture cheeses. With little water available, bacteria have a harder time growing in them. That makes a wedge of cheddar or a block of Parmesan less hospitable to bacteria than a soft cheese.

Brie, fresh mozzarella and queso fresco sit at the other end of the scale. They hold more moisture, and they belong to the higher-risk group.

The specific concern with soft cheese is Listeria. The FDA and the CDC both flag Listeria in soft cheese as a particular worry for three groups. Those groups are pregnant people, people with weakened immune systems and adults 65 and older.

That warning works differently for a food gift than for a cheese someone buys for themselves. The sender chooses what goes in the box. The recipient — or the people sitting at the recipient's table — may belong to one of those groups. A cheese board shared at a holiday gathering can end up in front of a guest who is pregnant or over 65 without anyone stopping to think about it.

The practical step is to sort a cheese gift by type as soon as it comes out of the box. Read the label on each piece and note which cheeses are hard and which are soft. An assortment can include both, and the soft ones are the pieces to inspect first and most closely.

If the temperature check on arrival raises any doubt, that doubt weighs most heavily on the soft cheeses. A hard cheese and a soft cheese that traveled in the same box under the same conditions do not carry the same level of risk.

For a household that includes someone in a higher-risk group, the soft cheeses in a gift call for a separate decision. That decision rests on the FDA and CDC Listeria warning, whatever the condition of the hard cheeses packed alongside them.

USDA advises cutting at least one inch around and below a mold spot on a hard cheese, then keeping the rest. A soft cheese that has grown mold should be thrown out.

That split matters for a gift box holding several cheeses at once. A wedge of cheddar and a round of Brie can arrive side by side and still call for opposite responses.

For a hard cheese such as cheddar or Parmesan, the cut works in two directions. The one-inch margin applies to the sides of the spot. It also applies to the cheese underneath it. Shaving off only the visible surface leaves the area below in place.

The knife needs attention too. USDA advises keeping the blade out of the mold itself while cutting. A blade that passes through the spot can drag it into the clean cheese left behind. The goal is to cut around the problem, not through it.

Soft cheeses follow a simpler rule. A Brie, fresh mozzarella or queso fresco that shows unexpected mold goes in the trash rather than under the knife. USDA guidance offers no trimming margin for soft cheese.

Intentional mold is a separate case. The blue veins in a blue cheese come from mold that is part of the cheese. The white rind on a Brie is also mold that belongs there. Neither one is a reason to trim or discard the cheese on its own.

The practical question is whether a mold belongs to the cheese or arrived uninvited. A new spot on a cheddar or Parmesan does not belong, and the hard-cheese cut applies.

The gift card, packing slip or seller's product listing can help sort this out. A description that names a blue cheese or a Brie tells the recipient which mold to expect. A cheese described with no mold at all falls under the hard-or-soft rule if a spot appears.

Sorting each cheese into one of these groups before cutting helps avoid two mistakes. One is throwing away a sound blue cheese. The other is keeping a moldy fresh mozzarella.

Some dry-cured meats, such as certain salami and country hams, are made to be shelf-stable. Fresh and cooked meats marked "keep refrigerated" are not. The package label settles which group each product in a mail-order gift belongs to.

That split matters. One food gift can hold both kinds. A cured sausage can arrive in the same box as sliced cooked ham or a pack of fresh links. Those items share a shipment, but they do not share storage rules.

The word "certain" carries weight here. Not every salami is shelf-stable, and not every ham is a country ham. Two products that look alike on a cutting board can come from different processes. Appearance, texture and a familiar product name are not reliable guides to how an item must be stored.

The label is the guide. Before anything goes into the pantry, read each package for its storage language. The label states whether a product needs refrigeration. If the wording is missing, smudged or unclear, the conservative choice is to treat the item as perishable.

Sort the box as soon as it is opened. Unpack every item, read each label and divide the contents into two groups. Items marked "keep refrigerated" get their temperature checked and go straight into the refrigerator. Items whose labels confirm they are shelf-stable can wait on the counter while the rest is handled.

The refrigerated group is held to the same 40°F threshold as any other perishable in a delivery. A cooked ham in that group gets no exception for traveling beside a cured salami. Ice packs and insulation in the box show how the shipment was packed, not which items needed the cold.

Seller descriptions and gift cards can help, but they do not replace the package itself. A product page may describe a sampler as a whole. The label on each item describes that item. Where the two differ, the label is the more specific instruction.

A recipient who shares a sampler or regifts a salami should keep each item in its original wrapping. The next person needs the same label to store it correctly.

A perishable shipment that arrives above 40°F with no sign of cold should be thrown away. After that, document what arrived and contact the seller promptly, while the evidence is still on hand.

The phrase "no sign of cold" describes a box where nothing inside is still holding a chill. The meat or cheese reads above 40°F, and no part of the product or packaging still feels cold to the touch. A shipment in that condition has failed the basic temperature test for perishable food.

A USDA rule of thumb covers the decision: when in doubt, throw it out. A box that looked fine from the outside does not change the thermometer reading. Neither does the price of the gift or the person who sent it. If the reading and the condition of the package both point the wrong way, the food goes.

Take photographs before anything goes in the trash. Three images cover the essentials. The first shows the packaging as it arrived, including the outer box and whatever insulation and cooling material sat inside. The second shows the thermometer reading, with the number clearly legible. The third shows the shipping label, which carries the tracking number, the carrier and the delivery address.

Those images create a record of the shipment's condition at the moment it was opened. Once the food is discarded and the box is recycled, that record is the only proof of what arrived.

The message to the seller works best with specifics. It should include the order number, the delivery date and the photographs. It should also state the temperature the thermometer showed and where on the product the reading was taken. Those details give the seller what it needs to look into the shipment.

When the gift came from someone else, the recipient may not have the order number or the seller's contact details. Telling the sender about the problem lets whoever placed the order raise it with the company.

For questions about whether a specific meat or poultry product is still safe, USDA runs the Meat and Poultry Hotline at 1-888-MPHotline (1-888-674-6854). The line offers a direct route to federal food-safety guidance when a package falls into a gray area. A call can help settle a borderline case before the food is eaten or thrown away.

#5589. Accrete Signs Data Agreement with TenderAlpha to Deepen Supply Chain Risk Insight for Federal Customers

NEW YORK, Nov. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Accrete, the cognitive infrastructure company building Knowledge Engines for autonomous work, today announced that it has signed an agreement with TenderAlpha, a global provider of government contracting and supply chain data. The agreement brings TenderAlpha data into Accrete's Argus for Supply Chain Influence, giving defense and civilian agency customers greater visibility into the companies, suppliers and component parts behind the products and systems they rely on.

Across the government, supply chain visibility has become a priority. The National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) requires closer scrutiny of defense suppliers, and civilian agencies face growing pressure to understand risk in critical food, agricultural and medical product supply chains. Agencies need a clearer view of the sub-tier relationships and sources where risk often goes unseen.

"Supply chain risk isn't a data aggregation problem. It's a judgment and tacit knowledge problem," said Prashant Bhuyan, Founder and CEO of Accrete. "Human expertise doesn't scale fast enough to get ahead of foreign influence threats, and burying analysts under mountains of disconnected data only makes it worse. Accrete's Knowledge Engine captures and scales the tacit knowledge of individual analysts and the organization itself. It grounds reasoning models in that judgment so they become trusted agents. With TenderAlpha's data in Argus, those agents can do in minutes what would ordinarily take teams of exceptional analysts months or years."

"Our customers need to understand supply chain risk faster and at a deeper level than ever before," said Bill Wall, CEO of Accrete AI Government. "Adding TenderAlpha data gives us greater insight into the obscured vulnerabilities and threats inherent in complex global supply chains. It gives defense and civilian agency teams a robust picture of who is really behind the products and components they depend on, so they can act before a vulnerability becomes a problem."

By combining TenderAlpha data with Argus for Supply Chain Influence, powered by the Accrete Knowledge Engine and its supply chain expert agent, Accrete customers will be able to:

"Exposing complex supply chain risk requires connecting the dots across disparate layers that are very rarely combined," said Martin Tsanov, CEO and co-founder of TenderAlpha. "The fusion of TenderAlpha's global B2B relationship and trade data with government contracting and subcontracting data within Argus' cutting-edge multi-tier graph architecture equips national security agencies with the comprehensiveness and visibility needed to proactively identify hidden dependencies and secure critical supply chains."

The TenderAlpha agreement is part of Accrete's ongoing investment in the data and analytics that federal customers need to protect the Defense Industrial Base and the critical supply chains Americans depend on. Customers using Argus for Supply Chain Influence will gain access to these expanded insights in early 2027.

Accrete builds cognitive infrastructure for government and enterprise customers. Founded in 2017, Accrete's Knowledge Engine platform unifies fragmented systems, siloed data, tacit knowledge, and decision-making into a continuously learning universal system of intelligence. Knowledge Engines give agents the shared context to reason, collaborate, decide, and act across the full complexity of an organization. As AI makes intelligence abundant, judgment is the scarce resource, and Accrete's Knowledge Engines encode the expert judgment organizations accumulate over decades so agents can be trusted with consequential decisions. Accrete's customers span Fortune 500 enterprises as well as U.S. defense and national security agencies. From commercial operations to national security missions, Accrete's platform enables expert agents that deliver superintelligence designed for high-stakes environments. Accrete AI Government LLC, based in Alexandria, VA, is the federal subsidiary of New York-based Accrete, Inc.

Founded in 2014, TenderAlpha delivers high-quality, structured data products designed to support investment analysis, risk assessment, and market intelligence. TenderAlpha serves financial institutions, asset managers, and risk-rating and research professionals, offering deep insights into global G2B and B2B transactional trends.
