#5588. Thinking Machines debuts Inkling 2 Small amid reported $5B fundraising push

Thinking Machines Labs Inc. has released a new large language model that can automate artificial intelligence training tasks.

The algorithm, Inkling 2 Small, made its debut late Thursday. Around the same time, Business Insider reported that Thinking Machine is in the process of raising a $5 billion funding round led by Accel. The company, which was founded last year by former OpenAI Group PBC Chief Technology Officer Mira Murati, is expected to receive a $40 billion valuation.

Thinking Machines trained Inkling 2 Small on a cluster of GB300 NVL72 racks. Each system contains 72 Blackwell Ultra graphics cards and half as many central processing units. The company completed the initial pre-training phase in 68 hours and subsequently refined the model through a nine-day reinforcement learning workflow. There were also a number of intermediate training steps.

Thinking Machines honed Inkling 2 Small’s programming capabilities by giving it hundreds of thousands of long-horizon coding challenges. The task collection included a number of particularly complicated “autoresearch” exercises. They required the model to post-train neural networks, optimize LLM components called kernels and perform other AI research work.

Thinking Machines put Inkling 2 Small’s machine learning skills to the test by asking it to fine-tune Qwen3.5-4B. The goal was to improve the open-source LLM’s ability to make predictions such as weather forecasts. According to the company, Inking 2 Small doubled the model’s forecasting score in 4.5 hours.

The LLM is also adapt at automating business tasks. It outperformed Spark Open, Kimi K3 and several other open-source models on three popular knowledge work benchmarks. Additionally, it earned higher scores across several financial task datasets.

Inkling 2 Small includes a vision encoder that can analyze images. Moreover, it enables the LLM to visually verify the quality of the graphics that it generates. If a user asks the model to create an e-commerce store, it can not only check the website’s code for bugs but also visually inspect product pages to check that they render correctly.

The vision encoder accounts for 292 million of Inking 2 Small’s 594 billion parameters. About 17 billion of those parameters activate when a user enters a prompt. Inking 2 Small can adjust the amount of computing power that it spends on tasks, which enables developers to trade off output quality for increased cost-efficiency or vice versa.

Particularly savvy users can extend the model’s capabilities by post-training, or customizing it, using their own data. Thinking Machines says that Inkling 2 Small learns faster than its earlier models. That should translate into more cost-efficient post-training runs.

Inkling 2 Small is available via Thinking Machines’ Tinker cloud service on launch. The company plans to release the model’s weights under an open-source license next week.

Trump Media has moved $343 million in Bitcoin to Crypto.com, raising fresh questions if Donald Trump’s media company could be selling its crypto holdings. The transfer comes as Democrats prepare investigations into Trump’s family crypto ventures following their midterm election victories.

The company sent 4,259 BTC in two transactions, according to blockchain data tracked by Arkham. The coins came from wallets labeled as collateral for convertible notes, adding another layer of uncertainty around the Trump Media Bitcoin transfer.

The timing is difficult to ignore. Trump Media faces a potential $1 billion debt repayment deadline later this month, while incoming Democratic lawmakers are preparing to scrutinize Trump’s crypto businesses. A sale has not been confirmed, but this move puts the company’s Bitcoin treasury under pressure.

Arkham data showed Trump Media-linked wallets transferring 4,259 BTC to Crypto.com just a few hours ago. The coins were moved in two batches of more than 2,000 BTC each. The transfer represents around $343 million at recent prices. It also accounts for 30% of the 14,139 BTC Trump Media previously held, including pledged coins.

However, the destination does not confirm a sale. It is known that Trump Media has used Crypto.com for custody and trading-related transfers before, including transactions in May and August.

The latest movement is particularly notable because the Bitcoin came from wallets associated with convertible-note collateral. Trump Media’s previous filings identified 4,260.73 BTC as collateral for its notes.

A November 2 filing also disclosed that noteholders can require cash repayment on November 30. If all eligible holders exercise that option, the company could face approximately $1 billion in repayments.

Trump Media warned that refinancing or other measures might not be sufficient. In that scenario, the company could be forced to sell Bitcoin or other digital assets to meet its obligations.

This disclosure gives the Crypto.com transfer a potentially more serious explanation than routine custody management. The company may be positioning assets ahead of a major liquidity decision. Although the reason remains unconfirmed, Trump Media could be selling its Bitcoin.

Democrats are expected to gain subpoena power when the new Congress begins in January. Reuters previously reported that investigations into Trump family businesses could begin as early as February.

The current political environment could complicate the outlook for Trump-linked companies. Congressional scrutiny may increase pressure on financial relationships, crypto holdings, and business operations connected to the president’s family.

#5586. Flu, COVID, RSV and measles: how to tell the four viruses apart

Free daily briefing on global business news.

How to tell flu, COVID, RSV and measles apart, from onset speed and rash timing to incubation periods, testing options, vaccines and the warning signs that need urgent care

A fever and a cough in midwinter could signal any of four different viruses, and the first days of each can look much alike. Influenza, COVID-19, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and measles can all circulate at the same time in winter. All four can start with fever, cough or a runny nose. Yet the differences matter. The right test, the right treatment and the right precautions depend on which virus is responsible.

Flu has an antiviral that works best when started early. COVID-19 has its own antiviral option for higher-risk patients. RSV can cause severe illness in babies and in adults 65 and older. Measles is among the most contagious viruses known. A suspected case calls for a phone call to the clinic before anyone walks into a waiting room.

Knowing how to tell flu, COVID, RSV and measles apart starts with patterns, not certainties. Symptoms offer clues. Flu tends to strike suddenly. RSV often builds slowly, like a cold. A loss of taste or smell can point toward COVID-19. Measles has the most distinctive sign of the four: a red rash that begins on the face and spreads downward. Even so, symptoms alone cannot reliably separate these illnesses. A test is the only way to know for sure.

This guide compares those four viruses only. It is not a complete list of winter illnesses. Common colds, strep throat and norovirus fall outside its scope, and the list makes no claim about which illness is worst or most common.

The 10 slides that follow move from symptoms to action. The first five describe what each virus typically looks like, including how RSV differs in adults and infants and how measles progresses from early fever to rash. The next two cover timing — how quickly each illness comes on, how long each takes to appear after exposure and how easily each spreads. The final three explain testing options, the vaccines and preventive products available for each virus and the warning signs that call for urgent care.

The facts come from established public-health guidance, mainly from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the World Health Organization (WHO). None of it replaces a diagnosis. Anyone with trouble breathing, confusion or a fever that will not come down should seek care rather than wait for a test result.

Flu typically comes on abruptly, with fever, chills, muscle aches, headache and heavy fatigue. A cough and sore throat often come with them.

Influenza is a respiratory infection caused by influenza viruses. Types A and B drive the seasonal outbreaks that circulate in the U.S. during fall and winter. The infection affects the nose, throat and sometimes the lungs.

The CDC describes flu symptoms as generally more intense than those of the common cold. Colds tend to center on the nose and throat. Flu more often adds body aches, fever and exhaustion on top of them.

The exhaustion can be severe. It goes beyond ordinary tiredness and can leave people unable to work, study or handle routine tasks while sick.

Fever is common, and it often comes with chills or a feeling of feverishness. It is not universal, however. Some people with influenza never develop a raised temperature. A normal thermometer reading does not rule the infection out.

The cough linked to flu is usually dry, producing little or no mucus. A sore throat is common, and some people also have a runny or stuffy nose. Those symptoms can make the early days resemble a cold.

Children can show a somewhat different picture. Vomiting and diarrhea occur with flu more often in children than in adults. A child with fever and an upset stomach may still have influenza and not a gut infection.

The term "stomach flu" adds to the confusion. It usually refers to gastroenteritis, which influenza viruses do not cause. Norovirus is a common cause of that illness. Influenza remains mainly a respiratory infection, even when vomiting or diarrhea comes along with it.

Severity varies widely. The CDC notes that flu can cause mild to severe illness. Adults 65 and older, young children, pregnant people and those with chronic conditions such as asthma or heart disease face higher risk of complications.

COVID-19 shares most of its symptoms with the flu, including fever, cough, sore throat, fatigue and body aches. A new loss of taste or smell is one known feature that can point toward COVID-19 instead.

The disease is caused by SARS-CoV-2, a coronavirus first identified in late 2019. Like flu, it spreads mainly through respiratory droplets and smaller airborne particles. It is a different virus from influenza, though, which belongs to an unrelated virus family. Even so, the two illnesses can look almost the same in their first days.

Fever or chills, cough and muscle aches appear on the symptom lists for both infections. So do headache, sore throat and heavy tiredness. Nasal congestion and a runny nose can occur with COVID-19 as well. Those symptoms can make it resemble a common cold.

The CDC's list of COVID-19 symptoms also includes shortness of breath or difficulty breathing. Some people develop nausea, vomiting or diarrhea. Digestive symptoms like these can make the early illness look more like a stomach bug than a respiratory infection.

Loss of taste or smell drew wide attention early in the pandemic as a distinctive sign. It is not universal, though. A person whose sense of smell is normal can still have COVID-19.

COVID-19 can also come on more gradually than flu, with symptoms building over time instead of arriving all at once.

Severity covers a wide range. Some infected people never develop symptoms. People without symptoms can still pass the virus to others. Others have a mild illness, while some develop pneumonia and need hospital care. Older adults and people with certain chronic medical conditions face a higher risk of severe disease, according to the CDC.

A person can also be infected with flu and COVID-19 at the same time. Matching symptoms to one virus therefore does not rule out the other.

In healthy adults and older children, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) usually looks like an ordinary cold. In babies, the same virus can inflame the small airways and make breathing hard.

The typical adult picture is mild. A runny nose, cough, sore throat and low-grade fever are the common signs. Some people also sneeze or lose their appetite for a few days. Many adults recover without ever learning that the cold had a specific name.

That resemblance is why RSV often goes unrecognized in grown-ups. Nothing in the adult symptom list points to RSV in particular. The same set of complaints fits many other respiratory viruses.

Infants show a different pattern. A baby with RSV may become unusually irritable, feed poorly and start wheezing. Breathing can turn fast or labored. In very young infants, irritability, reduced activity and breathing difficulty may be the only signs. Fever does not always appear.

The difference comes down to where the infection settles. RSV is a leading cause of bronchiolitis in babies. Bronchiolitis is inflammation of the bronchioles, the smallest airways in the lungs. An infant's airways are already narrow. Swelling and mucus can restrict airflow quickly. RSV is also a leading cause of pneumonia in babies.

Feeding trouble is tied to the breathing problem. A baby working to breathe through a blocked nose and swollen airways has a harder time sucking and swallowing at once. Feeds can become shorter, and the baby may take in less fluid over a day.

Age matters at the other end of life too. Adults 65 and older face a higher risk of severe RSV disease than younger adults. People with chronic heart or lung disease and those with weakened immune systems are also at higher risk, according to the CDC. In these groups, an illness that starts like a cold can spread into the lower airways.

One bout of RSV does not give lasting protection. People can catch the virus repeatedly throughout their lives. Repeat infections in healthy older children and adults tend to be milder than a first infection in infancy.

Measles begins with a high fever, a cough, a runny nose and red, watery eyes. Tiny white spots inside the mouth, called Koplik spots, can appear before any rash does.

This opening stretch of the illness is known as the prodrome. It lasts a few days. During that time, measles can pass for a bad cold or a case of flu.

Clinicians often sum up the early signs as the "three Cs": cough, coryza and conjunctivitis. Coryza is the medical term for a runny, stuffy nose. Conjunctivitis is inflammation of the thin membrane that covers the white of the eye and lines the eyelids.

The eye symptoms are one of the more useful early clues. The eyes turn red and water, and bright light can feel uncomfortable. A cough and a runny nose show up in many respiratory infections. Red, watering eyes alongside a high fever narrow the picture.

Koplik spots are the most specific early sign of measles. They are small white or bluish-white dots on a red background, often compared to grains of salt. They usually appear on the inner lining of the cheeks, near the back teeth.

The spots are easy to miss. They are small and sit inside the mouth, out of view. They also tend to fade once the rash takes hold. A doctor who suspects measles will often check for them with a light during an exam. Other common respiratory viruses do not produce them, so their presence points strongly toward measles.

Measles is caused by the measles virus, a member of the paramyxovirus family. People in this early phase can already pass the virus to others. They often do so before anyone suspects measles, because the telltale rash has not yet appeared.

The pre-rash stage is when measles is hardest to identify by appearance. In that window, red eyes and Koplik spots carry the most weight as clues.

A red rash that starts on the face and spreads down the body sets measles apart from flu, COVID-19 and RSV. It typically appears a few days after the first symptoms.

The timing of the rash is part of the clue. Measles does not begin with the rash. It begins with high fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. That early stretch can resemble other winter infections. The rash arrives a few days later.

The rash's path is the second part of the pattern. It typically shows up first on the face. From there it moves downward over the rest of the body. As it spreads, the flat red spots can join together into larger patches. A fever followed by a rash that travels from the face downward is the sequence that points toward measles.

The other three viruses offer no comparable marker. Flu, COVID-19 and RSV overlap in fever, cough, sore throat and fatigue. None of them normally causes this kind of spreading red rash. That makes the rash the clearest outward sign separating measles from the other three.

A person's history adds weight to the clue. A fever followed by this rash leans more strongly toward measles in someone who is unvaccinated. The same holds after a known exposure, such as contact with a person who has measles. Someone with no vaccination record and a recent exposure who develops the rash fits the pattern closely.

The pattern is a reason to seek care, not a diagnosis on its own. Measles is confirmed through laboratory testing, not by the appearance of a rash.

How a person seeks care matters as much as when. Anyone who suspects measles should phone the doctor's office, clinic or emergency department before arriving. Walking into a waiting room unannounced can expose other patients to the virus. A call ahead gives staff time to prepare, for example by arranging a separate room for the visit.

An illness that strikes abruptly leans toward flu, one that builds slowly like a cold leans toward RSV, and a lost sense of smell leans toward COVID-19. Each clue is a tendency, not a diagnosis.

Flu is known for its speed. The illness often arrives all at once rather than creeping in over several days. Fever, chills and body aches can appear together within a few hours. That abrupt start is the most useful timing clue for influenza.

RSV usually follows a different arc. In healthy adults and older children, it tends to begin with a runny nose and a sore throat. A cough and sometimes a mild fever follow over the next few days. That gradual pattern closely resembles a common cold. As a result, RSV in an adult can easily be mistaken for one.

COVID-19 does not fit neatly at either end. It can start suddenly, much like flu. It can also come on more gradually. The speed of onset alone does little to separate COVID-19 from the other two.

Loss of taste or smell is the clue most closely tied to COVID-19. It is a recognized feature of the disease and is less typical of flu or RSV. It does not prove COVID-19, however. A badly congested nose from many respiratory infections can also dull the sense of smell.

The absence of that symptom proves nothing either. Not everyone with COVID-19 loses the sense of smell. How often it happens has also varied as different variants have circulated.

Other factors blur these patterns. People notice and describe the start of an illness differently. A mild first day is easy to overlook. One person can also be infected with more than one virus at once. A mixed infection can produce symptoms that match no single profile.

Timing still has practical value. Noting when symptoms began, and which ones came first, gives a clinician useful context. Some treatment decisions also depend on how many days have passed since the illness started.

These clues overlap too much to settle the question on their own. Confirming the virus responsible takes a test, not a symptom timeline.

Flu has the shortest incubation period of the four, at roughly one to four days, according to the CDC. COVID-19 has the widest range, and measles typically takes seven to 14 days to produce its rash.

An incubation period is the gap between catching a virus and feeling sick. During that window, the virus is multiplying, but the person usually has no sign that anything is wrong. Knowing the typical range helps answer a practical question: when did this infection most likely start?

For flu, the answer usually points to the past few days. Someone who falls ill on a Friday most likely caught the virus earlier that same week.

COVID-19 runs on a much less predictable clock. The CDC gives its incubation period as two to 14 days. That spread makes a single exposure harder to pin down. A gathering nearly two weeks before the first symptoms can still fall within the range.

RSV usually lands in a narrower band. Its incubation period is typically four to six days, according to the CDC. A runny nose and cough from RSV most often point to an exposure several days earlier, inside the past week.

Measles is slower to show itself. The CDC puts the typical gap between exposure and the appearance of the rash at seven to 14 days. An exposure at a clinic, airport or school can lead to a rash up to two weeks later.

Measles also spreads with unusual ease. The virus can stay in the air of a room for up to two hours after an infected person has left. Direct contact is not required. Someone who walks in afterward can still breathe it in.

The CDC estimates that about nine in 10 exposed people who are not immune will become infected. A person can be exposed without knowing it. A rash may not appear for up to two weeks after that.

These ranges describe the usual pattern, not a fixed rule. They help narrow down when an infection began. They cannot confirm which virus is responsible.

Only a test can reliably tell flu, COVID-19, RSV and measles apart. Their symptoms overlap too much for a clinician to sort them out by symptoms alone. A swab or blood sample turns a likely guess into a diagnosis.

Flu and COVID-19 can each be identified with two main kinds of test. A rapid antigen test detects proteins from the virus. A PCR test detects the virus's genetic material instead.

The two tests trade speed against sensitivity. Rapid antigen tests return results quickly and can be done in a clinic or at home. PCR tests are generally more sensitive. They are more likely to catch an infection when only a small amount of virus is present. Their samples are usually processed in a laboratory.

That difference matters when a rapid result is negative but symptoms continue. A negative antigen test does not rule out infection. A clinician may follow up with a PCR test or a repeat test.

Combination panels check for flu, COVID-19 and RSV at the same time. A single sample is tested for all three viruses. That spares a patient separate swabs when the cause of a respiratory illness is unclear. Some at-home kits also test for both flu and COVID-19 from one swab.

RSV testing is used more narrowly. It is mostly ordered for infants and for patients sick enough to be hospitalized. Healthy adults with mild, cold-like symptoms are tested for RSV less often.

Measles is handled differently. It is confirmed in a laboratory, usually with two kinds of sample. A throat or nasal swab is tested by PCR for the virus itself. A blood test looks for antibodies, including a type called IgM that signals a recent infection.

A suspected measles case also triggers a step that a routine flu or COVID-19 diagnosis does not. Clinicians report suspected cases to public-health authorities. That report lets health officials identify other people who may have been exposed to the virus.

Each of the four viruses in this guide has a vaccine or preventive product. Flu vaccination is recommended for nearly everyone, RSV protection centers on older adults and babies, and the MMR vaccine prevents measles.

No single shot covers all four. Each product targets one virus. Which ones apply to a given person depends largely on age and, for RSV, on pregnancy.

In the U.S., an annual flu vaccine is recommended for everyone six months and older. There are few exceptions to that recommendation. The advice applies every season. A dose from a past season does not stand in for the current one.

Updated COVID-19 vaccines are also available. An updated vaccine is a revised version of the shot, not a repeat of the original formula. It is a separate product from the flu vaccine, and one does not substitute for the other.

RSV prevention focuses on the people most likely to become seriously ill. RSV vaccines are approved for older adults, who face a risk of severe disease from the virus. A separate vaccine is approved for use during pregnancy. The pregnant parent receives the shot, but its purpose is to protect the newborn.

Infants have a second route to protection. Nirsevimab, sold under the brand name Beyfortus, is an antibody product given directly to babies. It works differently from a vaccine. A vaccine prompts the body to build its own defenses, while an antibody product supplies protective antibodies ready-made.

Measles is prevented with the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, usually called MMR. Two doses are about 97 percent effective against measles, according to the CDC. One dose is about 93 percent effective, according to the same agency.

Those figures can be read another way. Roughly seven in 100 people who receive a single dose are left unprotected against measles. After two doses, that share falls to roughly three in 100. Because MMR is a combination vaccine, the same doses also guard against mumps and rubella.

These products prevent illness or lower its risk. They are not treatments for someone who is already sick with any of the four viruses.

Difficulty breathing, bluish lips, chest pain that will not ease, confusion, dehydration and a fever that will not come down all call for urgent medical care. These warning signs apply whether the illness turns out to be flu, COVID-19, RSV or measles.

Several of these signs point to specific problems. Struggling to breathe or turning blue around the lips suggests the body is not getting enough oxygen. Confusion in someone who was alert earlier is a change in mental state. It is not a routine part of a respiratory infection. Dehydration can build quietly when fever, vomiting or a poor appetite keep a person from drinking enough.

Babies need closer monitoring because they cannot say how they feel. Poor feeding and pauses in breathing are danger signs in infants. A baby who refuses the bottle or breast, or who stops breathing for moments at a time, should be seen right away.

Treatment depends on which virus is responsible. Oseltamivir, sold under the brand name Tamiflu, is a prescription antiviral for influenza. It works best when started within 48 hours of the first symptoms. That time limit is one reason to contact a clinician early instead of waiting several days to see whether flu improves.

Paxlovid is an antiviral pill for COVID-19. It is used for patients at higher risk of severe illness, such as older adults and people with certain chronic medical conditions. It is a prescription drug, and a clinician decides whether it suits a given patient. Paxlovid can interact with a range of other medications. The prescriber reviews what a patient already takes before recommending it.

RSV and measles are managed with supportive care. At home, that means rest, fluids and medicine to bring down fever. In a hospital, supportive care can extend to extra oxygen or fluids given through an IV.

Antibiotics do not work against any of these four viruses. They target bacteria, and taking them for a viral illness will not speed recovery. A doctor may still prescribe them if a bacterial infection, such as some cases of pneumonia, develops on top of the virus.

#5584. Zebec ZBCN Buyback: 40.5M Tokens Held, Not Burned, as Supply Stays Unchanged

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zebec says it bought back 40.5 million ZBCN in the third quarter and is keeping them "out of circulation."

On-chain, those tokens didn't reach Zebec's buyback treasury wallet during the quarter. They arrived on October 21, three weeks after Q3 ended, the same day Zebec announced the buyback, sent from what Solscan labels a Crypto.com hot wallet.

The amount matches Zebec's claim almost to the token. But the wallet's history also shows something "out of circulation" doesn't usually suggest: it has moved 59 million ZBCN out before. Let's go through the wallet to check what Zebec's buyback claim actually covers.

Zebec Network announced on October 21, in an X post, that it repurchased 40,536,539 ZBCN in Q3 for about $100,000. That implies an average price of roughly $0.00247. The money came from Zebec Cards and payroll fees across Zebec Enterprise and the SuperApp.

Zebec's explainer, Inside the ZBCN Buyback Program, says buybacks are "funded by operating revenue" from payroll, payments, cards and related services, not from treasury reserves. That's a real point in Zebec's favor.

The scale is small. ZBCN has a 100 billion maximum supply, so 40.5 million tokens is about 0.04% of it.

Zebec says the repurchased tokens "will not re-enter circulation." They weren't burned. ZBCN's total supply is exactly the same as it was before the buyback.

That's a deliberate policy. The program began in 2023 under the old ZBC token and originally included burns. In early 2024, the Zebec DAO approved ZIP-4, which paused burns while keeping recurring buybacks. Zebec says the DAO expects to decide by the end of 2026 whether to propose bringing burns back. Governance happens through the Zebec DAO portal.

The practical difference matters. A burn permanently destroys tokens. "Out of circulation" depends on Zebec continuing to hold them and on data providers leaving them out of circulating supply. The blockchain doesn't enforce either one.

Zebec's blog says repurchased tokens are held "in the designated on-chain Buyback Treasury Wallet and with Uphold Institutional," but doesn't give the address. The account linked with the announcement is EkXEg6de172aoLvr7w86YzQ2rf5oEFD3iUt8uQsLQuQW. ZBCN's Solana mint address is ZBCNpuD7YMXzTHB2fhGkGi78MNsHGLRXUhRewNRm9RU.

As of October 22, Solscan shows the wallet holding 108,256,701.48 ZBCN, worth about $246,157 at $0.002273.

The Q3 check passes. On October 21 at about 14:11 UTC, the wallet received two ZBCN transfers from an address Solscan labels "Crypto.com Hot Wallet":

Together, that's 40,535,224.09 ZBCN, just 1,315 ZBCN (about $3) short of Zebec's figure. That's a 99.997% match. The small difference is likely due to fees or rounding.

One detail stands out: the account is off-curve. Solscan shows "isOnCurve: FALSE," which means the address is derived by a program and has no private key of its own. Accounts like this are usually controlled by a program such as a multisig, so moving tokens requires that program's approval. That's a better setup than a single person's wallet, but it isn't a lock.

The timing shows how the program works. The wallet's transfer history suggests a repeating pattern, with each batch arriving after its quarter has ended:

Those three batches add up to the wallet's current balance within 0.01 ZBCN. So the "buyback treasury" holds the last three quarters of deliveries and nothing else.

This means that during each quarter, the purchased tokens weren't in the on-chain treasury. The pattern points to buying on an exchange, with tokens sitting in an exchange account until they're withdrawn to the treasury around announcement time. The chain doesn't show when the Q3 purchases actually happened, so for July 1 to September 30, the "$100,000 Q3 buyback" can't be checked on-chain. Only the October 21 delivery can.

That's common practice and not a sign of wrongdoing. But it means the on-chain record confirms delivery, not the purchases themselves.

If the balance only covers the last three batches, what happened to earlier buybacks? The transfer history answers that, too. The wallet has sent ZBCN out twice, both times to the same address, shown on Solscan as 9Sq2nZ...4TEine:

That's about 58.97 million ZBCN moved out of a wallet described as holding tokens that "will not re-enter circulation."To be fair, Zebec says tokens are "periodically consolidated with Uphold Institutional for custody," and these outflows may be exactly that. There's no confirmation that 9Sq2nZ...4TEine belongs to Uphold. Once tokens leave this wallet, readers can't follow them using Zebec's disclosures. These transfers also show what a burn would prevent: tokens in this wallet can, and do, move.

The Q3 claim holds up better than I expected. The wallet received almost exactly 40.5 million ZBCN, and the balance reconciles to the token. What the chain can't show is when the tokens were bought, or where earlier buybacks are now.

Three disclosures would close those gaps:

For now, Zebec did buy and deliver its Q3 tokens, and the supply is the same as it was before.

#5583. Rinsing, thawing and stuffing: 10 Thanksgiving turkey habits USDA guidance disputes

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These 10 Thanksgiving food safety myths, from rinsing raw turkey to leaving pumpkin pie out, run against USDA and CDC guidance on thawing, cooking and storing the holiday meal

Much of what happens in a Thanksgiving kitchen is inherited. Cooks rinse the turkey because a parent did. They leave it on the counter to thaw because a grandparent did. They judge doneness by the color of the juices because an old recipe card says so. Several of those habits run directly against the food safety guidance published by the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

The holiday meal is built differently from an ordinary dinner. It centers on a large raw bird that can take days to thaw in a refrigerator. It is often prepared in a crowded kitchen by several people at once. Raw poultry, vegetables and finished dishes end up sharing the same counters. Dishes also tend to stay on the table for hours after the meal ends.

Each of those conditions creates an opening for bacteria. Raw turkey can carry Salmonella and Campylobacter. Those germs multiply fastest when food sits between 40°F and 140°F, a range the USDA calls the danger zone. A frozen bird left out to thaw spends time in that range. So does a stuffing that never gets hot enough at its center. So does a platter of sliced meat left out for hours.

The guidance that addresses those risks is specific. It names a target internal temperature of 165°F and a minimum oven setting. It lists approved thawing methods with timings per pound. It sets clear limits on how long cooked food can sit out. Much of it depends on one tool: a food thermometer.

This list covers 10 Thanksgiving food safety myths drawn from that federal guidance. It is a selection rather than a complete catalog. The myths follow the order of the day. They start with preparing the raw bird, including whether you should wash a turkey and how to thaw it. They move through stuffing, oven temperatures and the tests cooks use to decide when the meat is done. They then cover cross-contamination, how long leftovers and pumpkin pie can stay out and the hazards of deep-frying a turkey that is not fully thawed.

Each slide explains what the common belief gets wrong, what the USDA or CDC recommends instead and why the recommended step matters.

The USDA tells home cooks not to rinse a raw turkey before it goes in the oven. Rinsing does not make the bird safer, and it can spread bacteria around the kitchen.

The concern is the bacteria raw poultry can carry, including Salmonella and Campylobacter. When water from the faucet hits the turkey, it can carry those germs off the skin and onto whatever surrounds the sink.

That includes the basin itself, the faucet handles, the counters on either side and any food sitting nearby. A colander of vegetables, a bowl of cranberries or a plate of bread left within reach of the splash can pick up raw-poultry juices.

The risk is greatest for food that will not be cooked again. The turkey goes into a hot oven, but a salad or a tray of cut fruit does not. Germs that land on those dishes have no heat step to kill them before they reach the table.

Should you wash a turkey at all? The USDA's answer is no. Cooking is what makes the bird safe, not water. A turkey cooked to 165°F has reached the temperature that kills those bacteria. Rinsing beforehand gives germs a way off the bird without removing any risk from the meat.

Surface moisture does not call for the faucet either. The USDA says patting the turkey dry with paper towels is fine. That method keeps the bird in one place instead of sending water and juices across the sink.

Those paper towels should go straight into the trash after use. Setting one down on the counter, or reusing it to wipe another surface, would move raw juices to the places the no-rinse advice protects.

A cook who has already rinsed a turkey can still limit the spread afterward. The sink, faucet handles and nearby counters should be cleaned with hot soapy water before any other food touches them. Produce should not go into that sink until it has been cleaned.

A frozen turkey should never thaw on the kitchen counter. The USDA approves only three thawing methods — the refrigerator, a cold-water bath and the microwave — and room temperature is not one of them.

The problem is uneven thawing. A large frozen bird warms from the outside in. Its outer layers can reach room temperature while the meat near the bone is still frozen solid. On a counter, the surface sits warm for hours before the center catches up.

Those hours matter because of what the USDA calls the danger zone, the range between 40°F and 140°F. Bacteria multiply fastest at those temperatures. A turkey on the counter spends much of its thaw inside that range. A refrigerator keeps it below 40°F.

Refrigerator thawing is the slowest approved method and the one that takes the most planning. The USDA estimates about 24 hours for every four to five pounds of turkey. At that pace, a 20-pound bird needs roughly four to five days. For a Thursday dinner, a turkey that size would have to leave the freezer by the Saturday or Sunday before.

A cold-water thaw is much quicker but needs more attention. The turkey goes into a bath of cold water, and the USDA says to change the water every 30 minutes. Thawing takes about 30 minutes per pound. The same 20-pound bird would need about 10 hours.

The microwave is the third approved option, and it carries the same condition as cold water. The USDA says a turkey thawed in cold water or in the microwave should be cooked right away. Of the three methods, only the refrigerator keeps the bird consistently cold from start to finish.

A turkey that is still frozen on the holiday morning does not have to be thawed at all. The USDA says it can be cooked straight from frozen. That takes roughly 50 percent longer. A bird that would roast for four hours thawed would need about six hours from frozen. It still has to reach 165°F, measured with a food thermometer.

Cooking stuffing inside the turkey is safe only when the stuffing itself reaches 165°F at its center. A bird that has hit its target temperature does not guarantee that the stuffing packed inside it has done the same.

The reason lies in what the stuffing does during the roast. It sits in the cavity of a raw bird and soaks up the juices that drain from the meat. Those juices come from raw poultry and can carry its bacteria. A moist bread mixture saturated with them has to be heated all the way through before it is safe to serve.

The stuffing also sits at the core of the bird, surrounded by meat. Heat reaches it last. As a result, stuffing can stay cooler than the turkey around it, even late in the roast. A cook who judges doneness by the meat alone may serve stuffing that never climbed out of the bacterial danger zone.

Anyone asking whether it is safe to stuff a turkey should plan on a separate check for the stuffing. The answer depends on a food thermometer placed in the middle of the stuffing, not on how long the bird has been in the oven. If the meat is ready and the stuffing is not, the stuffing has not finished cooking.

The USDA describes baking stuffing in a separate dish as the simpler route. In its own baking dish, the stuffing heats independently and never absorbs raw turkey juices. The cook also has one temperature target per dish instead of two inside a single bird.

For households that want a traditional stuffed bird, the USDA guidance comes down to two practical steps. The first is timing. Stuff the turkey just before it goes into the oven, not the night before or hours ahead. That limits how long the mixture sits against raw meat before cooking starts.

The second is packing. Spoon the stuffing in loosely rather than pressing it down. A loose fill lets heat travel through it more easily than a dense, compacted mass does. That gives the center a better chance of reaching 165°F.

A turkey's plastic pop-up timer is not a trustworthy sign that the bird is safe to eat. The device can fail or trigger at the wrong time, and a food thermometer reading of 165°F is the check that counts.

Some turkeys come from the store with the timer already pressed into the meat. When it pops, a cook may pull the bird from the oven without a second look. That habit hands the final safety call to a small piece of plastic that may not work as intended.

A timer that fails in one direction never pops, and the cook gets no signal at all. A timer that fails in the other direction pops too soon. That second error carries the real risk. The turkey can leave the oven before it is safe to eat.

The USDA points to a food thermometer as the reliable alternative and names three places to take the reading. The first is the innermost part of the thigh. The second is the innermost part of the wing. The third is the thickest part of the breast.

All three spots need to reach 165°F. One passing number is not enough on its own. A reading in the breast says nothing about the thigh, and a reading in the thigh says nothing about the wing.

A pop-up timer, by contrast, sits in a single spot in the bird. Even when it works, it reports on that one location and not on the rest of the turkey. The thermometer checks give the cook a reading from each part the USDA singles out.

A cook who leaves the timer in place can treat its pop as a cue to reach for the thermometer, not as the final word on doneness.

If any of the three readings falls short of 165°F, the turkey goes back into the oven. The cook then checks again in the same three places until each one reaches the target.

A turkey's color cannot tell a cook whether it is safe to eat. Clear juices, golden-brown skin and the shade of the meat can all point the wrong way. The USDA's standard is a food thermometer reading of 165°F.

The juice test is a long-standing kitchen habit. A cook pierces the thigh, watches what runs out and calls the bird finished once the liquid looks clear. Juice color, though, is not a reliable stand-in for the temperature inside the meat. Clear juice can show up before the bird has reached a safe point.

Skin color fails for a similar reason. Browning happens on the outside of the bird, where it meets the oven's heat directly. The surface can turn deep gold while the thickest meat underneath is still short of 165°F. A turkey can look ready for the table and still be undercooked inside.

Meat color misleads in both directions. White meat can look cooked before it is hot enough to be safe. Turkey that still shows some pink can be safe if it has reached 165°F.

Each of these cues describes how the turkey looks. None of them measures how hot it is. That gap is the core problem with every visual test. A cook can watch the juices, the skin and the meat closely and still learn nothing certain about the temperature at the center.

The temperature matters because heat is what makes raw poultry safe. Bringing turkey to 165°F kills the harmful bacteria that raw poultry can carry. A glance at color cannot confirm that those bacteria are gone.

The two possible errors carry different costs. Serving a bird too early can leave live bacteria in the meat. Roasting a finished bird longer than needed adds no safety benefit.

A thermometer reading is the only check that confirms the turkey has reached 165°F.

The USDA recommends roasting a turkey in an oven set no lower than 325°F. Overnight roasting at a very low setting, such as 200°F, can keep the meat in the bacterial danger zone for too long.

The overnight method has practical appeal. A cook puts the bird in before bed and expects a finished turkey by morning. The oven is then free for side dishes the next day. The risk lies in what happens inside the meat during those first slow hours.

A turkey taken straight from the refrigerator starts near the bottom of the 40°F to 140°F range, where bacteria multiply fastest. Before the meat reaches 165°F, the temperature that makes poultry safe to eat, its core has to climb through that entire range.

Heat enters a turkey from the outside in. Hot oven air warms the skin and the outer layers of meat first. That heat then moves inward toward the center of the thigh and the deepest part of the breast. A whole bird is a large, dense mass of muscle and bone. Its center is the last part to warm.

The oven setting controls how quickly that happens. Heat flows faster when the gap between the oven air and the cold meat is large. At 325°F, that gap is wide, and the interior warms at a steady pace. At 200°F, the gap is much smaller. The surface heats gently, and the center falls further behind.

That slower climb is where the risk comes from. The inside of the bird spends more hours in the danger zone than it would at a standard roasting temperature. Those extra hours give bacteria in the raw meat more time to grow before the heat rises high enough to kill them.

Time in the oven does not settle the question on its own. A turkey that has roasted all night can seem finished by morning. Hours of cooking are still no substitute for the target temperature. The bird is safe to serve only when a food thermometer reads 165°F.

The 325°F minimum applies whatever the size of the bird. A larger turkey needs more time in the oven at that setting. The answer for a big bird is a longer roast at 325°F or higher, not a lower dial left on through the night.

Raw turkey juices can carry germs onto cutting boards, knives, platters and serving utensils. From there, they can reach food that will not be cooked again. Any surface or plate that held the raw bird needs a wash in hot soapy water before cooked food touches it.

The danger comes after the cooking is finished. Heat makes the meat safe, but it never reaches the board where the raw bird was trimmed. It also misses the knife that cut away excess skin and the tray that carried the bird to the oven. Those items still hold whatever was in the raw juices.

Raw poultry can carry Salmonella and Campylobacter. Neither can be seen with the naked eye. A board that looks clean after a quick wipe can still pass those germs to the next food placed on it.

The serving platter shows how this can happen on Thanksgiving. A cook may carry the raw turkey to the roasting pan on a large serving dish. Hours later, the same dish comes back out for the carved meat. Unless it was washed in between, the cooked slices sit on residue from the raw bird.

Knives and carving boards follow the same pattern. A knife used to open the packaging or trim the raw turkey should not go straight to carving. The same applies to a board used to prep raw meat and then to slice bread, chop salad greens or cut cooked turkey. Washing each one with hot soapy water between jobs breaks the chain.

Serving utensils need the same attention. Tongs or forks that touched the raw bird while it was placed in the pan should be washed before they serve anything at the table.

Hands carry raw juices as easily as tools do. The CDC advises washing hands with soap and running water for at least 20 seconds after handling raw poultry. That step comes before touching the refrigerator handle, a phone or an ingredient for another dish. A quick rinse without soap does not meet that standard.

The working principle is short. Anything that touched the raw turkey gets washed before it touches anything else.

Cooked turkey and other Thanksgiving leftovers should not sit out for more than two hours, according to the USDA. When the room is warmer than 90°F, that limit drops to one hour.

The rule answers a question many hosts face after the meal: how long can turkey sit out? It covers the side dishes as well as the bird. Stuffing, mashed potatoes and gravy follow the same two-hour limit.

Time on the serving table and time on the kitchen counter add up together. A platter moved from the table back to the counter does not get a fresh start.

The limit exists because food at room temperature sits in the danger zone, the range where bacteria multiply fastest. The longer a dish stays there, the more time those bacteria have to grow.

The one-hour limit applies in hot settings. An outdoor meal in a warm climate can push the air above 90°F. So can a small kitchen packed with people and running ovens.

Food that has stayed out past either limit should be thrown away rather than refrigerated. Chilling it afterward does not undo the time it already spent warm.

The USDA recommends packing leftovers into shallow containers. A thin layer of food loses heat faster than a deep pot or a whole carcass. A full roasting pan of stuffing or a stockpot of gravy holds heat in its center for a long time. Splitting it into smaller, flatter portions lets the cold reach the middle sooner.

The refrigerator itself should be set at 40°F or colder. A thermometer placed inside the refrigerator shows whether it is actually holding that temperature.

Refrigerated leftovers should be used within three to four days. For a meal cooked on a Thursday, that window closes around Sunday or Monday. Writing the date on each container makes the deadline easier to track.

Reheating has its own standard. The USDA recommends warming leftovers to 165°F, the same internal temperature a raw turkey must reach in the oven. A food thermometer pushed into the center of the dish confirms it has gotten there.

Yes. The USDA says pumpkin pie belongs in the refrigerator once it has cooled. The filling is an egg-rich custard, and it can spoil like any other perishable dish.

A classic pumpkin pie filling combines pumpkin puree with eggs, milk or cream, sugar and spices. During baking, the egg proteins firm up and set the mixture into a smooth custard. That is the same basic chemistry behind a flan or a baked custard cup. The result is a moist, protein-rich food, and bacteria grow readily in that kind of food.

Baking heats the filling enough to set it. It does not protect the pie for the rest of the day. Once the pie leaves the oven, it cools into the 40°F to 140°F danger zone. A pie on the counter of a warm, crowded holiday kitchen can stay in that band for hours.

The same limit that governs turkey and side dishes applies here. A pumpkin pie should not sit out for more than two hours. The time it spends cooling on a rack is time at room temperature. The cooled pie should go into the refrigerator before the two hours are up. A refrigerator kept at 40°F or colder holds it below the danger zone.

Pecan pie needs the same treatment. Its sweet, gooey filling is bound with eggs. It falls into the same perishable category as pumpkin, even though it looks less like a custard on the plate.

Pies made without eggs are a separate case. Most fruit pies, such as apple or cherry, are built on fruit and sugar rather than an egg custard. The egg-based caution does not apply to them in the same way.

A make-ahead pumpkin pie depends on refrigerator space cleared in advance. A pie baked the day before Thanksgiving can be cooled, covered and chilled overnight. Once it comes out for serving, the time it spends on the table counts against the two-hour limit.

A turkey headed for a deep fryer must be completely thawed and patted dry before it goes in. Any ice or water left on the bird can make hot oil boil over violently and ignite in a flash fire.

The danger comes from the gap between two temperatures. Frying oil is heated far above 212°F, the point at which water boils. When ice or surface water touches that oil, it turns to steam almost instantly.

Steam takes up far more space than the water it came from. As it forms beneath the oil's surface, it pushes the oil upward and out of the pot. Oil that spills over the rim can reach the burner flame below and catch fire.

A bird that feels thawed on the outside can still hold ice deep inside. The cavity and the meat closest to the bone are the last parts to thaw. A turkey with any frozen spots is not ready for the fryer, even if the skin feels soft.

Drying matters as much as thawing. Water left in the cavity or clinging to the skin sets off the same reaction as ice. Patting the bird dry, inside and out, removes that moisture before it meets the oil.

The amount of oil in the pot is the next variable. Lowering a whole turkey into the pot raises the oil level. The bird pushes aside its own volume of oil as it goes in. A pot filled too close to the top has no room for that rise. The excess goes over the edge.

Where the fryer sits is part of the safety plan. It belongs outdoors, on flat, level ground. A heavy pot of hot oil on uneven footing can tip. The fryer also needs distance from houses, garages, decks and other structures. That gap keeps a fire from spreading to them.

A safe setup does not guarantee a safe bird. A fried turkey must still reach 165°F, the same standard that applies to a roasted one. A food thermometer reading is the way to confirm it before carving.

#5582. TEN Holdings Reports Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results

NEW YORK, Nov. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- TEN Holdings, Inc. (Nasdaq: XHLD), through its subsidiary, Ten Events, Inc., the technology company behind TEN, a Digital Experience Platform that powers the next generation of enterprise digital engagement, today announced its financial results for the quarter ended September 30, 2026.

"Third quarter revenue increased 17.9% year over year to $640,000, as we completed customer engagements that had been initiated in prior periods and added revenue from new customers," said Virgilio Torres, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of TEN Holdings. "Our performance reflects continued demand for our digital engagement solutions and our ability to serve both existing and new customers. As we look ahead, our focus remains on expanding recurring revenue, strengthening our technology platform, and accelerating our transition toward a scalable, SaaS-driven business model."

"Our third-quarter results reflect two significant expenses that we consider non-recurring: a $1.8 million write-off of previously capitalized service contracts and approximately $0.5 million in legal expenses. Excluding these items, our underlying selling, general and administrative expenses declined compared to the same period last year, reflecting the progress we have made in improving operational efficiency. Over the past 12 months, we have reduced our annual operating cost structure by approximately $2.5 million through strategic cost reductions, process improvements, and the integration of AI-driven tools to streamline engineering and accelerate product development. With these efficiencies largely implemented and a leaner operating structure in place, we are now shifting our focus toward accelerating revenue growth, expanding customer relationships, and scaling TEN, our new platform."

"We also made significant progress in strengthening our balance sheet, reducing short-term related-party borrowings from $4.6 million at the beginning of the year to approximately $0.1 million as of September 30, 2026. Total liabilities declined by approximately 74%, from $7.7 million at year-end 2025 to $2.0 million, reflecting our continued efforts to simplify our capital structure and improve our financial position."

"One of our most significant milestones this year was the launch of TEN, our next-generation Digital Experience Platform, whose development was accelerated by investments made possible through the proceeds of our June common stock offering, consistent with our previously communicated commitment to product development. TEN represents an important step in our evolution toward a scalable, SaaS-driven business model, bringing together the tools organizations need to create, manage, deliver, and measure digital experiences within a unified platform.

At launch, TEN provides enterprises with a self-service solution for webinars, virtual events, and continuing education programs, with the capacity to support up to 50,000 concurrent attendees. Building on our longstanding relationships with enterprise customers, many of whom rely on our technology for recurring digital engagement initiatives, we see a meaningful opportunity to transition these relationships toward subscription-based arrangements. We believe this approach will deliver greater flexibility and value to our customers while creating a more predictable and recurring revenue stream for TEN Holdings."

"Looking ahead, we are focused on three priorities: continuing the transition of our business from a managed services provider to a SaaS company, investing in TEN so that it remains competitive, and executing an acquisition strategy aimed at accretive businesses that add revenue and EBITDA, products our sales team can scale, and technology that complements our own. With TEN now in the market, a leaner cost structure, and a simplified balance sheet, we believe TEN Holdings is positioned to build a more scalable, recurring revenue business and create long-term value for our shareholders."

Selected Balance Sheet and Cash Flow Results

(Nasdaq: XHLD) is a New York-based technology company focused on developing enterprise software solutions that enable organizations to create, manage, deliver, and measure digital experiences. Building on more than a decade of experience serving Fortune 500 companies, TEN Holdings is evolving its platform into a broader, AI-enabled enterprise technology ecosystem. Its product roadmap includes marketing automation, CRM integrations, advanced engagement analytics, AI-powered capabilities, and content management solutions designed to help organizations streamline workflows, strengthen customer engagement, and generate actionable business insights.
