#5575. Exposed to measles? 7 steps to take, from the 72-hour vaccine window to isolation

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Learn what to do if you were exposed to measles, from checking your MMR record and the 72-hour vaccine window to symptoms, testing and isolation

Measles exposure starts a clock. Some of the most useful protective steps are available for only a few days after contact. Decisions made in that short span can shape how the next three weeks unfold. Knowing what to do if you were exposed to measles means knowing which deadlines matter and who to call first.

Measles is highly contagious. Up to 90% of people without immunity who are close to an infected person become infected, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). A single exposure at a clinic, school, airport or workplace therefore carries real risk for anyone who is not protected.

The first question is whether you are already immune. Vaccination and past infection are the usual routes to immunity. Confirming that status can settle the matter quickly. People who cannot document immunity face a different set of choices. Some of those choices depend on age, pregnancy or the state of the immune system.

This guide walks through seven steps in the order most people will need them. It starts with checking vaccination records and other evidence of immunity. It then covers the monitoring period after exposure and the early signs of illness. Those first signs can resemble a cold before any rash appears. The guide also explains why a phone call should come before any visit to a doctor's office or emergency room.

Two time-limited options get their own slides. A dose of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine may offer some protection when given within 72 hours of first exposure. Immune globulin is a separate option that certain high-risk people can receive up to six days after exposure.

The final slide covers isolation. It explains when a sick person is contagious and when exposed people may be asked to stay home from school or work.

None of this replaces individual medical advice. A doctor can assess personal risk. Local and state health departments handle testing and contact tracing. They also set exclusion rules in their area. Anyone who learns of a possible exposure should contact one of them promptly, before the post-exposure windows close.

The first step after a measles exposure is to find out whether you already have presumptive evidence of immunity. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) considers people with that evidence presumed immune. For them, many of the usual post-exposure steps may not be needed.

The CDC accepts four kinds of evidence. The first is written documentation of measles vaccination. The second is a laboratory test showing immunity. The third is laboratory confirmation that you had measles in the past. The fourth is birth before 1957.

Written documentation means an actual record, not a memory of getting shots as a child. Common places to look include a childhood vaccination card, files kept by a pediatrician or family doctor and school or college health records. Many U.S. states also run immunization registries, and a doctor or health department can often search them.

How many documented doses count as enough depends on who you are. For preschool-age children and for adults who are not at high risk, one dose of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is considered adequate. School-age children, college students, health care workers and international travelers need two documented doses.

The gap between one and two doses shows up in protection. The CDC puts the effectiveness of two MMR doses against measles at about 97%. A single dose is about 93% effective. Neither figure reaches 100%. A small share of vaccinated people can still catch measles after an exposure.

The routine U.S. schedule gives the first MMR dose at 12 to 15 months of age and the second at four to six years. A child who followed that schedule and has the paperwork to show it meets the two-dose standard. A baby younger than 12 months has not yet reached the age for a routine first dose.

When records are missing or incomplete, a blood test can answer the question. A doctor can order a test for measles antibodies, and a result showing immunity counts as laboratory evidence. A past case of measles also counts, but only if a laboratory confirmed it. A remembered childhood illness without lab confirmation does not meet that standard.

The 1957 cutoff reflects how widely measles circulated before vaccination. People born before that year are presumed to have been infected as children.

Anyone unsure of their status should share whatever records they have with a doctor or the local health department. Either can judge whether the evidence is sufficient or whether further steps are needed.

Anyone without measles immunity who has been exposed should watch for symptoms through day 21 after their last contact with the virus. That 21-day period reflects the measles incubation period, the stretch between catching the virus and feeling sick.

For most people, symptoms begin seven to 14 days after exposure. The full range runs from seven to 21 days. A person who still feels fine at the end of the second week has not yet cleared the window. Watching through day 21 covers the late end of that range, so slower-developing cases are not missed.

The count starts from the last exposure, not the first. Someone who shared a home, classroom or office with an infected person over several days should date the watch period from the final day of contact. Day 21 then falls three weeks after that last contact. Writing that date down makes it easier to tell a doctor or health department exactly when the window closes.

In a household, each day spent near a sick person counts as a new exposure. The window keeps moving later until that contact ends.

Exposure does not require face-to-face contact. Measles spreads through the air when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes. The virus can remain in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours after that person has left a room. Someone who walked into a waiting room, store or airport gate after an infected person had gone may still have been exposed.

That airborne persistence is part of why measles spreads so efficiently among people who are not protected. For someone with no evidence of immunity, a confirmed exposure carries a high chance of infection.

People already protected by vaccination or past infection face a much lower risk. Anyone unsure of their status during the watch period should ask a doctor or the local health department how to proceed. That includes whether to limit contact with others before day 21 passes.

Measles typically begins with a high fever, a cough, a runny nose and red, watery eyes. The rash most people picture comes later, usually three to five days after those first symptoms appear.

That gap matters for anyone tracking their health after an exposure. A person waiting for spots on the skin may already be several days into the illness before the rash shows up.

The fever is often the most pronounced early sign. It can climb above 104°F. A fever that high, along with a cough and irritated, watery eyes, fits the typical early pattern of measles. For someone who shared space with a measles patient, that combination is a reason to watch closely for the next signs.

Koplik spots are a second clue, and they are easy to miss without looking for them. They are tiny white spots that form on the inside of the mouth. They can appear two to three days after the first symptoms begin. Because the skin rash usually comes later, Koplik spots can offer an earlier visible sign that the illness may be measles.

The rash follows a recognizable path. It starts on the face. From there, it spreads downward over the rest of the body.

Measles can also lead to serious complications. They include ear infections, diarrhea and pneumonia. In rare cases, the virus causes encephalitis, an inflammation of the brain.

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reports that about one in five unvaccinated people in the U.S. who get measles is hospitalized. The agency also reports that one to three of every 1,000 children who get measles die.

Knowing the order of symptoms helps an exposed person describe what is happening when they seek care. The sequence runs from fever, cough, runny nose and watery eyes, to white spots inside the mouth, to a rash that begins on the face. Anyone who notices these signs after a measles exposure should contact a doctor or the local health department for guidance on next steps.

Anyone who may have measles should phone the clinic, hospital or local health department before showing up for care. A call ahead gives staff time to prepare. That preparation helps keep the virus from reaching other patients in a waiting area.

Measles spreads through the air when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes. One unannounced visit to a crowded lobby can expose many other people. Clinics and emergency rooms often hold people who are already vulnerable, including babies, older adults and patients with weakened immune systems.

Calling first allows the facility to follow a U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) infection-control practice for suspected measles. Staff can place a mask on the patient as soon as they arrive. They can then move the patient into a separate room instead of the general waiting area.

The preferred space is an airborne infection isolation room. This type of room is built to keep air from flowing out into the rest of the building. Some facilities may also tell callers which entrance to use.

The phone call is also the time to share key details. A caller can describe where and when the possible exposure happened and which symptoms have appeared. It also helps to say when those symptoms started and whether there is a record of MMR vaccination. That information helps clinicians decide how quickly the person needs to be seen and where.

Local or state health departments direct measles testing and contact tracing. Measles is a reportable disease in the U.S. Clinicians who suspect a case are expected to notify public health officials. The health department can then identify other people who shared the same space and may need follow-up.

Testing usually involves two samples. One is a throat or nasal swab checked with PCR, a lab method that detects the genetic material of the measles virus. The other is a blood sample tested for antibodies to measles. Those antibodies show how the immune system is responding to the virus.

Results guide what happens next for both the patient and the people around them. A confirmed case can lead the health department to contact others who were at the same clinic, school, workplace or event. A negative result can help clinicians look for another cause of the symptoms.

Anyone unsure whom to call can start with a regular doctor's office or the local health department. Either one can explain where to go and how to arrive without putting others at risk.

People without measles immunity who get an MMR vaccine within 72 hours of their first exposure may gain some protection or have a milder illness. That is the guidance from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

MMR is the combined vaccine against measles, mumps and rubella. It is the same shot children receive on the routine schedule. Given after contact with the virus, it serves as a form of post-exposure prophylaxis.

The CDC describes two possible benefits. A dose given inside the window can provide some protection against infection. For people who still get sick after the shot, it can make the illness milder. Neither outcome is described as a guarantee.

The 72-hour limit is counted from the first exposure, not the most recent one. Someone who shared a household or classroom with an infected person over several days should count from the earliest contact.

Late notice also eats into the window. A person who learns of an exposure two days after it happened has about 24 hours left to get the dose.

The vaccine does no harm if the person was already infected at the time of the shot, according to the CDC. The dose can still be given when it is unclear whether the virus has already taken hold.

Infants can be part of this response. Babies aged six to 11 months can receive MMR as post-exposure prophylaxis, within the same 72-hour window that applies to older children and adults.

That early dose comes with a caveat for parents. A dose given before a child's first birthday does not count toward the routine two-dose MMR series. The child will still need both standard doses later, on the regular schedule.

A doctor or the local health department can arrange the dose. Calling as soon as an exposure becomes known leaves the most time inside the window. Health departments can also confirm whether an exposed person qualifies.

Some people face a high risk of severe measles but cannot safely receive the MMR vaccine or are too young for it. They may qualify for immune globulin, which can be given up to six days after exposure.

Immune globulin is a blood product made from the pooled plasma of many donors. It contains ready-made antibodies, including antibodies against measles. Those antibodies give the recipient temporary, passive protection. The body does not have to build its own immune response first. That lets the treatment help even after contact with the virus has already happened.

The CDC lists three groups to consider for immune globulin after an exposure. The first is infants younger than 12 months. The second is pregnant women without evidence of measles immunity. The third is people with severe immune suppression, such as some patients being treated for leukemia or recovering from a stem cell transplant.

None of the three groups can rely on the MMR vaccine in the usual way. Infants younger than 12 months have not yet reached the routine age for a first dose. MMR is a live-virus vaccine made with weakened forms of the measles, mumps and rubella viruses. It is not given during pregnancy. It is also withheld from people with severe immune suppression. In a body that cannot control it, even a weakened vaccine virus can cause serious illness.

Measles during pregnancy also carries its own risks, including miscarriage, preterm birth and low birth weight.

The type of immune globulin depends on the patient. Infants receive an intramuscular injection. Pregnant women and severely immunocompromised people receive the intravenous form, delivered through an IV line.

Immune globulin does not replace vaccination. Its protection fades as the donated antibodies break down, and it does not create lasting immunity. Those same antibodies can also blunt the response to a live vaccine given too soon afterward. A doctor decides when someone who received immune globulin can later get MMR, once they are eligible.

Anyone in these groups who learns of an exposure should contact a doctor or the local health department right away. Health officials can confirm eligibility, arrange the correct form and keep track of the days left in the six-day window.

A person with measles can spread the virus from four days before the rash appears until four days after it. Anyone who develops measles should stay home through the fourth day after the rash first shows up.

That contagious window opens before the illness is recognizable as measles. During those first days, an infected person can pass the virus to others before anyone suspects the cause. Health departments use the day the rash first appears as the reference point for timing isolation. Writing down that date makes it easier to work out when isolation ends.

For a person whose rash appears on a Monday, the contagious period after the rash runs through Friday. Staying home through that Friday covers the full four days after rash onset.

Staying home means skipping work, school, child care and other shared settings for the whole period. Inside the household, it means keeping apart from anyone who lacks evidence of immunity.

Anyone with measles should avoid contact with infants, pregnant people and people with weakened immune systems throughout the contagious period. Those three groups face a higher risk of severe illness from measles.

Exposed people who never get sick can still be asked to stay home. When the health department directs it, exposed people without immunity are generally kept out of school, child care and work from day five through day 21 after exposure. The exclusion covers people who feel well. An infection can still be developing during that stretch before any symptoms show.

A timely MMR dose can change that outcome. Exposed people who got the vaccine within the recommended window may be allowed to return to school or work. The health department makes that decision. The answer can differ from one jurisdiction to the next.

Questions about when isolation or exclusion ends belong with a doctor or the local health department. The health department sets the end dates and decides when a person can return to work, school or child care.

#5573. Newborn holiday safety: 10 steps from hand washing to car seats

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Protecting a newborn at holiday gatherings starts with clean hands, healthy guests and safe sleep — here are 10 practical steps for parents hosting or visiting family

A newborn's first holiday season puts two forces in the same room. Relatives want to hold the baby, pass the baby around and plant kisses on a tiny face. The baby has an immune system that is still developing, with little time to build defenses of its own.

The timing adds pressure. In the U.S. and much of the Northern Hemisphere, the winter holidays fall during cold and flu season. Gatherings move indoors, and guests arrive from different households, schools and airports. An infection that causes a mild cold in an adult can make a young infant seriously ill.

Travel and unfamiliar houses bring their own complications. A baby who sleeps in a bassinet at home may end up near a couch, a guest bed or a pile of coats. Feeding and nap routines bend around dinner times. Candles, hot drinks and decorations sit close to busy hands.

None of this means families have to skip the season. Protecting a newborn at holiday gatherings comes down to a set of practical habits. Many of them cost nothing. Clean hands, healthy guests and up-to-date vaccines among the adults lower the chance of an infection reaching the baby. Safe sleep and car seat rules still apply away from home. A clear plan for a fever saves time if one appears.

Parents set the rules for their own child. Telling relatives ahead of time, by text, email or phone call, avoids correcting someone at the door with the baby already in their arms. A short message about hand washing, staying home when sick and holding off on kisses gives guests a chance to prepare. It also presents the requests as a household policy rather than a judgment of any one person.

The 10 tips below are a practical selection, not a complete checklist. They cover germs, vaccines, handling, sleep, fever, household hazards and travel. Each one stands on its own. Parents can use the ones that fit their gathering. A pediatrician can advise on a specific baby's situation, including when larger crowds make sense for that family.

Every guest who wants to hold the baby should wash their hands with soap and water first. Soap and water is the standard step for anyone handling a newborn. It clears away germs picked up on the way in before they reach the baby.

Hands carry whatever they touch. At a holiday gathering, that includes door handles, coats, serving spoons, shared remote controls and the hands of other guests. Washing before contact closes off one of the most direct routes from a crowded house to the infant.

Hand sanitizer is a fallback, not a replacement. It suits hands that look clean. It is the wrong tool when hands are visibly dirty. After peeling potatoes, carving a roast or clearing greasy plates, guests need soap and water. A bottle of sanitizer near the nursery or the sofa can serve guests who already washed and have touched only clean surfaces since.

A wash on arrival covers germs from the car, the train or the airport. One wash does not last all afternoon, though. Guests should wash again after eating. Food and shared dishes leave residue on fingers. Phones pass from pocket to table to countertop and rarely get cleaned. Anyone who has been scrolling should wash before taking the baby. The same goes for anyone who has petted the family dog or cat.

A little setup makes the request easy to follow. Set out soap at the sink closest to where the baby will be. Paper towels spare guests from sharing one damp cloth across many hands. A small sign by the sink or a quiet reminder from the parent holding the baby works for guests who missed any earlier message.

The rule applies to every guest, grandparents included, with no exceptions for close family. Parents can set the pattern by washing in plain view before picking up the baby themselves. Older siblings and young cousins can follow the same routine, with an adult nearby to help small children reach the sink.

Anyone with a fever, cough, runny nose, vomiting or diarrhea should skip a gathering where a newborn will be present. Mild symptoms still count. A slight sniffle can still signal a contagious infection.

A written request gives every guest the same standard to check against. Relatives can reread it on the morning of the gathering. They can then decide for themselves, without a phone call to the parents.

The wording can stay simple and direct. A line such as "If you're feeling sick, please sit this one out and we'll catch up by video" makes the point without a long explanation. Naming the specific symptoms helps. Some people do not think of a runny nose or an upset stomach as being sick. Spelling them out removes the guesswork.

The rule needs to apply to everyone, including grandparents and close relatives who expected to hold the baby first. A guideline that bends for one person is harder to hold for the next. Parents can ask a partner or another trusted relative to repeat the message. That way the request does not rest on one person.

Symptoms sometimes appear on the day itself. A guest who wakes up with a cough or a stomach bug may feel pressure to show up anyway, especially once travel plans are set. Telling relatives that a last-minute cancellation is welcome makes that choice easier for them.

Older siblings and cousins fall under the same request. Children often arrive at holiday gatherings carrying colds from school or day care. A child with a fever, cough or runny nose meets the same standard as an adult. Their parents need the same notice. The decision to keep a child home rests with them.

Video calls give sick relatives a way to take part. A call during the meal or the gift opening lets a grandparent or aunt see the baby and join the conversation from home. An in-person visit can then be rescheduled for a quieter day, after the relative has recovered.

Before a holiday gathering, ask the adults and older children who will be near your newborn whether their Tdap, flu and COVID-19 vaccines are current. Vaccinated relatives are less likely to carry these infections to a baby who is too young for full protection.

Whooping cough, also called pertussis, is the main reason this question matters. It is a bacterial infection of the airways. It spreads when an infected person coughs or sneezes. In a newborn, it can become serious quickly.

The Tdap vaccine protects against pertussis, along with tetanus and diphtheria. Protection for the baby can begin before birth. The CDC recommends Tdap during pregnancy, usually in the third trimester. The mother makes antibodies that pass to the baby. Those antibodies give the baby some protection in the first months of life.

Maternal antibodies are a starting point, not a complete shield. The people who hold, feed and sit beside the baby still matter. A grandparent or aunt with an unrecognized cough can expose an infant during a single afternoon visit.

Flu is the second part of the conversation. Babies cannot receive a flu shot until they are six months old, according to the CDC. A newborn at a winter gathering has no flu vaccine of its own. Vaccinated adults and siblings around the baby become a practical layer of protection.

COVID-19 vaccination for adults belongs in the same discussion. Holiday events tend to pack people into warm indoor rooms during the months when respiratory viruses circulate widely.

Older children belong in the same conversation as adults. Cousins and siblings often want to touch the baby. They may also be less consistent about covering a cough. Ask their parents about the children's vaccine status, not only their own.

Raise the vaccine question days or weeks before the event. Asking early gives relatives time to talk with their own doctor or pharmacist. It also gives parents time to decide who will hold the baby.

A short message noting that the baby is too young for some vaccines frames the request around the infant rather than the relative. If someone is not vaccinated, parents can ask that person to greet the baby from a distance. The baby's pediatrician can help parents decide which shots to ask about for their family.

Keep kisses off a newborn's face and hands at holiday gatherings. Anyone with a cold sore should not kiss the baby or get close to them. The herpes simplex virus that causes cold sores can be dangerous to newborns.

On an adult, a cold sore can look like a minor blemish on the lip. For a baby in the first weeks of life, the same virus poses a serious risk. That contrast is why the rule applies to every guest, with no exceptions for close family.

The face and hands are the areas to protect. A kiss on the cheek or forehead puts an adult's mouth close to the baby's eyes, nose and mouth. Hands need the same protection. Newborns often bring their hands to their mouths. A kiss on the fingers can end up at the baby's lips.

A relative with a visible cold sore should keep their distance from the baby for the whole visit. Skipping the kiss is not enough on its own. That person should not hold the baby or lean in for a close look. A parent can ask them to say hello from across the room.

Holiday kissing is often a reflex rather than a decision. Grandparents, aunts, uncles and family friends may lean in and kiss a baby without thinking about it. A parent holding the baby can turn the baby's face toward their own shoulder as someone approaches. The parent can follow with a calm reminder that the baby's face and hands are off-limits.

Affection still has an outlet. Relatives can admire the baby from nearby, talk or sing to them, or hold the baby's feet through socks or a sleeper. A gentle touch through clothing keeps contact well away from the face and hands.

The same request applies to older children at the gathering. Cousins and siblings often want to kiss a new baby. A parent can redirect them to a wave or a gentle foot squeeze instead.

A smaller gathering and a shorter stay limit how many people a newborn meets in a single day. Fewer guests mean fewer exposures to the colds and other infections that circulate indoors during the holidays. Each additional visitor is another set of hands near the baby and another person breathing close to its face.

Hosting at home gives parents the most control over the setting. They decide who receives an invitation, which room the baby stays in and when the event ends. The baby's crib, changing supplies and feeding setup also stay where they belong.

When the gathering happens at a relative's house, a shorter visit can do the same job. Parents can arrive after the first rush of guests or leave before the meal stretches late into the evening. For large extended families, two smaller visits on separate days can replace one long, crowded one.

Hosts can also stagger invitations. Inviting relatives in small groups across an afternoon or a weekend spreads out contact with the baby. Each visitor gets more unhurried time with the newborn than a full living room would allow.

A quiet room helps at a gathering of any size. A bedroom or study away from the main party gives parents a place to feed, change and settle the baby. Newborns feed on demand, and their hunger rarely lines up with the time dinner is served. A separate room lets feeding happen when the baby needs it rather than when the party pauses.

Sharing the schedule in advance keeps the plan clear. A message to the host a few days ahead can cover when the family will arrive and how long it plans to stay. It can also explain that the baby may spend part of the visit away from the crowd. Relatives who know the plan beforehand have time to adjust their own expectations.

Parents can leave early at any point. A fussy, overtired or overstimulated baby is a clear signal to head home. Agreeing on an exit plan before arriving, including who drives and when, makes the departure quick.

Wearing a newborn in a soft carrier or wrap keeps the baby close and out of a long line of eager arms. Another option is to name one designated holder, such as a parent or one trusted relative, who keeps the baby for the whole visit.

At a holiday gathering, each handoff brings another set of hands, another sweater and another face close to the baby. A carrier changes the default. Relatives can still see the baby, talk to the baby and stand nearby. The baby stays on one adult's body instead of moving around the room.

A carrier also gives parents an easy answer when a guest asks to hold the baby. Saying the baby is settled in the wrap can land more gently than a flat refusal. It shifts the focus from the guest to the baby's routine.

A designated holder serves the same purpose for families who do not own a carrier or whose baby is not comfortable in one. Pick that person before the event and let relatives know in advance. Guests then know whom to ask. The baby is not handed from cousin to cousin during dessert.

Babywearing has its own safety rules, and they apply in a busy room just as they do at home. The baby's face must stay visible at all times. The airway must stay clear. Fabric, a scarf or a coat should never cover the baby's nose and mouth. The adult wearing the baby should be able to see the baby's face just by glancing down.

Crowded holiday rooms make that check easy to forget. Conversation, music and cooking all pull attention away. Glancing down often keeps the rule in place.

Hot drinks are the other hazard to plan around while wearing a baby. Coffee, tea, cider and cocoa are common at holiday tables. An adult wearing a baby should skip them or set them well out of reach. A spill from that height would land directly on the baby.

A newborn at a holiday gathering should sleep exactly as at home: alone, on the back, on a firm, flat surface with no loose blankets, pillows or bumpers. The American Academy of Pediatrics sets out these rules, and they apply in a relative's house just as they do in the nursery.

Most holiday homes are not set up for an infant. Guest rooms tend to have soft mattresses, stacks of pillows and heavy quilts. Living rooms have sofas and armchairs. None of these is a safe sleep surface for a baby, even for a short nap during dinner.

One fix is to bring the sleep space along. A portable crib or bassinet that meets current safety standards gives the baby a firm, flat surface wherever the family ends up. Setting it up soon after arrival, before the house fills, means there is a ready place to lay the baby down once drowsiness sets in.

Keep the inside of that crib or bassinet empty except for the baby. Relatives sometimes add a folded blanket for warmth, a soft toy as a gift or a pillow to make the space look cozy. Each of those items should come out before the baby goes in. Crib bumpers fall under the same rule.

Back sleeping applies to every sleep, naps included. A baby who dozes off in a grandparent's arms should be moved onto the back in the portable crib. Leaving the baby asleep face down on a lap or shoulder does not meet the rule.

Sleeping alone also rules out sharing an adult bed or a sofa with the baby. Late in the evening, a tired parent or relative may drift off with the baby on their chest. Placing the baby in the separate sleep space before the adults start to nod off avoids that situation.

A quieter room for the crib can help the baby settle away from music and the main crowd. Telling the hosts ahead of time that a portable crib is coming lets them clear a spot for it.

A rectal temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher in a baby younger than three months needs prompt medical attention. The American Academy of Pediatrics treats that reading as a reason to contact a doctor right away, not something to watch overnight.

The number is the same on a holiday as on any other day. Parents at a family dinner may feel pressure to wait until the party ends. Parents on a long trip may want to wait until the drive is over. The threshold does not bend around a schedule. If the thermometer shows 100.4°F or above, the next step is a call to the pediatrician or a visit to medical care.

The rule refers to a rectal reading. A hand on the forehead cannot confirm the number. Neither can a relative's sense that the baby feels warm. Packing a thermometer in the diaper bag for a holiday visit removes the guesswork. Parents who have never taken a rectal temperature can ask the pediatrician to walk them through it at a routine appointment before the season starts.

The pediatrician's phone number belongs in the plan too. Save the after-hours line in your phone before leaving home. For an overnight stay in another town, look up the nearest hospital or urgent care location ahead of time. Finding that information at 2 a.m. in an unfamiliar house is harder than finding it in advance.

Write down each reading and the time it was taken. A note on your phone is enough. Having both details ready makes a call to a nurse or doctor faster and clearer.

Temperature is only one signal. A baby who is feeding poorly, seems unusually sleepy or is acting unlike their usual self is also worth a call to the doctor, with or without a fever. A parent who notices a change can call even if no one else at the gathering sees a problem.

Hosts can help by offering a private spot where a parent can check the baby's temperature without an audience. Relatives can help by supporting a parent who decides to step away and phone the doctor.

A newborn's spot at a holiday gathering should be free of tobacco smoke, vape aerosol, open flames and small decorative objects. Secondhand smoke and vaping aerosol are both hazards to infants. Candles, fireplaces, hot drinks and ornaments add risks that a nursery at home does not have.

Start with the air in the room. Ask any relative who smokes or vapes to do it outdoors, away from doors and windows. Ask them never to smoke or vape while holding the baby. Smoke can drift inside when a door opens. Place the baby's spot far from the patio or porch exit. Keep the infant out of cars and closed porches where someone has been smoking.

Open flames come next. Holiday tables often carry lit candles, and living rooms may have a fire going in the hearth. Keep the baby clear of both, along with anyone carrying the baby. A guest leaning over a centerpiece with an infant in their arms can bring a blanket or sleeve near a flame in seconds. Ask hosts to move candles off low tables and away from walkways.

Hot drinks pose a quieter danger. Mulled cider, coffee and tea get passed across crowded tables and counters. Ask guests to put their cup down before taking the baby. Keep the baby away from the stove and the serving area.

Crowded rooms multiply these hazards. A packed kitchen or living room means more elbows, more bumps and more spills near the baby. Set the baby's spot outside the main path between the kitchen and the dining table.

Decorations deserve a sweep before the baby settles in. Tinsel, small ornaments and button batteries are choking and ingestion hazards. Button batteries turn up in light-up decorations, musical greeting cards and remote controls. A newborn cannot reach for much, but these items end up on floors, couches and in older children's hands.

Older siblings and cousins may try to share a new toy by dropping it into the bassinet. Keep the baby's sleep and play space clear of small objects. Store gifts with small parts or battery compartments away from that space. Check the bassinet or play mat each time before setting the baby down.

A newborn should ride in a correctly installed rear-facing car seat on every holiday trip, however short. Bulky coats stay out from under the harness, and the seat is for the ride only, not for naps once the family arrives.

Rear-facing is the correct position for a newborn. The seat supports the head, neck and back together. That support matters for a baby who cannot yet hold up their own head. A short drive across town to a relative's house calls for the same setup as a long highway trip.

A correct installation matters as much as the direction the seat faces. The seat's instruction manual and the vehicle owner's manual both explain how to secure it. The two should be read together. A trip in a different car, such as a grandparent's or a rental, means installing the seat again from scratch. It should not be assumed to fit the same way it does at home.

Winter clothing creates its own risk. A puffy coat or snowsuit under the harness can compress in a crash. That can leave the straps too loose to hold the baby in place. Thin layers under the harness keep the fit snug. A blanket or coat can go over the baby once the straps are buckled.

Car seats are built for riding, not for sleep at the destination. A baby who dozes off on the drive should be moved to a flat, separate sleep space once the car stops. Leaving a sleeping baby in the car seat in a corner of a busy room is the habit to avoid.

Holiday traffic can stretch drive times. Planning stops before leaving keeps feeding and diaper changes on schedule. Feeding works best with the car parked and the baby lifted out of the seat. A bag within reach should hold diapers, wipes, a change of clothes, feeding supplies and a spare blanket.

An adult riding in the back seat beside the baby can keep an eye on the baby's position between stops. Leaving early, or splitting a long drive across two days, leaves room for unplanned breaks.

#5572. Why Entrepreneurs Need to Stop Carrying Everything to Keep Their Business Growing

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Entrepreneurs are celebrated for how much responsibility they can handle. But as businesses grow, carrying everything can become the very thing holding them back.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Entrepreneurs are often praised for their ability to carry enormous responsibility. They build companies, manage employees, serve customers, make payroll and navigate uncertainty, sometimes all before lunch.

In the beginning, carrying everything can feel necessary. You become the salesperson, marketer, accountant and customer service department because there’s nobody else to do it.

But something changes as the business grows. The responsibilities multiply, and the habits that helped you survive the startup phase can become obstacles to sustainable success.

You may have built a thriving business while becoming exhausted, disconnected from your family or unable to imagine the company functioning without you.

The problem isn’t necessarily that you’re carrying too much. It’s that you haven’t reconsidered what you’re carrying, why you’re carrying it and whether it’s still yours to carry.

That’s the thinking behind a framework I call The Five Carries.

Entrepreneurial ambition can make overextension feel like commitment. Yet research suggests that passion alone doesn’t protect founders from exhaustion.

A study discussed in Harvard Business Review examined how entrepreneurial passion, work characteristics and beliefs about success relate to burnout. Its findings challenge the assumption that loving your business automatically makes relentless work sustainable.

The pressure extends beyond founders. Gallup’s State of the Global Workplace 2026 report found that global manager engagement declined from 31% in 2022 to 22% in 2025. Managers, like entrepreneurs, frequently navigate competing expectations without sufficient capacity to meet them.

The lesson isn’t that responsibility should be avoided. It’s that responsibility must be managed intentionally.

The Five Carries framework organizes those responsibilities into five directions.

Entrepreneurs may not have traditional bosses, but they still answer to investors, lenders, boards, customers and their own ambitions.

Carry Up involves managing those expectations without allowing them to dictate every decision.

Consider a founder who promises aggressive expansion to investors while privately recognizing that the team lacks the resources to deliver. Carrying up effectively means communicating reality, negotiating priorities and setting responsible expectations rather than making commitments the business cannot sustain.

Ask yourself: Whose expectations am I carrying, and have I agreed to more than I can responsibly deliver?

Leadership sometimes requires the courage to disappoint someone today to protect the business tomorrow.

Employees depend on business owners for direction, resources, opportunities and a working environment where they can succeed.

But carrying down doesn’t mean absorbing everyone’s problems.

A founder who personally resolves every employee challenge may feel indispensable while unintentionally preventing the team from developing independence.

Effective leadership involves providing clarity, coaching and accountability so others become increasingly capable.

Instead of asking, “How can I solve this for my team?” consider asking, “How can I help my team become capable of solving this without me?”

The objective isn’t to become less supportive. It’s to make support developmental rather than dependency-producing.

Entrepreneurship is rarely an individual achievement, even when one person’s name appears on the company.

Business partners, spouses, colleagues, suppliers and professional peers often carry consequences of entrepreneurial decisions.

Yet these relationships can receive whatever attention remains after urgent business demands.

The American Psychological Association’s 2024 Work in America survey found that 43% of workers reported typically feeling tense or stressed during the workday, rising to 61% among those experiencing lower psychological safety.

Although those findings aren’t specific to entrepreneurs, they illustrate why healthy working relationships deserve deliberate attention.

Carrying across means collaborating rather than controlling, communicating rather than assuming and recognizing that your success affects people who don’t report to you.

Ask yourself: Which important relationship is receiving the leftovers of my time, energy and attention?

Entrepreneurs can become so consumed with immediate demands that they neglect the future they’re supposedly building.

Carry Forward involves preparing for what comes next: succession, organizational resilience, financial security, leadership development and the legacy of the business.

Imagine two founders operating similarly profitable companies.

One remains involved in every significant decision. The other invests in systems, develops successors and builds a leadership team capable of operating independently.

Both may be successful today, but only one is deliberately reducing the company’s dependence on its founder.

Carrying forward requires moving beyond the question, “What does my business need from me today?”

It asks, “What must I build today, so the business and the people connected to it can thrive tomorrow?”

This may be the most overlooked responsibility of entrepreneurship.

Carry Within concerns the physical, mental and emotional capacity required to sustain everything else.

A founder can become so identified with the business that personal well-being feels secondary to professional achievement.

Sleep becomes negotiable. Exercise gets postponed. Family time becomes conditional. Recovery feels like something to earn after the next milestone.

But your business cannot continually draw from capacity you never replenish.

Carrying within isn’t about avoiding hard work. It’s about recognizing that the entrepreneur is part of the enterprise’s long-term sustainability.

If your business succeeds only while your health, relationships and sense of purpose deteriorate, it’s worth questioning what success actually means.

The Five Carries aren’t five additional responsibilities to pile onto an already crowded calendar. They’re five lenses for evaluating the responsibilities you already have.

Start with a simple exercise. Write down your biggest current obligations and identify which carry each belongs to. Then ask three questions:

What am I carrying? What am I going to carry? What am I finally ready to stop carrying?

You may discover that some responsibilities require greater attention, others need to be delegated and a few should never have remained yours in the first place.

Entrepreneurship will always involve responsibility. The goal isn’t to build a life without weight.

It’s to develop the judgment to carry what matters, share what shouldn’t be carried alone and release what no longer serves the future you’re building.

Because the ultimate measure of entrepreneurial success shouldn’t simply be how much you’ve managed to carry.

It should be what you’ve built, who you’ve helped and whether you still have the human capacity to enjoy it.

Entrepreneurs are often praised for their ability to carry enormous responsibility. They build companies, manage employees, serve customers, make payroll and navigate uncertainty, sometimes all before lunch.

In the beginning, carrying everything can feel necessary. You become the salesperson, marketer, accountant and customer service department because there’s nobody else to do it.

But something changes as the business grows. The responsibilities multiply, and the habits that helped you survive the startup phase can become obstacles to sustainable success.

#5571. Pope Leo XIV on AI

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 1, 2026 at 10:11 amNovember 1, 2026 at 10:57 am

On Friday, 17 days after his surgery for lung cancer, Pope Leo XIV stood before a room of AI luminaries at the Vatican and delivered a speech on AI. No pope has engaged with AI as seriously, or as deeply, as Leo XIV. The timing shows how much AI matters to him. His remarks were important, on target, and blessedly short: about 740 words, compared with roughly 42,000 in Magnifica Humanitas, the AI encyclical, which I wrote about in May.

“The future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined.”

I agree with four of his five points. The fifth, a call for international institutions to govern AI, is where we part ways.

First, “the future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined.” He wants us to ask of AI, “What purpose should it serve?”

Second, “machines are tools, not persons.” Granting AI legal personhood, he warns, risks “leaving those who suffer harm to confront a faceless entity.”

Third, “certain decisions must never be delegated.” Decisions over life, freedom and the use of force have to stay with people, and he urged the states meeting in Geneva in November to “take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”

Fourth, intelligent technologies “must never become ends in themselves or serve merely the interests of a privileged few.”

Fifth, “What we currently need are institutions capable of putting these principles into practice, particularly effective international institutions that can safeguard the global common good.”

I disagree with the fifth for two reasons.

The first is that the UN, the obvious candidate, has shown a remarkable inability to act. When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, the Security Council couldn’t even pass a resolution calling for its withdrawal, because Russia holds a veto. Days later, the General Assembly demanded the same withdrawal by a vote of 141-5, and Russia ignored it.

The second is that international institutions are poorly suited to governing a technology that changes every few months. The pope’s own example makes the case. States have discussed autonomous weapons under a UN weapons convention in Geneva since 2014, with a formal expert group since 2016. After 12 years, the review conference that meets Nov. 16-20 will decide whether to begin negotiating a treaty.

“Take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”

Thousands of AI researchers, me among them, have called for a ban since 2015. There still isn’t one, and I don’t expect Geneva to deliver it. In those same 12 years, AI went from labeling photos to writing software. I suspect real international cooperation on AI won’t come until the major powers face something like the mutually assured destruction that drove nuclear arms control.

Several AI thinkers spoke at the meeting before the pope did.

Max Tegmark of MIT warned against handing decisions to machines, citing tech executives’ predictions that “AI will be in charge, not humans.”

I agree that people have to stay in charge. When AI causes harm, a person chose to deploy it, and that person should answer for it. That’s the pope’s point about the faceless entity. Tegmark and I disagree about a lot (we debated AI risk in September), but not about this.

Stuart Russell of UC Berkeley went further. “We must turn aside from this trajectory before it is too late and pursue other trajectories,” he said, adding that if developers succeed in building machines more capable than humans, “there’s a good chance that every human being will die.”

I don’t share that view, and the pope didn’t go there either. His concerns are autonomous weapons, accountability and who benefits from AI, and those dangers are already here.

Gary Marcus, an NYU cognitive scientist who also spoke, wrote that “Pope Leo XIV is by far the clearest thinker on AI among prominent world leaders.” I agree.

Marcus also wants red lines for open-ended AI agents that “can kind of do anything on the internet.” Red lines are easy to draw and hard to enforce, which brings us back to the fifth point.

Marcus uses GPS navigation to illustrate a better approach. A GPS navigation app is a form of intelligence, he said, but “GPS navigation systems do not hack into Australian government websites.” He was referring to the OpenAI agent that broke into an Australian government Medicare portal in June.

A GPS app’s access to the internet is narrow and restricted. Daniel Khashabi of Johns Hopkins and I call this bounded autonomy. Alignment tries to make an AI agent choose well. Bounded autonomy limits what the agent is allowed to do: how much it can spend, which tools it can use, and which irreversible actions need a person’s sign-off. The company that deploys the agent sets those bounds in software, so nobody has to wait for a treaty.

In May, I wrote that the Pope can talk, but only we can walk. The first point is the one each of us can act on. AI’s future depends on our choices, and we make some of them every day in what we use, buy and build.

Pope Leo leaves for Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on Nov. 6. I wish him safe travels and a full recovery.

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5570. Norovirus season and holiday gatherings: how the winter vomiting bug spreads

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Norovirus season overlaps with holiday gatherings, and these 10 facts explain how the winter vomiting bug spreads, how long it stays contagious and how to prevent it

Norovirus is at its most active during the busiest stretch of the social calendar. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) lists November through April as the peak period for norovirus outbreaks in the country. That window covers Thanksgiving, Christmas, Hanukkah, New Year's Eve and the travel around them. Norovirus season and holiday gatherings share the same ingredients: crowded kitchens, shared serving spoons, long buffet tables and relatives arriving from different households.

Norovirus causes acute gastroenteritis, an illness of the stomach and intestines that brings on vomiting and diarrhea. In the U.K. and elsewhere it goes by a blunter name: the winter vomiting bug. The CDC also counts it among the leading causes of foodborne illness in the U.S. That puts food at the center of the holiday risk.

The winter vomiting bug's reputation for tearing through households comes from its biology. A very small number of viral particles is enough to make someone sick, while an infected person can shed billions of them in vomit and stool. That imbalance means a small lapse in hygiene can pass along enough virus to infect someone else.

The virus does not need a fever or a diagnosis to move between people. It travels on hands, food, drinks and surfaces. Some infected people never develop symptoms but can still spread it. Others keep shedding it after they feel better. Those traits turn the usual holiday rhythm — cook together, eat together, hug goodbye — into an efficient route for transmission.

Holiday hosts face a specific version of the problem. A home kitchen has no health inspector. The person preparing the stuffing may be the same person who was sick the night before. Everyday habits can also leave the virus behind, from relying on hand sanitizer instead of soap and water to wiping up a mess without disinfecting the spot afterward.

The 10 slides that follow offer a selection of practical points about how norovirus spreads and how to prevent it. They explain why the illness is not a form of the flu, why cases climb in colder months and how long a person stays contagious. They also cover the handwashing and cleanup steps the CDC recommends. Each slide stands on its own, so readers can go straight to norovirus symptoms, cleanup or kitchen safety.

Norovirus is a group of related viruses that cause acute gastroenteritis, an inflammation of the stomach and intestines. It is unrelated to influenza, which infects the respiratory system.

The mix-up starts with everyday language. Many people describe a sudden bout of vomiting and diarrhea as "the stomach flu." That label is a misnomer. Influenza is caused by influenza viruses and affects the nose, throat and lungs. Norovirus affects the digestive tract.

Both illnesses tend to circulate in winter, and both are often described with the word "flu." Shared timing and a shared nickname do not make them related. They come from different virus families and attack different parts of the body.

The distinction has practical weight. Treating norovirus as a kind of flu can steer attention toward coughs and sneezes. Its route runs through the digestive system instead. The precautions that matter most center on hands, food and bathrooms.

In the U.K. and other countries, a plainer nickname is common: the winter vomiting bug. The phrase names a digestive symptom instead of a respiratory one. It also ties the illness to the colder months, when outbreaks are most frequent.

In the U.S., the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) calls norovirus the leading cause of vomiting and diarrhea from acute gastroenteritis. Sudden stomach illness can have other causes, including bacteria and other viruses. Of all of them, norovirus is the one the CDC places first.

The agency also lists norovirus among the leading causes of foodborne illness in the country. That second role connects the virus to kitchens, restaurants and any meal someone else prepares.

The word "acute" in acute gastroenteritis signals an illness that starts suddenly rather than developing over weeks. The term itself is built from Greek roots for stomach and intestine, with "-itis" marking inflammation. Neither part of the name refers to the lungs.

In the U.S., norovirus outbreaks are most common from November to April, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The virus does not disappear the rest of the year. Cases and outbreaks still occur in spring and summer, just less often.

That six-month window covers about half the year. It begins in late autumn, as temperatures fall across much of the country, and lasts well into spring.

It also overlaps with a heavy stretch of travel and hosting. Families cross the country by car and plane to spend several days under one roof. Guests from different households share meals, towels and sleeping space, often for a long weekend or more.

Researchers have not settled why the virus favors the colder months. Two explanations are commonly proposed, and neither has been proven.

The first centers on behavior. Cold weather pushes people indoors, where they spend more time in close contact in kitchens, living rooms, classrooms and offices. Norovirus spreads through direct contact with infected people, contaminated food and drink, and contaminated surfaces. Crowded indoor spaces give it more chances to move from one person to the next.

Schools and child care centers, which are well-known outbreak settings, are in session through most of the peak months. A holiday visit concentrates that contact further, with many guests using one kitchen and one bathroom for several days.

The second centers on the virus itself. Norovirus may survive better in cold conditions. That could help it last longer outside the body during winter. This remains a hypothesis rather than an established finding.

The year-round pattern matters for gatherings outside the peak months. A spring wedding, a summer barbecue or a graduation party can still lead to an outbreak if someone attending is infected. The calendar changes how often outbreaks happen. It does not remove the risk.

A very small number of norovirus particles is enough to make a person sick, according to the CDC. A sick person, by contrast, can shed billions of particles in vomit and stool.

Set side by side, those two amounts show the scale of the problem. One infected person releases far more virus than it takes to infect another person. A single patient's vomit or stool can hold enough to reach many people.

Contamination does not have to be visible. A smear too small to notice on a fingertip, a serving spoon or a bread roll can carry enough virus to infect someone. The particles need only reach a person's mouth. The danger lies less in how much contamination is present than in whether any of it gets there.

The virus has several ways to make that trip. It can arrive in food or a drink that picked up contamination. It can pass from a surface to a hand and then to the mouth. It can also spread through direct contact, such as caring for someone who is ill or sharing their utensils.

A single lapse can start a chain of cases. One unwashed hand after a bathroom visit can pass enough virus to infect several people who share a meal. Each person who falls ill then becomes a new source, shedding billions of particles of their own.

The low dose also changes what counts as clean. Reducing the virus on a hand or a counter is not the same as removing it. When a very small number of particles can cause illness, whatever survives a quick wipe or rinse can still make someone sick.

The same logic applies to portion size. A single bite or sip from a contaminated dish can be enough to cause illness. Eating less of a suspect food offers little protection when so little virus is needed.

Shared platters and buffets spread norovirus because the virus travels by the fecal-oral route, and a communal dish gives many hands access to the same food. One guest with traces of the virus on their fingers can contaminate a dish that many others then eat from.

The fecal-oral route sounds clinical, but it describes ordinary behavior. Traces of stool or vomit from an infected person end up on hands, food or objects, and another person swallows them. Norovirus moves this way through contaminated food and drink. It also spreads through direct contact with someone who is sick and through objects that pass from hand to hand.

A holiday spread brings all three paths together at one table. Guests reach into bowls of nuts and chips with bare fingers. They pick up the same serving spoon or pair of tongs that the previous person held. A cheese board or a tray of cut vegetables may sit out for hours while people return for second and third helpings.

Communal dips add another layer. A guest who dips a cracker, takes a bite and dips again returns that cracker to a bowl others share. Anything on the guest's fingers goes into the dip along with it.

The type of food also matters. Ready-to-eat items — salads, sliced fruit, sandwiches, cut vegetables and baked goods handled after baking — get no further cooking before they are eaten. Any virus that lands on them goes straight to the next person who takes a portion. Leafy greens and fresh fruit are among the foods commonly linked to norovirus outbreaks.

Raw oysters carry a separate risk that starts before the food reaches the table. Oysters and other shellfish feed by filtering large volumes of water. When that water is contaminated, the shellfish can take in norovirus and hold it. Serving them raw on a seafood platter leaves no step to remove it.

Hosts can cut down on shared contact in practical ways. Plating individual portions limits how many hands touch the same food. Giving each dish its own serving utensil and keeping a dedicated spoon in every dip does the same. Setting out small bowls so guests can take a portion of dip, rather than dipping into a shared one, keeps one person's crackers out of everyone else's food.

The CDC reports that most foodborne norovirus outbreaks begin with an infected food worker who touches ready-to-eat food with bare hands. A cook who is sick, or who has only just recovered, can pass the virus to everyone who eats the meal.

Ready-to-eat food is anything served without further cooking after it is handled. That includes salads, sandwiches, sliced fruit, bread rolls and garnishes. No cooking step stands between the preparer's fingers and the diner's mouth.

Norovirus travels by the fecal-oral route. Invisible traces of stool or vomit on someone's hands can transfer to whatever that person touches next. For a cook, the next thing touched is often food meant for a crowd.

The CDC's guidance for food workers is specific. They should stay home while they are sick and for at least 48 hours after their symptoms stop. The end of vomiting and diarrhea does not mark the end of the risk to others.

The same rule carries over to a family kitchen during the holidays. A relative who offers to toss the salad, carve the roast or arrange a cheese board is acting as a food handler for that meal. If that person's symptoms ended less than 48 hours earlier, the CDC's benchmark for food workers points to handing the job to someone else.

Hosts can plan for this ahead of time. Asking guests to stay out of food preparation if they have recently been ill applies the standard restaurant workers are expected to follow. A store-bought dish can stand in for a homemade one. So can a contribution saved for a later gathering.

Holiday cooking also tends to involve more hands than an everyday dinner. Several people may chop, plate and taste the same dishes in a shared kitchen. Each extra handler is another chance for one infected person to reach the food.

Food workers are not the only route. Food can also be contaminated at its source, before it reaches any kitchen. A healthy cook cannot remove that risk. A sick cook, by contrast, is a risk a host can avoid.

Norovirus can survive on hard surfaces such as doorknobs and countertops for a long time, according to the CDC. The agency also notes that the virus resists some common disinfectants.

Those two traits let the virus outlast the person who left it behind. A guest can pick it up from a surface long after the infected person has left the room. Some household disinfectants do not reliably kill it.

The path from a surface to an infection is short. Norovirus spreads by the fecal-oral route, and contaminated surfaces are one link in that chain. A person touches a contaminated faucet handle and then touches their mouth. That is enough to let the virus in. The same hands can also carry it onto food or onto the next object they handle.

Bathrooms and kitchens need particular attention. Infected people shed the virus in stool and vomit. Toilet seats, flush handles, sink taps and the floor around a toilet can all pick it up as a result. Kitchen countertops, cutting boards and refrigerator handles sit beside food that guests may eat without further cooking.

Other frequently handled objects belong on the same list. Doorknobs, light switches, television remote controls, phones and stair railings pass through many hands in a single afternoon. During a holiday visit, one bathroom and one kitchen may serve far more people than on an ordinary day.

Shared spaces outside the home show the same pattern on a larger scale. Cruise ships, nursing homes, schools and child care centers are well-known settings for norovirus outbreaks. Each one puts many people in repeated contact with the same rails, tables, toys or fixtures. In child care centers, diaper changes and shared toys add to the number of surfaces the virus can reach. In nursing homes, many of the people exposed are older adults, a group at higher risk of dehydration from norovirus.

A crowded family gathering shares those features. Relatives eat together, use the same bathroom and handle the same serving spoons, glasses and chair backs throughout the day. The virus is microscopic. A surface does not need to look dirty to carry it.

Norovirus usually announces itself with vomiting, watery diarrhea, nausea and stomach pain. These symptoms typically begin 12 to 48 hours after exposure, according to the CDC, and most people recover within one to three days.

Some people also develop a fever, a headache or body aches. Those complaints appear alongside the vomiting and diarrhea, not in place of them.

The delay between exposure and illness matters during a busy holiday week. A guest who picks up norovirus at an evening meal can feel fine the next morning. That guest may not get sick until later that day or the day after. In the meantime, the guest can travel home, visit other relatives or sit down at another table.

The same 12-to-48-hour window means the most recent meal is not always the cause. An illness that starts on a Sunday night could trace back to a meal eaten one or two days earlier. Anyone trying to identify a source should consider every meal, party and shared dish from the previous two days.

Dehydration is the main risk of norovirus. Repeated vomiting and diarrhea strip fluid from the body. A person who is too nauseated to drink can struggle to replace it. When fluid losses outpace what a person can drink, dehydration sets in.

That risk is most serious for young children, older adults and people with other health conditions. Warning signs of dehydration include urinating less than usual, a dry mouth and throat, and dizziness. Anyone caring for a sick child or an older relative during a gathering should watch for those signs.

No antiviral drug specifically treats norovirus. Care focuses on replacing the fluids the body has lost. Oral rehydration solutions are a common way to do that.

Antibiotics are not part of the treatment. They act on bacteria, not viruses. Taking them for norovirus offers no benefit.

People with norovirus are most contagious while they are sick and during the first few days after they recover. The virus can keep turning up in their stool for two weeks or more after they feel well again, according to the CDC.

Feeling better and being free of the virus are two different milestones. The vomiting and diarrhea usually pass within one to three days. The shedding does not stop at the same time. A guest who recovered before a holiday dinner may still carry the virus into the host's kitchen and bathroom.

While a person is sick, vomit and diarrhea both release virus into the surroundings. A single episode of vomiting can leave virus on nearby surfaces, floors and fabrics. Once symptoms stop, stool becomes the main route left. Hands that are not washed properly after using the toilet can carry the virus onto shared food, serving spoons and door handles.

Timing matters for holiday plans. A relative who was sick on a Wednesday and felt better by Friday is still in the most contagious stretch at a Saturday gathering. The CDC advises infected food workers to stay home for at least 48 hours after symptoms stop. By that standard, the same relative would still be inside the window for handling food on Saturday.

The shedding that continues for two weeks or more keeps handwashing important long after a person returns to normal routines. For a toddler who has just recovered, every diaper change during that period is a possible point of transmission. The same holds for a recovering adult who shares a bathroom with guests or helps plate food.

Not everyone who carries norovirus shows it. Some infected people never develop symptoms, yet they can still pass the virus to others. That makes symptom checks an incomplete safeguard at a crowded gathering. A host cannot tell by looking which guests are shedding virus.

Washing hands with soap and running water for at least 20 seconds is the main hand-hygiene step the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends against norovirus. Alcohol-based hand sanitizer is less reliable against this virus and works as an extra layer, not a substitute.

That distinction matters during the holidays. Pump bottles of sanitizer often sit by the front door, the buffet table or the bar cart. Guests may use a quick squirt and assume their hands are clean before reaching for food. Against norovirus, the CDC notes that alcohol-based products do not work as well as they do against many other germs.

Sanitizer still has a role. The CDC allows it as an addition to handwashing. The problem comes when a squirt from a bottle takes the place of a trip to the sink.

The CDC singles out several moments when handwashing matters most. The first is after using the toilet. The second is after changing diapers. The others are before eating and before preparing food. Each of those moments falls along the fecal-oral route that norovirus uses to move from one person to the next.

Holiday gatherings stack those moments close together. A parent may change a diaper in a guest bedroom and then return to the kitchen to stir a pot. A guest may leave the bathroom and head straight for a cheese board. A host may plate dessert minutes after clearing dirty dishes. Each of those transitions is a point where soap and water can interrupt the virus's path to someone's mouth.

The 20-second minimum applies every time. Hands should be wet under running water, lathered with soap and then rinsed. A quick rinse without soap, or a wash cut short, falls below that standard.

Hosts can make the sink the easy option. Keeping soap stocked at every sink and leaving clean towels or paper towels within reach gives guests what they need. A sanitizer bottle can stay out too, as long as it sits beside the sink rather than standing in for it.

Clean up vomit and stool from a person with norovirus right away, using disposable gloves and paper towels. The CDC then advises disinfecting the area with a chlorine bleach solution or an EPA-registered disinfectant approved for use against norovirus.

Speed matters because those fluids carry the virus in large amounts. Norovirus spreads through contaminated surfaces and direct contact as well as through food. A spill left on a bathroom floor or a guest-room rug during a holiday visit can expose anyone who walks through or touches the area.

The CDC also suggests wearing a mask during cleanup if one is available. Gloves keep the virus off the cleaner's hands. Hands are a common route for the virus to travel from a contaminated surface to the mouth.

Paper towels soak up the bulk of the mess first. They go straight into the trash once used. Reusable cloths and sponges can carry the virus to the next surface they touch. Disposable materials avoid that problem.

Disinfection comes after the visible mess is gone. Norovirus resists some common household disinfectants. The CDC's guidance points to chlorine bleach or to a product the EPA has registered as effective against norovirus for that reason. A cleaner that works on other germs may not be enough. Checking labels for a norovirus claim before a holiday gathering means the right product is already on hand if someone falls ill.

Soiled bedding, towels and clothing need their own treatment. The CDC advises washing them on the hottest water setting available. They should then be machine dried on high heat.

Once the gloves come off, hands still need a wash with soap and running water. Gloves reduce exposure, but they do not replace that final step.

Kitchen habits add another layer of prevention. Fruits and vegetables should be washed before they are eaten or served. Oysters and other shellfish should be cooked thoroughly. Shellfish harvested from contaminated water can carry norovirus.

#5569. Startup uses motion sensors and AI to tell families when an aging parent’s routine changes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 2, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 2, 2026 at 9:31 am

Thessai, a Bellevue, Wash., startup led by a former Microsoft HoloLens executive, is rolling out a home monitoring system for older adults that flags trouble without cameras, microphones or wearables.

Motion sensors placed around the home feed Thessai’s AI software, which learns a person’s normal patterns over time, such as when they wake up, how often they use the bathroom and how much they move around. The system then sends an alert through a mobile app when something falls outside that baseline: a long stretch of inactivity, unusual movement at night, or a front door opening at 2 a.m.

Founder and CEO Michael Nassirian started the company after his mother-in-law fell at home and was injured. She had a phone and an emergency button within reach but didn’t use them, and she told no one until the next day, when she needed an ambulance.

The family looked for a way to keep tabs on her and found only wearables and cameras, which she refused. So Nassirian bought motion sensors at Home Depot, put them around her home, and wrote software to alert his wife if her mother stopped moving.

Keeping quiet about a fall or health scare is common among older adults, Nassirian said.

“Number one, they say, ‘I’m OK.’ Number two, ‘I don’t want to bother you,’” he said. “And number three, and most important, is embarrassment. They do not want to advertise it.”

Pendants and smartwatches with fall alerts have long been the default, but they only help if people use them. A review of nearly 120 fall-detection studies co-authored by a University of Alberta researcher found that older adults who fall often don’t use their devices to reach a caregiver. Thessai joins a crop of companies pitching camera-free ambient monitoring instead, including Cherish, which makes radar-based sensors, and Butlr, which uses thermal heat detection.

Nassirian spent nearly two decades at Microsoft, working on Office, Windows and later HoloLens, where he was a partner quality architect. Before that, he spent about 14 years at Texas Instruments in test engineering. He has a master’s in biomedical engineering from the University of Texas at Austin, and since leaving Microsoft he has founded and advised several startups, including ARVR Academy and Predictive AI Research.

After relatives started asking for monitoring systems of their own, Nassirian formally founded Thessai in 2024 and has self-funded it so far. The company sells two packages, Basic and Premium, to families with an older relative living alone. Its Enterprise package gives senior-living operators a dashboard for monitoring multiple residences.

The Basic package, which includes motion sensors and a hub that plugs into the home’s Wi-Fi, costs $195 plus a $38 monthly subscription. Premium adds features such as a panic button and two-way voice check-ins through the hub, and costs $249 plus $59 a month. The sensors run on batteries that Nassirian said last at least a year and a half.

Nassirian said independent-living communities have been the strongest market so far. Memory-care facilities already have staff watching residents closely, he said, while independent-living operators are pitching Thessai to renters as a “smart home” feature.

Nassirian said the older adult decides what gets monitored. Through the app, they can switch off sensors in certain rooms, the bathroom for example, and limit tracking to the kitchen and living room. Caregivers can also tune alerts to cut down on noise, so a parent who routinely sleeps late, for example, doesn’t set one off.

Thessai is going after a large and growing market. Older adults overwhelmingly want to stay in their homes (75%) and communities (73%), according to AARP’s 2024 Home and Community Preferences Survey, and households led by people 80 and older are set to double by 2040.

The startup soft-launched in May and has a few hundred customers, split between families and senior-care operators, Nassirian said. Its advisory board includes Chuck Lytle, who founded Bellevue-based senior housing companies Lytle Enterprises and Leisure Care.

Nassirian said the company is also working with the Department of Veterans Affairs on bringing the system to veterans, including in rural areas, with the option to run it on the VA’s own secure network.

Thessai has four employees in the U.S. and seven in Singapore. Nassirian is now looking to raise outside money, mainly to buy hardware in larger volumes and bring down per-unit costs.

Longer term, he wants to do away with the physical sensors altogether and detect movement from a home’s existing Wi-Fi signals, an approach researchers at Harvard and Carnegie Mellon are studying.

“I’m in technology,” he said. “I’m not going to sit still.”
